changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: An experiment is a measurable sample space (X,A) together with a set Θ of parameter labels and a family (P_θ)_{θ∈Θ} of probability measures on (X,A). The family consists of sampling laws; it does not assert that Θ is measurable, that θ↦P_θ is measurable, or that all laws are realized on one specified probability space. If data are realized as a random element, its law is the pushforward law in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]].
changes.after:
An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: For an experiment on (X,A), write P(X,A) for its set of probability measures. A parametric statistical model is the parameter map P:Θ→P(X,A), θ↦P_θ, regarded together with its parameter set Θ and sample space. The map need not be injective. Unless a measurable structure on Θ is supplied separately, no measurability of this map is asserted.
changes.after:
For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: If (Θ,T) is a measurable parameter space, a Markov (probability) kernel representation of an experiment on (X,A) is a function K:Θ×A→[0,1] such that K(θ,·) is a probability measure on (X,A) for every θ and, for every A∈A and every Borel set C⊆[0,1] (the sigma-algebra generated by relatively open subsets U∩[0,1] with U open in R), {θ∈Θ:K(θ,A)∈C}∈T. It represents the given model exactly when K(θ,A)=P_θ(A) for every θ and A. This is an additional parameter-measurability condition, not part of an arbitrary experiment.
changes.after:
Suppose an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ also has a measurable
parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measurable-space]]). A
**Markov kernel** (or **probability kernel**) representation is a function
$$
K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]
$$
such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, the set function
$A\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
and, for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and every Borel set $C\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$
\{\theta\in\Theta:K(\theta,A)\in C\}\in\mathcal T.
$$
Here the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,1]$ is generated by its relatively open
subsets $U\cap[0,1]$, where $U$ is open in $\mathbb R$. Thus the second
condition says that each event-probability map $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is
measurable. The kernel represents the given experiment exactly when
$K(\theta,A)=P_\theta(A)$ for every $\theta$ and $A$
([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-probability-measure]]).

This is an optional parameter-measurable version of a model. An arbitrary
experiment does not include a measurable structure on $\Theta$ or imply this
kernel condition.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: In a parametric model P:Θ→P(X,A), parameters θ and η are observationally equivalent, written θ∼η, exactly when P_θ=P_η as measures; equivalently, P_θ(A)=P_η(A) for every A∈A. Thus equivalent parameter values give the same sampling law, even when θ≠η.
changes.after:
In a parametric model $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
two parameter values $\theta,\eta\in\Theta$ are **observationally
equivalent**, written $\theta\sim\eta$, if and only if
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta,
$$
that is, $P_\theta(A)=P_\eta(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). Equivalent parameter values therefore
give exactly the same sampling law. No distinctness of $\theta$ and $\eta$ is
required.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: For a parametric model with parameter set Θ, an estimand (parameter target) is a specified function ψ:Θ→T₀ into a target set T₀. No measurable structure on Θ or T₀ is assumed by this definition.
changes.after:
For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: An estimand ψ:Θ→T₀ is identifiable in the model P if ψ(θ)=ψ(η) whenever θ∼η (equivalently, whenever P_θ=P_η). The model itself is identifiable when its identity estimand id_Θ is identifiable, which is equivalent to injectivity of θ↦P_θ.
changes.after:
An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Let P:Θ→P(X,A) be a parametric model, ψ:Θ→T₀ an estimand, and M=P(Θ) the set of model laws. The following are equivalent: (i) ψ is identifiable; (ii) ψ is constant on every observational equivalence class [θ]={η∈Θ:η∼θ}; (iii) there is a unique function ψ̄:M→T₀ such that ψ=ψ̄∘P. No measurable structure or measurable factorization is asserted.
changes.after:
Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ be an estimand, and set
$\mathcal M:=\mathsf P(\Theta)$, the set of laws in the model. For
$\theta\in\Theta$, write
$$
[\theta]_\sim:=\{\eta\in\Theta:\eta\sim\theta\}.
$$
Then the following are equivalent: **(i)** $\psi$ is identifiable; **(ii)**
$\psi$ is constant on every observational equivalence class $[\theta]_\sim$;
and **(iii)** there is a unique function $\bar\psi:\mathcal M\to\mathcal T_0$
such that $\psi=\bar\psi\circ\mathsf P$.

The factorization is a statement about sets and functions. It asserts no
measurable structure or measurable factor map.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: On X={0,1} with all subsets measurable and parameter set Θ=[0,1], define P_p({1})=p and P_p({0})=1−p. This is an identifiable statistical model, and the target ψ(p)=p is identifiable.
changes.after:
Let $\mathcal X=\{0,1\}$ with $\mathcal A=2^{\mathcal X}$, let
$\Theta=[0,1]$, and, for $p\in\Theta$, define
$$
P_p(A):=p\,\mathbf 1_{\{1\in A\}}+(1-p)\,\mathbf 1_{\{0\in A\}}\qquad(A\in\mathcal A),
$$
where each indicator is $1$ when its stated membership holds and $0$
otherwise. This is the Bernoulli model with success probability $p$. Its
parameter is identifiable, and the target $\psi(p)=p$ is identifiable.

changes.heading: Statement refuted
changes.before: Let Θ={(u,v)∈[0,1]^2:u+v≤1}, X={0,1}, and P_{u,v}({1})=u+v, P_{u,v}({0})=1−u−v. The first-coordinate target ψ(u,v)=u is not identifiable.
changes.after:
For every parametric statistical model with parameter $(u,v)\in\Theta\subseteq
[0,1]^2$, the first-coordinate target $\psi(u,v)=u$ is identifiable.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: For a statistical experiment with data measurable space (X,A) and an action measurable space (D,G), a randomized procedure is a probability kernel K from (X,A) to (D,G): for every x, K(x,.) is a probability measure on (D,G), and for every B in G, x maps to K(x,B) is A-measurable. K(x,B) is the probability of an action in B after observing x; K does not depend on the unknown parameter.
changes.after:
Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable **action space**: a set of available
actions equipped with a sigma-algebra of action events, hence a measurable
space ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **randomized procedure** (or
randomized decision rule) is a probability kernel $K$ from
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$, in the pointwise sense
of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Thus $K(x,\cdot)$ is a
probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$,
and $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable for every $B\in\mathcal G$.
After observing $x$, the procedure assigns probability $K(x,B)$ to taking an
action in $B$. The kernel is specified without reference to the unknown
parameter. This definition imposes no measurable structure on $\Theta$. The
kernel is the specification of the procedure; no representation by a separate
random seed is asserted for arbitrary measurable action spaces.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Let K be a randomized procedure for an experiment ((X,A),Theta,(P_theta)) with action space (D,G). Give [0,infinity] its Borel sigma-algebra. For every nonnegative G/B([0,infinity])-measurable g:D->[0,infinity], x maps to integral g(a) K(x,da) is A-measurable. For each theta, Q_theta(B)=integral K(x,B) P_theta(dx) is a probability measure on (D,G), and integral g dQ_theta equals integral [integral g(a)K(x,da)] P_theta(dx), with extended nonnegative values allowed.
changes.after:
Let $K$ be a randomized procedure for the experiment
$\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
with action space $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$. Give $[0,+\infty]$ its Borel
sigma-algebra. For every nonnegative $\mathcal G/\mathcal B([0,+\infty])$-
measurable function $g:\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$, the function
$$h_g(x)=\int_{\mathsf D}g(a)\,K(x,da)$$
is $\mathcal A$-measurable. In particular, $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is measurable
for every action event $B\in\mathcal G$. For each $\theta\in\Theta$, the
set function
$$Q_\theta(B)=\int_{\mathcal X}K(x,B)\,P_\theta(dx),\qquad B\in\mathcal G,$$
is a probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$, and for every such $g$,
$$\int_{\mathsf D}g\,dQ_\theta=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}g(a)\,K(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
with nonnegative extended values allowed.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: In a statistical experiment with data measurable space (X,A), a statistic with target measurable space (Y,B) is an A/B-measurable map T:X→Y. For an estimand psi:Theta→Y whose target set Y is equipped with B, an estimator of psi is a statistic with that same target space; its value at x is an estimate. The parameter map psi need not be measurable, since the experiment imposes no measurable structure on Theta.
changes.after:
Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: A randomized test is a randomized procedure with binary action space ({0,1},2^{ {0,1} }), where 1 means reject and 0 means do not reject. Its test function is phi(x)=K(x,{1}), a measurable map X→[0,1]; phi(x) is the probability of rejection conditional on observed data x, and 1-phi(x) is the probability of no rejection.
changes.after:
A **randomized test** is a randomized procedure with binary action space
whose action set is $\{0,1\}$, equipped with its full sigma-algebra
$2^{\{0,1\}}$ (the power set, which is a sigma-algebra by
[[def-sigma-algebra]]), where $1$ means reject and $0$ means do not reject
([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its **test function** is
$$\varphi(x)=K(x,\{1\}),\qquad x\in\mathcal X.$$
Since $K(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure and $\{0\},\{1\}$ partition the
action set, $K(x,\{0\})+K(x,\{1\})=1$. Thus $\varphi(x)\in[0,1]$ and
$1-\varphi(x)=K(x,\{0\})$ is the probability of not rejecting. Give $[0,1]$
the trace of the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,+\infty]$, namely
$\{C\cap[0,1]:C\in\mathcal B([0,+\infty])\}$. By
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], $x\mapsto K(x,\{1\})$ is
measurable; since it has range in $[0,1]$, its preimage of $C\cap[0,1]$ equals
its preimage of $C$ and is measurable for every such $C$. Hence $\varphi$ is a
measurable map in the preimage sense of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Its value is the
rejection probability after observing $x$.
The convention $1=\text{reject}$ is fixed here. No null or alternative
hypothesis is part of this definition.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: Let T:(X,A)->(Y,B) be a statistic in a statistical experiment. The procedure K(x,C)=delta_{T(x)}(C)=1_C(T(x)) is a probability kernel and always takes the action T(x).
changes.after:
Let $T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ be a statistic in
an experiment. Define
$$K(x,C)=\delta_{T(x)}(C)=\begin{cases}1,&T(x)\in C,\\0,&T(x)\notin C,\end{cases}\qquad C\in\mathcal B.$$
Then $K$ is a randomized procedure that assigns probability one to the
statistic value $T(x)$ after observing $x$.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: On the one-point data space {x0}, let the experiment have one parameter theta and sampling law delta_{x0}. For any p in [0,1], the binary procedure K(x0,{1})=p and K(x0,{0})=1-p is a randomized test whose rejection probability is p.
changes.after:
Let the data space be the one-point space $\mathcal X=\{x_0\}$ with its full
sigma-algebra, let $\Theta=\{\theta_0\}$, and take
$P_{\theta_0}=\delta_{x_0}$. For any $p\in[0,1]$, define a binary procedure by
$$K(x_0,B)=p\,1_{\{1\in B\}}+(1-p)\,1_{\{0\in B\}},\qquad B\subseteq\{0,1\}.$$
It is a randomized test with rejection probability $p$.

changes.heading: Statement refuted
changes.before: The claim that every set map from a statistical data space to the binary action space is a statistic or a randomized test function is false. Let X={0,1} carry the trivial sigma-algebra and let phi(x)=x into {0,1} with its full sigma-algebra. Then phi is not measurable.
changes.after:
Every set map from a statistical data space to the binary action space is a
statistic or a randomized test function.

changes.before:
Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$
changes.after:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$ and let $C$ be a
nonempty closed convex subset of $\mathbb R^d$, with closedness in the Euclidean
topology ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]) and convexity as in
[[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]. Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on
its Borel sets, and assume $\int_C\|a\|_2\,\mu(da)<\infty$, where $\|\cdot\|_2$
is the Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Define the barycenter
$b=\int_Ca\,\mu(da)$ coordinatewise and assume $b\in C$. If
$f:C\to[0,+\infty]$ is Borel measurable and convex, then
$$f(b)\leq\int_C f(a)\,\mu(da).$$
Here convexity uses [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]],
and the barycenter is the vector of coordinate integrals.
changes.after:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$ and let $C$ be a
nonempty closed convex subset of $\mathbb R^d$, with closedness in the Euclidean
topology ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]) and convexity as in
[[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]. Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on
its Borel sets, and assume $\int_C\|a\|_2\,\mu(da)<\infty$, where $\|\cdot\|_2$
is the Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Define the barycenter
$b=\int_Ca\,\mu(da)$ coordinatewise and assume $b\in C$. If
$f:C\to[0,+\infty]$ is Borel measurable and convex, then
$$f(b)\leq\int_C f(a)\,\mu(da).$$
Convexity for this possibly extended-valued $f$ uses the extended-functional
convention of
[[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functionals-on-a-banach-space]], including its
endpoint convention for $0\cdot(+\infty)$. On a convex restriction where
$f$ is finite, this inequality reduces to the real-valued Euclidean convention of
[[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]], as used in the
subgradient step of the proof. The barycenter is the vector of coordinate
integrals.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before:
Let $\Theta$ be a nonempty measurable parameter space, let the model be a
probability kernel from $\Theta$ to the data space, and let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a nonempty measurable action space
([[def-measurable-space]]). Let $L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to\overline{\mathbb R}$
be measurable from the product measurable space with sigma-algebra
$\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal G$ to the extended real line with its Borel
sigma-algebra, and assume $L(\theta,a)\geq0$ for all $(\theta,a)$
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], [[def-extended-reals]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra-on-the-extended-real-line]]). A **prior** $\pi$ is a
probability measure on $\Theta$. The risk function $\theta\mapsto R(\theta,\delta)$ is measurable
under these hypotheses by kernel integration
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]],
[[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]). The **Bayes risk** of
$\delta$ under $\pi$ is
$$r_\pi(\delta)=\int_\Theta R(\theta,\delta)\,\pi(d\theta)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Its **worst-case risk** is $R^*(\delta)=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}
R(\theta,\delta)$, and the **minimax value** is
$$V_{\rm mm}=\inf\{R^*(\delta):\delta\text{ is a measurable randomized rule from data to actions}\}.$$
A rule is minimax if its worst-case risk equals this infimum. These definitions
make no assertion that a minimizer exists. Nonemptiness of $\mathsf D$ ensures
the rule class is nonempty: fixing any $a_0\in\mathsf D$ gives the constant
point-mass rule $x\mapsto\delta_{a_0}$.
changes.after:
Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable
parameter and data spaces, with $\Theta$ nonempty, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel, writing
$P_\theta=K(\theta,\cdot)$ for the sampling law
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). Let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a nonempty measurable action space
([[def-measurable-space]]). Let $L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to\overline{\mathbb R}$
be measurable from the product measurable space with sigma-algebra
$\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal G$ to the extended real line with its Borel
sigma-algebra, and assume $L(\theta,a)\geq0$ for all $(\theta,a)$
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], [[def-extended-reals]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra-on-the-extended-real-line]]). A **prior** $\pi$ is a
probability measure on $\Theta$. The risk function $\theta\mapsto R(\theta,\delta)$ is measurable
under these hypotheses by kernel integration
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]],
[[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]). The **Bayes risk** of
$\delta$ under $\pi$ is
$$r_\pi(\delta)=\int_\Theta R(\theta,\delta)\,\pi(d\theta)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Its **worst-case risk** is
$$R^*(\delta)=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}R(\theta,\delta)\in[0,+\infty],$$
and the **minimax value** is
$$V_{\rm mm}=\inf\{R^*(\delta):\delta\text{ is a measurable randomized rule from data to actions}\}\in[0,+\infty].$$
These suprema and infima are taken in the extended order on $\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]]); they exist by
[[lem-extended-reals-complete]]. The parameter set is nonempty and the rule
class is nonempty under the action-space hypothesis, so these are suprema and
infima of nonempty sets of nonnegative extended risks.
A rule is minimax if its worst-case risk equals this infimum. These definitions
make no assertion that a minimizer exists. Nonemptiness of $\mathsf D$ ensures
the rule class is nonempty: fixing any $a_0\in\mathsf D$ gives the constant
point-mass rule $x\mapsto\delta_{a_0}$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$ and let the
action space be a nonempty closed convex set $\mathsf D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$,
with its Borel sigma-algebra ([[def-measurable-space]]). Closedness is in the
Euclidean topology ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]) and convexity
uses [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]. Let
$\delta(x,da)$ be a randomized decision rule and let $L(\theta,\cdot)$ be a
nonnegative Borel convex loss on $\mathsf D$
([[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]). Assume for
every $\theta$ that $\int_\mathsf D\|a\|_2\,\delta(x,da)<\infty$ and the
barycenter $b_\delta(x)=\int_\mathsf D a\,\delta(x,da)$ belongs to $\mathsf D$
for $P_\theta$-almost every $x$. Then there is a measurable deterministic
rule $d$ such that
$$R(\theta,d)\leq R(\theta,\delta)\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
The barycenter is taken coordinatewise; finite first moment in the Euclidean
norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] makes each
coordinate integral finite. No claim is made for nonconvex action sets or when
the barycenter condition fails.
changes.after:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$ and let the
statistical experiment be
$\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$,
([[def-statistical-experiment]]), with a nonempty closed convex action set
$\mathsf D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$,
with its Borel sigma-algebra ([[def-measurable-space]]). Closedness is in the
Euclidean topology ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]) and convexity
uses [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]. Let $\delta(x,da)$ be a
randomized decision rule, and let $L(\theta,\cdot):\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$
be a nonnegative Borel loss convex in the extended-functional sense of
[[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functionals-on-a-banach-space]]. On its
convex finite-valued domain this inequality agrees with the real-valued Euclidean
convention of
[[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]], used in the
Jensen proof's subgradient step. Define
$$m_\delta(x)=\int_\mathsf D\|a\|_2\,\delta(x,da),\qquad E_0=\{x:m_\delta(x)<\infty\}.$$
For $x\in E_0$, define the coordinatewise barycenter
$$b_\delta(x)=\left(\int_\mathsf D a_j\,\delta(x,da)\right)_{j=1}^d.$$
Assume that for every $\theta\in\Theta$,
$$P_\theta\bigl(\{x\in E_0:b_\delta(x)\in\mathsf D\}\bigr)=1.$$
Then there is a measurable deterministic rule $d$ such that
$$R(\theta,d)\leq R(\theta,\delta)\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
On $E_0$, finite first moment in the Euclidean norm of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]] makes each coordinate integral finite. No claim
is made for nonconvex action sets or when the parameterwise almost-sure
barycenter condition fails.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a probability
kernel from a standard-Borel parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to a
standard-Borel data space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, where standard Borel means
measurably isomorphic to a Polish space
([[def-standard-borel-space]]). Let $\pi$ be a prior,
and let $L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$ be jointly measurable for a
measurable action space $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$. Let $J$ be the joint prior-data
law of [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]], let $M$ be its data
marginal, and let $\Pi_x(d\theta)$ be a regular posterior distribution of
$\theta$ given $x$ (the disintegration is supplied by
[[thm-disintegration-of-a-joint-law-on-standard-borel-spaces]]).
Define posterior risk
$$q(x,a)=\int_\Theta L(\theta,a)\,\Pi_x(d\theta).$$
Suppose a measurable deterministic rule $d^*:\mathcal X\to\mathsf D$
attains the posterior minimum for $M$-almost every $x$; that is,
$q(x,d^*(x))\leq q(x,a)$ for every $a\in\mathsf D$ on one $M$-full-measure
set. Then $d^*$ minimizes prior-integrated risk among all randomized decision
rules $\delta$:
$$r_\pi(d^*)\leq r_\pi(\delta).$$
No conclusion is asserted when a measurable posterior minimizer does not
exist. All risks may be $+\infty$.
changes.after:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a probability
kernel from a standard-Borel parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to a
standard-Borel data space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, where standard Borel means
measurably isomorphic to a Polish space
([[def-standard-borel-space]]). Let $\pi$ be a prior,
and let $L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$ be jointly measurable for a
measurable action space $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$. Let $J$ be the joint prior-data
law of [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]], let $M$ be its data
marginal, and let $\Pi_x(d\theta)$ be a regular posterior distribution of
$\theta$ given $x$ (the disintegration is supplied by
[[thm-disintegration-of-a-joint-law-on-standard-borel-spaces]]).
Define posterior risk
$$q(x,a)=\int_\Theta L(\theta,a)\,\Pi_x(d\theta).$$
Suppose a measurable deterministic rule $d^*:\mathcal X\to\mathsf D$
attains the posterior minimum for $M$-almost every $x$; that is,
$q(x,d^*(x))\leq q(x,a)$ for every $a\in\mathsf D$ on one measurable
$M$-full-measure set. Then $d^*$ minimizes prior-integrated risk among all randomized decision
rules $\delta$:
$$r_\pi(d^*)\leq r_\pi(\delta).$$
No conclusion is asserted when a measurable posterior minimizer does not
exist. All risks may be $+\infty$.

changes.before:
Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$
changes.after:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

changes.before:
Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$
changes.after:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Let ν be a finite positive measure and μ a positive measure on the same measurable space. If ν=ν_ac+ν_s with ν_ac absolutely continuous with respect to μ and ν_s singular with respect to μ, then ν_ac and ν_s are positive measures.
changes.after:
Let $
u$ be a finite positive measure and $\mu$ a positive measure on the same
measurable space. If $
u=
u_{\mathrm{ac}}+
u_{\mathrm{s}}$ with
$
u_{\mathrm{ac}}\ll\mu$ and $
u_{\mathrm{s}}\perp\mu$, then
$
u_{\mathrm{ac}}$ and $
u_{\mathrm{s}}$ are positive measures.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Assume AC. If μ and ν are sigma-finite positive measures on the same measurable space and ν is absolutely continuous with respect to μ, then the Radon–Nikodym class dν/dμ has a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative. Every finite-valued representative of that class is nonnegative μ-almost everywhere.
changes.after:
Assume AC. If $\mu$ and $\nu$ are sigma-finite positive measures on the same
measurable space and $\nu\ll\mu$, then the Radon–Nikodym class
$d\nu/d\mu$ has a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative. Every
finite-valued representative of that class is nonnegative
$\mu$-almost everywhere.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: A statistical experiment on (X,A) is dominated if one supplied sigma-finite positive measure μ on that same measurable space dominates every sampling law P_θ, meaning P_θ≪μ for every θ. The definition adds no parameter measurability.
changes.after:
Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).
The dominating measure is part of the specified setup. This condition adds no
measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: For probability measures P₁ and P₀ on the same measurable space, take the unique Lebesgue decomposition P₁=P₁,ac+P₁,s relative to P₀ and define the likelihood-ratio density to be the P₀-almost-everywhere class dP₁,ac/dP₀. The components are positive, P₁,ac is finite, and a nonnegative measurable representative may be chosen under AC. This class is a full likelihood ratio for P₁ versus P₀ only when P₁≪P₀; otherwise the singular component is retained separately. No pointwise canonical function is specified.
changes.after:
Let $P_0$ and $P_1$ be probability measures on the same measurable space.
Assume AC. Their Lebesgue decomposition relative to $P_0$ is the unique
decomposition
$P_1=P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}+P_{1,\mathrm{s}}$ with
$P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}\ll P_0$ and $P_{1,\mathrm{s}}\perp P_0$
([[thm-lebesgue-decomposition-exists-for-sigma-finite-signed-measures]],
[[thm-lebesgue-decomposition-is-unique-for-sigma-finite-signed-measures]]).
Both components are positive by
[[lem-positive-lebesgue-components-of-a-positive-measure]], and
$P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}$ is finite because their sum has mass one. Define the
**likelihood-ratio density** of $P_1$ against $P_0$ to be the
$P_0$-almost-everywhere class
$$
\frac{dP_{1,\mathrm{ac}}}{dP_0}
$$
of [[def-radon-nikodym-derivative]]. Under AC this class has a nonnegative
measurable representative by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

This is a full density of $P_1$ with respect to $P_0$ only in the
absolutely continuous case $P_1\ll P_0$. If that condition fails, the
singular component remains separate. A displayed representative is not a
canonical pointwise function: its values are determined only
$P_0$-almost everywhere.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: Under AC and a dominated experiment with fixed sigma-finite positive measure μ, choose simultaneously for each θ a finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative p_θ of the Radon–Nikodym class dP_θ/dμ. For observed x the likelihood is L_x(θ)=p_θ(x), with no implied measurability in θ. Each p_θ is determined only μ-almost everywhere; no pointwise canonical version or common exceptional null set for an arbitrary uncountable Θ is implied. A likelihood is not a probability distribution on Θ.
changes.after:
Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Assume AC and let P₀,P₁ be probability measures on one measurable space. Let r be a nonnegative representative of the likelihood-ratio class for P₁ versus P₀. If P₁≪P₀, then P₁=r dP₀ and E_{P₀}[g r]=E_{P₁}[g] for every nonnegative measurable g, and also for every real g integrable under P₁. Here E_{Pᵢ} means integration with respect to Pᵢ. Without P₁≪P₀, this identity need not hold because the singular component may be nonzero.
changes.after:
Assume AC and let $P_0,P_1$ be probability measures on one measurable space.
Let $r$ be a nonnegative measurable representative of the likelihood-ratio
class for $P_1$ versus $P_0$. If $P_1\ll P_0$, then
$$
E_{P_0}[g r]=E_{P_1}[g]
$$
for every nonnegative measurable $g$, and also for every real-valued
$P_1$-integrable measurable $g$. Here $E_{P_i}[h]$ means
$\int h\,dP_i$. Without $P_1\ll P_0$, this identity need not hold because the
singular component may be nonzero.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Assume AC. Let μ and ν be mutually absolutely continuous sigma-finite positive measures on one measurable space, and let (P_θ) be a statistical experiment dominated by both. Choose nonnegative density representatives p_θ^μ=dP_θ/dμ, p_θ^ν=dP_θ/dν, and h=dν/dμ. For each θ, p_θ^μ=h p_θ^ν μ-almost everywhere; h is positive μ-almost everywhere and depends only on the two dominators. Thus for each fixed pair θ,η, p_θ^μ/p_η^μ=p_θ^ν/p_η^ν μ-almost everywhere wherever the denominator is positive. No common exceptional null set for all pairs in an arbitrary uncountable Θ, no pointwise canonical versions, and no ratio value at a zero denominator are asserted.
changes.after:
Assume AC. Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be mutually absolutely continuous sigma-finite
positive measures on one measurable space, and let
$\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by both. Choose nonnegative density representatives
$p_\theta^\mu=dP_\theta/d\mu$, $p_\theta^\nu=dP_\theta/d\nu$, and
$h=d\nu/d\mu$. Then $h>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere and, for each fixed
$\theta$,
$$p_\theta^\mu=h\,p_\theta^\nu\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$
Thus, for each fixed pair $\theta,\eta$, the ratios
$p_\theta^\mu/p_\eta^\mu$ and $p_\theta^\nu/p_\eta^\nu$ agree
$\mu$-almost everywhere wherever the denominator is positive. The factor
$h$ depends only on the two dominating measures. For an arbitrary uncountable
$\Theta$, no single exceptional null set valid for every pair is asserted;
the density versions are not pointwise canonical, and no ratio value is
specified at a zero denominator.

changes.heading: Statement refuted
changes.before: For P₀=δ₀ and P₁=δ₁ on {0,1}, the P₁-absolutely-continuous component relative to P₀ is zero and its P₀-a.e. likelihood-ratio class is zero, while the singular component is P₁. At x=1 the elementary quotient of counting-measure masses has denominator zero, and no function can represent all of P₁ as a density with respect to P₀.
changes.after:
On a finite sample space with counting measure, for any probability laws
$P_0,P_1$, the pointwise quotient $r(x)=p_1(x)/p_0(x)$ is finite at every
point and represents $P_1$ as a density with respect to $P_0$.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: On X={0,1} with counting measure and parameter set Θ={0,1}, let P₀({1})=1/3, P₀({0})=2/3, P₁({1})=2/3, and P₁({0})=1/3. Both laws are dominated by counting measure. The likelihood ratio is r(0)=1/2 and r(1)=2, and for every real function g on this finite space, E_{P₀}[g r]=E_{P₁}[g].
changes.after:
Let $\mathcal X=\{0,1\}$, $\mathcal A=2^{\mathcal X}$, and let $\mu$ be
counting measure. Set $\Theta=\{0,1\}$ and define the experiment's probability
measures by
$$
P_0(\{1\})=\frac13,\quad P_0(\{0\})=\frac23,\qquad P_1(\{1\})=\frac23,\quad P_1(\{0\})=\frac13.
$$
Both are dominated by $\mu$. Their likelihood-ratio density is
$r(0)=1/2$ and $r(1)=2$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: A finite complex measure with an exponential moment whose Laplace transform vanishes on a real neighborhood of zero is the zero measure.
changes.after:
Assume AC and let $k\ge0$. Let $
u$ be a finite complex Borel measure on $\mathbb R^k$. Suppose there is $\delta>0$ such that $\int e^{\delta\|x\|_1}\,|
u|(dx)<\infty$. If the Laplace transform $L(z)=\int e^{z\cdot x}\,
u(dx)$ is zero for every real $z$ in an open neighborhood of $0$, then $
u=0$.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: On a countable common positive support, x and y are equivalent when pθ(x)/pθ(y) is constant in θ.
changes.after:
Let $\mathcal X$ be countable with its full $\sigma$-field, so it is standard Borel under the discrete metric. Let $\Theta\ne\varnothing$, and let $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ be dominated by a fixed $\sigma$-finite positive measure $\mu$. Choose the finite-valued densities $p_\theta=dP_\theta/d\mu$ as in [[def-likelihood-density]]. Let $X_0\subseteq\mathcal X$ satisfy $P_\theta(X_0)=1$ and $P_\theta(\{x\})>0$ for every $x\in X_0$ and every $\theta$. Write $m_\theta(x)=P_\theta(\{x\})$. For each $x\in X_0$, $0<\mu(\{x\})<\infty$ and $p_\theta(x)=m_\theta(x)/\mu(\{x\})$: positivity follows from $m_\theta(x)>0$, finiteness from sigma-finiteness, and the value is fixed by the density integral on the positive-measure singleton. Consequently

$$\frac{p_\theta(x)}{p_\theta(y)}=\frac{m_\theta(x)}{m_\theta(y)}\frac{\mu(\{y\})}{\mu(\{x\})}.$$

For $x,y\in X_0$, define $x\sim y$ if there is a constant $c(x,y)>0$ such that $m_\theta(x)/m_\theta(y)=c(x,y)$ for every $\theta$. The displayed fixed singleton factor shows this is equivalent to constancy of the common-reference density ratio. This is an equivalence relation: the constants for $(x,x)$, $(y,x)$ and $(x,z)$ are respectively $1$, $c(x,y)^{-1}$ and $c(x,y)c(y,z)$. Its equivalence classes form a countable quotient. Equip that quotient with its discrete $\sigma$-field; it is standard Borel because the discrete metric is complete and the countable space itself is dense. Since $\Theta\ne\varnothing$ and $P_\theta(X_0)=1$, $X_0$ is nonempty; define the class statistic by mapping each point of $X_0$ to its class and every point off $X_0$ to any fixed class. It is measurable because $\mathcal X$ has the full $\sigma$-field, and values off $X_0$ are null under every law.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Every nonempty family of probabilities dominated by one sigma-finite measure has a positive-weight countable mixture from the family that dominates every member.
changes.after: Assume AC. Let $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ be a nonempty family of probability measures dominated by a $\sigma$-finite positive measure $\mu$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. There are a finite or countable sequence $(\theta_j)$ from $\Theta$ and weights $w_j>0$ summing to one such that $Q=\sum_jw_jP_{\theta_j}$ satisfies $P_\theta\ll Q$ for every $\theta$. Repetitions are permitted if $\Theta$ is finite.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: A statistic is ancillary if its distribution is the same under every parameter.
changes.after: A statistic $U:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Z,\mathcal C)$ is **ancillary** for $(P_\theta)$ if its pushforward probability $P_\theta\circ U^{-1}$ does not depend on $\theta$. Equivalently, for every $C\in\mathcal C$, $P_\theta(U\in C)$ is constant in $\theta$.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: A statistic T is complete if every measurable g integrable under each model law with Eθg(T)=0 for all θ vanishes almost surely under every law.
changes.after: A statistic $T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is **complete** for $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ if, for every measurable real-valued $g$ such that $E_\theta|g(T)|<\infty$ for every $\theta$, the conditions $E_\theta[g(T)]=0$ for every $\theta$ imply $P_\theta(g(T)=0)=1$ for every $\theta$. Integrability is part of the premise; completeness is a property of the statistic relative to the specified family.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: A dominated family with density h exp(η·T−A(η)) is a full-rank exponential family when its parameter set contains an open subset and T has no nontrivial affine constraint.
changes.after:
Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be standard Borel, let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-finite positive measure, let $h:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable, and let $T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^k$ be a measurable statistic. For $\eta\in\mathbb R^k$ put

$$Z(\eta)=\int h(x)e^{\eta\cdot T(x)}\,\mu(dx),\qquad H=\{\eta:0<Z(\eta)<\infty\},\qquad A(\eta)=\log Z(\eta).$$

For a parameter set $\Omega\subseteq H$, the associated **exponential family** has laws $P_\eta$ with density

$$p_\eta(x)=h(x)\exp\{\eta\cdot T(x)-A(\eta)\}\quad(\eta\in\Omega).$$

The normalization $A(\eta)=\log Z(\eta)$ makes each density integrate to one. In this item **full-rank** means that $\Omega$ contains a nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^k$ and there do not exist $b\ne0$ and $c\in\mathbb R$ with $b\cdot T=c$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{h>0\}$. A parameter set containing an open subset is also called regular in some sources; terminology varies, so this definition controls here. The condition is stronger than needed for the completeness theorem below but rules out redundant displayed coordinates.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: For standard Borel data and statistic spaces, T is sufficient when one regular conditional law of the data given T works under every model law.
changes.after:
Let $((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta))$ be a statistical experiment, where $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ is standard Borel, and let $T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ be a statistic with standard Borel target. Write $P_\theta^T=P_\theta\circ T^{-1}$. The statistic $T$ is **sufficient** if there is one probability kernel $K$ from $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ to $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, $A\in\mathcal A$, and $C\in\mathcal B$,

$$P_\theta(A\cap T^{-1}(C))=\int_C K(y,A)\,P_\theta^T(dy).$$

Thus $K(T(x),A)$ is a common version of the conditional probability of $A$ given $T$, under every parameter. The kernel is fixed independently of $\theta$. Under AC, standard Borelness gives each law an individual conditional law through [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]] and [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]]; sufficiency additionally asks that one kernel works across parameters.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: A sufficient sigma-field is minimal if it is contained modulo the model-wide null ideal in every sufficient sigma-field.
changes.after:
For a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a sub-$\sigma$-field $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal A$ is **sufficient** if for every bounded measurable $u:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ there is one $\mathcal G$-measurable bounded function $v_u$ such that

$$\int_A u\,dP_\theta=\int_A v_u\,dP_\theta\quad(A\in\mathcal G,\ \theta\in\Theta).$$

For each $\theta$, this says that $v_u$ is a version of $E_\theta[u\mid\mathcal G]$, with the same pointwise version used for every parameter. Define the family-null ideal $\mathcal N=\{N\in\mathcal A:P_\theta(N)=0\text{ for every }\theta\}$. We say $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal H\pmod{\mathcal N}$ if for every $A\in\mathcal G$ there is $B\in\mathcal H$ with $A\triangle B\in\mathcal N$. A sufficient $\sigma$-field $\mathcal G_*$ is **minimal sufficient** if $\mathcal G_*\subseteq\mathcal H\pmod{\mathcal N}$ for every sufficient $\mathcal H$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: If the dominating reference probability P0 is a member of the model, T is sufficient iff each RN derivative dPθ/dP0 has a σ(T)-measurable version.
changes.after: Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ be standard Borel, let $\Theta\ne\varnothing$, and let $T:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y$ be a statistic. Fix $\theta_0\in\Theta$ and set $P_0=P_{\theta_0}$. Assume $P_\theta\ll P_0$ for every $\theta$. Then $T$ is sufficient if and only if for every $\theta$ the Radon–Nikodym derivative $dP_\theta/dP_0$ has a $\sigma(T)$-measurable version. Equivalently, for each $\theta$ there is a Borel $g_\theta:\mathcal Y\to[0,\infty)$ with $dP_\theta/dP_0=g_\theta(T)$ $P_0$-almost surely. The null exceptional set may depend on $\theta$. The requirement $P_0\in\{P_\theta\}$ is essential; an arbitrary external dominating probability is not covered.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: In a full-rank exponential family whose natural parameter set contains an open subset, the canonical statistic is complete.
changes.after: Assume AC and let $(P_\eta)_{\eta\in\Omega}$ be a full-rank exponential family as in [[def-exponential-family]], with $\Omega$ containing a nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^k$. Then its canonical statistic $T$ is complete.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: On a nonempty countable discrete sample space, sufficiency is equivalent to pointwise factorization pθ(x)=gθ(Tx)h(x), with a zero-fiber convention.
changes.after:
Let $\mathcal X$ be a nonempty countable set with its full $\sigma$-field, let $\Theta\ne\varnothing$, let $T:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y$ be a statistic into a standard Borel space, and write $p_\theta(x)=P_\theta(\{x\})$. Then $T$ is sufficient if and only if there are nonnegative functions $h:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ and Borel $g_\theta:\mathcal Y\to[0,\infty)$ such that

$$p_\theta(x)=g_\theta(Tx)h(x)\quad(\theta\in\Theta,\ x\in\mathcal X).$$

The pointwise convention is $g_\theta(t)=0$ whenever $M(t)=0$, where $M(t)=\sup_{\theta}P_\theta(T=t)$ on the countable image $T(\mathcal X)$; outside that image set $g_\theta=0$.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: A standard Borel statistic is minimal sufficient when its generated sigma-field is minimal sufficient modulo the family-null ideal.
changes.after: A statistic $T$ into a standard Borel space is **minimal sufficient** for $(P_\theta)$ if $\sigma(T)$ is a minimal sufficient $\sigma$-field in the preceding sense. Minimality is modulo sets null under every model law. It does not assert literal pointwise equality with any other minimal sufficient statistic.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: For an exponential family on a standard Borel sample space, the canonical statistic T is sufficient.
changes.after: Assume AC. Let $(P_\eta)_{\eta\in\Omega}$ be the exponential family of [[def-exponential-family]] on a standard Borel sample space, with $\Omega\ne\varnothing$, and let $T$ be its canonical statistic. Then $T$ is sufficient.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: For a dominated family on standard Borel spaces with a common conditional kernel, sufficiency is equivalent to a countable-mixture reference factorization pθ=h gθ(T).
changes.after:
Assume AC. Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ be standard Borel, let $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ be a nonempty family dominated by a $\sigma$-finite positive measure $\mu$, and let $T:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y$ be a statistic. Then the family is dominated by a positive-weight countable mixture $Q=\sum_jw_jP_{\theta_j}$, and with $h=dQ/d\mu$, $T$ is sufficient if and only if for every $\theta$ there is a nonnegative Borel $g_\theta$ such that

$$p_\theta(x)=h(x)g_\theta(Tx)\quad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

The exceptional null set may depend on $\theta$. Here $Q$ is a member of the augmented family $\{Q\}\cup\{P_\theta\}$, which is why the common-reference criterion applies. No product-density formula for a singular joint law is used.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: For the Bernoulli family indexed by [0,1], the equal mixture of the two endpoint laws dominates every member.
changes.after: Let $\mathcal X=\{0,1\}$ and $P_\theta=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\theta)$ for $0\le\theta\le1$. The positive mixture $Q=\tfrac12P_0+\tfrac12P_1$ dominates every $P_\theta$.

changes.heading: Statement refuted
changes.before: Sufficiency does not imply measurability of dPθ/dR with respect to T for an arbitrary external dominating probability R.
changes.after: The implication “$T$ sufficient and $P_\theta\ll R$ for every $\theta$ imply $dP_\theta/dR$ is $\sigma(T)$-measurable” is false if the reference probability $R$ is not required to belong to the family (or to share its conditional law given $T$).

changes.heading: Statement refuted
changes.before: In the curved iid N(θ,θ²) family, T=(ΣXi,ΣXi²) is sufficient but incomplete.
changes.after: Assume AC. A curved exponential subfamily can have a sufficient canonical statistic that is not complete.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: For iid N(μ,1) observations, the sample mean is complete sufficient and independent of the ancillary residual vector.
changes.after: Assume AC. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid $N(\mu,1)$, $\mu\in\mathbb R$, with $n\ge1$. Put $\bar X=n^{-1}\sum_iX_i$ and $R=(X_i-\bar X)_{i=1}^n$. Then $\bar X$ is complete sufficient, $R$ is ancillary, and they are independent for every $\mu$.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: For Pk=δk on the positive integers with geometric mixture Q, the likelihood-ratio vector uniquely identifies each sample point.
changes.after: Assume AC. Let $\mathcal X=\mathbb N_{\ge1}$ with its discrete $\sigma$-field, $P_k=\delta_k$, and $Q=\sum_{k\ge1}2^{-k}P_k$. The vector statistic $T(j)=(dP_k/dQ(j))_{k\ge1}$ is minimal sufficient and injective.

changes.before:
Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$
changes.after:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

changes.before:
Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$
changes.after:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

changes.before:
Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$
changes.after:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

changes.before:
For a finite family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$,
$$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}X_i\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{Var}(X_i)+2\sum_{\{i,j\}\subseteq I}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j).$$
Equivalently, it is $\sum_{i,j\in I}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)$. The empty sum has variance zero, and the singleton formula is the identity.
In the first display, the second sum is over two-element subsets of $I$.
changes.after:
For a finite family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ of square-integrable real random variables on one common probability space,
$$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}X_i\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{Var}(X_i)+2\sum_{\{i,j\}\subseteq I}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j).$$
Equivalently, it is $\sum_{i,j\in I}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)$. The empty sum has variance zero, and the singleton formula is the identity.
The original finite-probability-space case is included, since every real random variable there is square-integrable and the covariance/variance definitions agree with the finite centered-product/square formulas.
In the first display, the second sum is over two-element subsets of $I$.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: For a dominated parametric model with selected differentiable density representatives, define the score as the derivative of the log density on the positive-density support. For d=1 define scalar Fisher information by the expected squared score; for d>1, when the vector score is square-integrable, define the information matrix by the expected score outer product. The definition adds no parameter measurability or common-support hypothesis.
changes.after:
Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment dominated by a fixed sigma-finite positive measure
$\mu$, and let $p_\theta$ be selected finite-valued measurable
Radon–Nikodym density representatives as in
[[def-likelihood-density]]. The simultaneous selection of this arbitrary-index
family uses the Axiom of Choice. No measurability of $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$
or common exceptional null set for an arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$ is
implied.

Let $\Theta$ be open in $\mathbb R^d$, and fix a parameter $\theta$ at
which the selected family $\eta\mapsto p_\eta(x)$ is differentiable for
$\mu$-almost every $x$, with measurable coordinate derivatives. On
$\{x:p_\theta(x)>0\}$, define the log-likelihood
$\ell_\theta(x)=\log p_\theta(x)$ and the **score**
$$S_\theta(x):=\nabla_\theta\ell_\theta(x) =\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_j}\log p_\theta(x)\right)_{j=1}^d.$$
Set $S_\theta(x)=0$ where $p_\theta(x)=0$, which is $P_\theta$-null.
For $d=1$, this is $S_\theta=\partial_\theta\log p_\theta$.

For $d=1$, the scalar **Fisher information** is
$$I(\theta):=\mathbb E_\theta[S_\theta(X)^2]\in[0,+\infty].$$
When $d>1$ and $S_\theta$ is square-integrable, the **Fisher information
matrix** is $I(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta[S_\theta(X)S_\theta(X)^\mathsf T]$;
its $i,j$ entry is $\mathbb E_\theta[S_{\theta,i}S_{\theta,j}]$. No scalar
information is defined here for a vector parameter.
The information matrix is a second-moment matrix by definition; it equals the
score covariance matrix when the score has mean zero.

The derivatives, score and information are defined relative to the specified
differentiable representative family. The Radon–Nikodym definition alone
does not supply parameter differentiability or a canonical score version.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: On an open parameter set, suppose a selected density family has a fixed positive support on a neighborhood, is twice continuously differentiable there, and its first and second parameter derivatives have local integrable envelopes. If the score has finite second moment, then its expectation is zero and the Fisher information matrix equals the negative expected log-likelihood Hessian. This is a sufficient regularity setup, not a necessary characterization.
changes.after:
Assume the Axiom of Choice for the selected density representatives. Let
$\Theta$ be open in $\mathbb R^d$, let $\mu$ be a fixed sigma-finite
dominating measure, and let $p_\eta$ be the selected densities of a
statistical model. Fix $\theta\in\Theta$. Suppose that on a neighborhood
$U$ of $\theta$ there are a fixed measurable support $S$ and a
$\mu$-null set $N$ such that, for every $x\in S\setminus N$,
$p_\eta(x)>0$ and $\eta\mapsto p_\eta(x)$ has continuous first and second
partial derivatives on $U$; outside $S\cup N$, $p_\eta(x)=0$ for all
$\eta\in U$. Suppose there are nonnegative $g_1,g_2\in L^1(\mu)$ that
uniformly dominate every first partial derivative and every second partial
derivative, respectively, on $U$. Also assume
$\mathbb E_\theta\|S_\theta(X)\|^2<\infty$.

Then $\mathbb E_\theta S_\theta(X)=0$, and, entrywise,
$$I(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta[S_\theta(X)S_\theta(X)^\mathsf T] =-\mathbb E_\theta[\nabla_\theta^2\ell_\theta(X)].$$
For a scalar parameter this reads
$\mathbb E_\theta S_\theta=0$ and
$I(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta S_\theta^2
=-\mathbb E_\theta[\ell_\theta''(X)]$.

This common-support, integrable-envelope setup is sufficient, not necessary:
the theorem does not claim that every model with valid score identities must
have common support or these envelopes.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: For a scalar parameter in an open interval, let T have finite variance and mean ψ(θ) locally, let the score have mean zero and finite positive information I(θ), and assume Covθ(T,Sθ)=ψ′(θ). Then Varθ(T)≥ψ′(θ)²/I(θ), with equality exactly when T−ψ(θ)=(ψ′(θ)/I(θ))Sθ almost surely. Common support and an integrable derivative envelope are one sufficient route to the score and covariance identities, not necessary hypotheses for every valid bound.
changes.after:
Assume AC for the selected density representatives. Let $\Theta$ be an open
interval, fix $\theta\in\Theta$, and let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be
differentiable at $\theta$. Let $T$ be a real-valued estimator
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]) with
$\mathbb E_\eta T=\psi(\eta)$ on a neighborhood of $\theta$ and
$\mathbb E_\theta[T^2]<\infty$. Let the score $S_\theta$ have
$\mathbb E_\theta S_\theta=0$ and Fisher information
$I(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta S_\theta^2\in(0,\infty)$. If
$$\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T,S_\theta)=\psi'(\theta),$$
then
$$\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)\ge\frac{\psi'(\theta)^2}{I(\theta)}.$$
Equality holds exactly when
$$T-\psi(\theta)=\frac{\psi'(\theta)}{I(\theta)}S_\theta \quad P_\theta\text{-almost surely}.$$

The covariance identity is an explicit hypothesis. One sufficient way to
establish it is to assume the regularity hypotheses of
[[thm-score-mean-zero-and-information-identity]] on a neighborhood, together
with a neighborhood $V$ of $\theta$, a nonnegative integrable $H$, and one $\mu$-null
set $N_H$ such that $|T(x)\partial_\eta p_\eta(x)|\leq H(x)$ for every
$x\notin N_H$ and every $\eta\in V$. The mean value theorem and dominated
convergence then differentiate $\mathbb E_\eta T=\int T p_\eta\,d\mu$ and
give the covariance identity. This is only one sufficient regularity route; the bound
itself does not require common support if its score and covariance identities
have been established by another valid argument. The theorem's hypotheses
also include every finite-variance unbiased estimator in the sense of
[[def-unbiased-estimator-and-umvu]] whenever its score-covariance identity
holds.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: For an open d-dimensional parameter set, let T be a k-vector estimator unbiased coordinatewise with finite covariance, let the score have mean zero and finite nonsingular information matrix I(θ), and assume Eθ[(T−ψ(θ))Sθᵀ]=Dψ(θ). Then Covθ(T)⪰Dψ(θ)I(θ)⁻¹Dψ(θ)ᵀ, where A⪰B means aᵀ(A−B)a≥0 for every a∈Rᵏ.
changes.after:
Assume AC for the selected density representatives. Let
$\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and fix $\theta\in\Theta$. Let
$T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^k$ be a measurable estimator
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]) with finite second moments and
$\mathbb E_\theta T=\psi(\theta)$ coordinatewise (this is the meaning of
unbiasedness here), where
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathbb R^k$ is differentiable at $\theta$. Let the score
vector $S_\theta$ be square-integrable, have mean zero, and have nonsingular
information matrix $I(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta[S_\theta S_\theta^\mathsf T]$.
Assume the vector score-derivative identity
$$\mathbb E_\theta[(T-\psi(\theta))S_\theta^\mathsf T]=D\psi(\theta),$$
where $D\psi(\theta)$ is the $k\times d$ Jacobian matrix with entries
$\partial\psi_a/\partial\theta_j$. Then
$$\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T)\succeq D\psi(\theta)I(\theta)^{-1}D\psi(\theta)^\mathsf T.$$
Here $A\succeq B$ means $a^\mathsf T(A-B)a\ge0$ for every
$a\in\mathbb R^k$, and $\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T)$ is the matrix whose
$a,b$ entry is $\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T_a,T_b)$. The mean-zero and
score-derivative identities are
explicit hypotheses; common support with suitable derivative-interchange
conditions is one sufficient regular route, not the only possible route. If each coordinate $T_a$ is a finite-variance unbiased estimator of the real
estimand $\psi_a$ in the sense of [[def-unbiased-estimator-and-umvu]],
then $T$ satisfies the pointwise mean and moment premises; the score-derivative identity remains a separate condition.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: For one Bernoulli observation with parameter p∈(0,1), the score is (X−p)/(p(1−p)), the information is 1/(p(1−p)), and the unbiased estimator T=X attains the scalar Cramér–Rao bound.
changes.after:
Assume AC. Let $X$ take values in $\{0,1\}$, with
$P_p(X=1)=p$, $P_p(X=0)=1-p$, and $p\in(0,1)$. With counting measure as
dominator, this is a one-parameter common-support model. The statistic $T=X$
is unbiased for $\psi(p)=p$, and it attains the scalar Cramér–Rao bound.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: For X∼N(μ,σ²) with known σ²>0, the score is (X−μ)/σ², the Fisher information is 1/σ², and T=X is unbiased with variance σ², so it attains the scalar Cramér–Rao bound.
changes.after:
Assume AC. Let $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, where $\mu\in\mathbb R$ is the
parameter and $\sigma^2>0$ is fixed. With Lebesgue measure as dominator, the
density is
$$p_\mu(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).$$
The estimator $T=X$ is unbiased for $\psi(\mu)=\mu$, and it attains the
scalar Cramér–Rao bound.

changes.heading: Statement refuted
changes.before: The scalar Cramér–Rao formula does not apply to every differentiable density family without its score-mean and derivative-interchange hypotheses. For X∼Unif[0,θ], θ>0, T=2X is unbiased for θ but has variance θ²/3, below the naive value obtained from the formal score.
changes.after:
For every differentiable one-parameter density family, the formal score
$S_\theta=\partial_\theta\log p_\theta(X)$ and its finite positive second
moment $I(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta S_\theta^2$ automatically give the
Cramér–Rao inequality
$\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)\ge\psi'(\theta)^2/I(\theta)$ for every
unbiased finite-variance estimator $T$, even when the support depends on
$\theta$.

changes.before:
Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$
changes.after:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

changes.before:
Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$
changes.after:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before:
Let $p$ be a valid p-value for a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0$ in a
statistical experiment. For every $\alpha\in[0,1]$, the deterministic test
with rejection function
$$\varphi_\alpha(x)=\mathbf 1_{\{p(x)\le\alpha\}}$$
has size at most $\alpha$, and therefore has level $\alpha$.
changes.after:
Let $p$ be a valid p-value for a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0$ in a
statistical experiment. For every $\alpha\in[0,1]$, the deterministic test
with rejection function
$$\varphi_\alpha(x)=\mathbf 1_{\{p(x)\le\alpha\}}$$
satisfies
$$P_\theta(p(X)\le\alpha)=E_\theta[\varphi_\alpha(X)]\le\alpha \qquad(\theta\in\Theta_0).$$
Consequently, whenever a nonempty alternative hypothesis
$\Theta_1\subseteq\Theta\setminus\Theta_0$ is specified, this test has size
at most $\alpha$ and hence level $\alpha$ in the sense of
[[def-test-size-and-power]].

changes.before:
Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$
changes.after:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a positive integer $k$, take the product probability law of an independent standard normal $G$ and an independent $Q_k\sim\chi_k^2$. The **Student t law with $k$ degrees of freedom**, denoted $t_k$, is the law of
$$
T_k=\frac{G}{\sqrt{Q_k/k}}.
$$
For positive integers $r,s$, take independent $Q_r\sim\chi_r^2$ and $Q_s\sim\chi_s^2$. The **Fisher F law with degrees $(r,s)$**, denoted $F_{r,s}$, is the law of
$$
F_{r,s}=\frac{Q_r/r}{Q_s/s}.
$$
The positive-degree chi-square lemma proves that the denominators are positive almost surely, so these are real-valued random variables with well-defined laws. Zero degrees are excluded from both definitions.
changes.after:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a positive integer $k$, take the product probability law of an independent standard normal $G$ and an independent $Q_k\sim\chi_k^2$. The **Student t law with $k$ degrees of freedom**, denoted $t_k$, is the law of
$$T_k=\begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{G}{\sqrt{Q_k/k}},&Q_k>0,\\ 0,&Q_k=0. \end{cases}$$
For positive integers $r,s$, take independent $Q_r\sim\chi_r^2$ and $Q_s\sim\chi_s^2$. The **Fisher F law with degrees $(r,s)$**, denoted $F_{r,s}$, is the law of
$$F_{r,s}=\begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{Q_r/r}{Q_s/s},&Q_s>0,\\ 0,&Q_s=0. \end{cases}$$
The displayed piecewise maps are Borel measurable: each quotient is continuous on its Borel positive-denominator region, and the value on the Borel zero set is constant. The positive-degree chi-square lemma proves that the denominators are positive almost surely, so these versions agree almost surely with the usual quotients. Zero degrees are excluded from both definitions.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Use the experiment with data space $(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n))$, parameter set $\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)$, and sampling law $P_{\mu,\sigma^2}=N(\mu,\sigma^2)^{\otimes n}$. Let $n\ge2$, $\sigma>0$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be the independent coordinates of the observation. Define
$$
\bar X=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i,\qquad S^2=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X)^2,\qquad S=\sqrt{S^2}.
$$
The map $x\mapsto\bar x$ is a statistic. The sample mean $\bar X$ and residual sum $S^2$ are independent,
$$
\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi_{n-1}^2,\qquad S>0\ \text{almost surely},\qquad \frac{\bar X-\mu}{S/\sqrt n}\sim t_{n-1}.
$$
For every $0<\alpha<1$, the interval
$$
\left[\bar X-q_{n-1}(1-\alpha/2)\frac{S}{\sqrt n},\ \bar X+q_{n-1}(1-\alpha/2)\frac{S}{\sqrt n}\right]
$$
has exact coverage $1-\alpha$, where $q_{n-1}(u)$ is the unique $u$-quantile of $t_{n-1}$ established in [[lem-student-t-and-f-cdfs-are-continuous-and-strictly-increasing]].
changes.after:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Use the experiment with data space $(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n))$, parameter set $\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)$, and sampling law $P_{\mu,\sigma^2}=N(\mu,\sigma^2)^{\otimes n}$. Let $n\ge2$, $\sigma>0$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be the independent coordinates of the observation. Define
$$\bar X=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i,\qquad S^2=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X)^2,\qquad S=\sqrt{S^2}.$$
The map $x\mapsto\bar x$ is a statistic. The sample mean $\bar X$ and residual sum $S^2$ are independent,
$$\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi_{n-1}^2,\qquad S>0\ \text{almost surely},\qquad \widetilde T:=\begin{cases} \dfrac{\bar X-\mu}{S/\sqrt n},&S>0,\\ 0,&S=0 \end{cases} \sim t_{n-1}.$$
For every $0<\alpha<1$, the interval
$$\left[\bar X-q_{n-1}(1-\alpha/2)\frac{S}{\sqrt n},\ \bar X+q_{n-1}(1-\alpha/2)\frac{S}{\sqrt n}\right]$$
has exact coverage $1-\alpha$, where $q_{n-1}(u)$ is the unique $u$-quantile of $t_{n-1}$ established in [[lem-student-t-and-f-cdfs-are-continuous-and-strictly-increasing]].

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a deterministic matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with $n>p\ge1$ whose $p$ columns are linearly independent. Use the experiment on $(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n))$ indexed by $(\beta,\sigma^2)\in\mathbb R^p\times(0,\infty)$, with observation $Y=X\beta+\varepsilon$ and independent errors $\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$. Define the least-squares statistic and residual sum of squares by
$$
\widehat\beta=(X^TX)^{-1}X^TY,\qquad P_X=X(X^TX)^{-1}X^T,\qquad RSS_X=\|(I_n-P_X)Y\|^2,\qquad S^2=\frac{RSS_X}{n-p}.
$$
For every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^p$,
$$
\frac{c^T\widehat\beta-c^T\beta}{S\sqrt{c^T(X^TX)^{-1}c}}\sim t_{n-p},\qquad \frac{RSS_X}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi_{n-p}^2,
$$
and $\widehat\beta$ is independent of $RSS_X$, with $S>0$ almost surely.

For nested deterministic full and reduced design spaces $W_R\subset W_U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of dimensions $p-q$ and $p$, where $q$ is an integer and $1\le q\le p<n$, let $P_R,P_U$ be the orthogonal projections onto these spaces and define $RSS_R=\|(I-P_R)Y\|^2$ and $RSS_U=\|(I-P_U)Y\|^2$. Under the null hypothesis that the mean vector belongs to $W_R$,
$$
\frac{(RSS_R-RSS_U)/q}{RSS_U/(n-p)}\sim F_{q,n-p}.
$$
The numerator and denominator chi-square contributions are independent. All t and F denominator degrees of freedom in the statement are positive.
changes.after:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a deterministic matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with $n>p\ge1$ whose $p$ columns are linearly independent. Use the experiment on $(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n))$ indexed by $(\beta,\sigma^2)\in\mathbb R^p\times(0,\infty)$, with observation $Y=X\beta+\varepsilon$ and independent errors $\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$. Define the least-squares statistic and residual sum of squares by
$$\widehat\beta=(X^TX)^{-1}X^TY,\qquad P_X=X(X^TX)^{-1}X^T,\qquad RSS_X=\|(I_n-P_X)Y\|^2,\qquad S^2=\frac{RSS_X}{n-p},\qquad S=\sqrt{S^2}.$$
For every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^p$,
$$\widetilde T_c:=\begin{cases} \dfrac{c^T\widehat\beta-c^T\beta}{S\sqrt{c^T(X^TX)^{-1}c}},&S>0,\\ 0,&S=0 \end{cases} \sim t_{n-p},\qquad \frac{RSS_X}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi_{n-p}^2,$$
and $\widehat\beta$ is independent of $RSS_X$, with $S>0$ almost surely.

For nested deterministic full and reduced design spaces $W_R\subset W_U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of dimensions $p-q$ and $p$, where $q$ is an integer and $1\le q\le p<n$, let $P_R,P_U$ be the orthogonal projections onto these spaces and define $RSS_R=\|(I-P_R)Y\|^2$ and $RSS_U=\|(I-P_U)Y\|^2$. Under the null hypothesis that the mean vector belongs to $W_R$,
$$\widetilde F:=\begin{cases} \dfrac{(RSS_R-RSS_U)/q}{RSS_U/(n-p)},&RSS_U>0,\\ 0,&RSS_U=0 \end{cases} \sim F_{q,n-p}.$$
The numerator and denominator chi-square contributions are independent. All t and F denominator degrees of freedom in the statement are positive.

changes.before:
Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. The orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]) gives

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp$$

associates to every $v\in V$ unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$. The **orthogonal projection onto $W$** is the function

$$P_W:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad P_Wv=w.$$

Equivalently, $P_Wv$ is the unique vector of $W$ such that $v-P_Wv\in W^\perp$.
