changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: A confidence-set procedure C:X→2^Theta has measurable membership sections C_eta={x:eta∈C(x)} for every eta. Under a nonempty experiment (X,A,(P_theta)), its coverage at theta is P_theta(C_theta), and its confidence level is the infimum of coverage over theta. Coverage is at least 1-alpha when every P_theta(C_theta)≥1-alpha.
changes.after:
Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment as in [[def-statistical-experiment]], and assume
$\Theta\ne\varnothing$. A **confidence-set procedure** is a map
$C:\mathcal X\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$, where
$\mathcal P(\Theta):=\{A:A\subseteq\Theta\}$, such that, for every
$\eta\in\Theta$, its
membership section
$$C_\eta:=\{x\in\mathcal X:\eta\in C(x)\}$$
belongs to $\mathcal A$. Its **coverage at $\theta$** is
$c_C(\theta):=P_\theta(C_\theta)$, and its **confidence level** is
$\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}c_C(\theta)$, the greatest lower bound of those
coverage values. For $0\le\alpha\le1$, it has coverage
at least $1-\alpha$ if $P_\theta(C_\theta)\ge1-\alpha$ for every
$\theta\in\Theta$.

Only membership sections need to be measurable; no sigma-algebra on the
parameter set is assumed. The parameter is fixed in the repeated-sampling
coverage probability.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: A family of measurable maps q_theta:X→S is a pivot in an experiment (X,A,(P_theta)) when the pushforward laws P_theta(q_theta^{-1}(·)) are one common probability measure on S. No measurability in the parameter is assumed.
changes.after:
Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment with $\Theta\ne\varnothing$, and let
$(S,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable space. A
family of measurable maps $q_\theta:\mathcal X\to S$, one for each
$\theta\in\Theta$, is a **pivot** if the pushforward law
$$\nu_\theta(B):=P_\theta(q_\theta^{-1}(B)),\qquad B\in\mathcal S$$
is the same probability measure $\nu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$.
Each section is a random element on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,P_\theta)$, so
its pushforward is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].
No measurability in $\theta$ is asserted or needed.

For $S=\mathbb R$, a pivot is a real-valued statistic whose sampling
distribution is parameter-free. A pivot need not be invertible in the
parameter, and its inversion need not be an interval.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: If q_theta is a pivot with common law nu and B is measurable with nu(B)≥1-alpha, then C(x)={theta:q_theta(x)∈B} has coverage at least 1-alpha. Equality nu(B)=1-alpha gives exact coverage. For interval acceptance sets with atoms, calibrate nu([a,b]) itself.
changes.after:
Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be an
experiment with nonempty $\Theta$. Let $q_\theta:\mathcal X\to S$ be a
pivot with common law $\nu$, and let $B\in\mathcal S$. Define
$$C(x):=\{\theta\in\Theta:q_\theta(x)\in B\}$$
If $\nu(B)\ge1-\alpha$, then $C$ is a confidence set with coverage at
least $1-\alpha$. If $\nu(B)=1-\alpha$, its coverage is exactly
$1-\alpha$ for every parameter value. For an interval $B=[a,b]$ in
$\mathbb R$, exactness requires calibration of the actual probability
$\nu([a,b])$; quantile labels alone do not remove endpoint atoms.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: For each eta in a nonempty parameter set, let A_eta be a measurable point-null acceptance event on the full observation space, including any auxiliary randomization, and assume Q_eta(A_eta)>=1-alpha. Then C(y)={eta:y in A_eta} is a confidence set with coverage at least 1-alpha.
changes.after:
Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal Y,\mathcal G),(Q_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be an
experiment with nonempty $\Theta$, and let $0\le\alpha\le1$. For each
$\eta\in\Theta$, let $A_\eta\in\mathcal G$ be the acceptance event of a
test of the point null $\theta=\eta$, on the full observation space,
including any auxiliary randomization. Suppose
$Q_\eta(A_\eta)\ge1-\alpha$ for every $\eta\in\Theta$.
Then $C(y):=\{\eta\in\Theta:y\in A_\eta\}$
is a confidence set with coverage at least $1-\alpha$.

The probability bound is the point-null level condition written in terms of
acceptance events. For a randomized test, a rejection-probability function on
the original data space is not itself an acceptance event; the auxiliary
randomization must be part of the observation before applying this statement.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: On the integer location model X=theta+Z with Z uniform on {-1,0,1}, the pivot X-theta has a parameter-free three-atom law. At nominal level 4/5, inversion of B=[-1,1] gives C(X)={X-1,X,X+1}, whose coverage is 1 because B contains all pivot atoms.
changes.after:
Let $\Theta=\mathbb Z$, let the measurable observation space be
$(\mathbb Z,2^{\mathbb Z})$, and for each $\theta\in\mathbb Z$ assign
probability $1/3$ to each of
$\theta-1,\theta,\theta+1$. Let $X$ have this law, put
$Q(X;\theta)=X-\theta$, choose nominal level $1-\alpha=4/5$, and use the
central pivot set $B=[-1,1]$. The inverted set is
$$C(X)=\{\eta\in\mathbb Z:|X-\eta|\le1\}=\{X-1,X,X+1\}$$
Its coverage is $1$, so it is conservative for the nominal $4/5$ level.
The atom masses prevent the equal-tail quantiles from calibrating the central
acceptance set to probability $4/5$.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: Assume AC and observe Y∼N(mu,sigma^2), mu∈R, known sigma>0. For 0<alpha<1 the interval [Y-z_{1-alpha/2}sigma,Y+z_{1-alpha/2}sigma] has exact coverage 1-alpha.
changes.after:
Assume AC as in the library's construction of the normal laws. Observe one
real-valued $Y\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, where $\mu\in\mathbb R$, the known
standard deviation $\sigma>0$, and $0<\alpha<1$. Define
$\Phi(t)=\int_{-\infty}^t e^{-u^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,du$, and let
$z_{1-\alpha/2}$ be its
$(1-\alpha/2)$-quantile. Then
$[Y-z_{1-\alpha/2}\sigma,\;Y+z_{1-\alpha/2}\sigma]$
has exact confidence level $1-\alpha$.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: Assume AC and iid N(mu,lambda) observations with n>=2. Restrict the normal product law to the full-measure Borel set where the sample standard deviation is positive. For every fixed lambda>0, inversion of the exact t_(n-1) pivot gives the usual mean interval with coverage 1-alpha.
changes.after:
Assume AC and let $n\ge2$. For each fixed variance $\lambda=\sigma^2>0$, let $\widetilde P_{\mu,\lambda}=N(\mu,\lambda)^{\otimes n}$ be the full product law on $\mathbb R^n$, with mean parameter $\mu\in\mathbb R$ and independent coordinates. Use the common sample space
$D_n:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:s(x)>0\}$, where
$\bar x=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i$ and
$s(x):=\sqrt{(n-1)^{-1}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2}$ is the nonnegative square root, with the trace Borel sigma-algebra; write $P_{\mu,\lambda}$ for the restriction of $\widetilde P_{\mu,\lambda}$ to this sample space. Let $\nu=n-1$, and write $t_{\nu,u}$ for the unique $u$-quantile of the $t_\nu$ law. For $0<\alpha<1$, the interval
$$I(X)=\left[\bar X-t_{\nu,1-\alpha/2}\frac{S}{\sqrt n},\;\bar X+t_{\nu,1-\alpha/2}\frac{S}{\sqrt n}\right]$$
has exact coverage $P_{\mu,\lambda}\{\mu\in I(X)\}=1-\alpha$, for every $\mu\in\mathbb R$ and every fixed $\lambda>0$. The same formula works for all unknown variances.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: For n≥1 independent Uniform(0,theta) observations and M=max_i X_i, P_theta(M/theta≤u)=u^n for 0≤u≤1. The interval [M,M/alpha^(1/n)] has exact coverage 1-alpha for 0<alpha<1.
changes.after:
Let $n\ge1$, $\theta>0$, and take the experiment with sample space
$\mathcal X=\mathbb R^n$ and its Borel sigma-algebra, where under each
$\theta$ the coordinate random variables $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are independent,
each with
$P_\theta(X_i\le t)=0$ for $t<0$, $P_\theta(X_i\le t)=t/\theta$ for
$0\le t\le\theta$, and $P_\theta(X_i\le t)=1$ for $t>\theta$.
Write $M=\max_iX_i$ and let $0<\alpha<1$. The pivot $M/\theta$ has
distribution function $u^n$ on $[0,1]$. Setting $v=\alpha^{1/n}$ gives
the exact confidence set $C(X)=[M,M/v]\cap(0,\infty)$
with coverage $1-\alpha$.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: For X∼Bin(n,p), define F_p(k)=P_p(X≤k). The lower-tail level-alpha tests reject p=p0 when F_{p0}(X)<alpha. Inverting them gives C(X)=[0,U_X], where F_{U_k}(k)=alpha for k<n and U_n=1; coverage is at least 1-alpha.
changes.after:
Let the observation space be $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ with its full power set,
$n\ge1$, $p\in[0,1]$, $0<\alpha<1$, and let $X$ have mass
$P_p(X=j)=\binom njp^j(1-p)^{n-j}$, $j=0,\ldots,n$, with $0^0=1$.
Define $F_p(k)=\sum_{j=0}^k\binom njp^j(1-p)^{n-j}$.
For $k<n$, let $U_k\in(0,1)$ be the unique solution of
$F_{U_k}(k)=\alpha$, and set $U_n=1$. Then $C(X)=[0,U_X]$ is the
confidence set obtained by inverting the lower-tail tests that reject
$p=p_0$ when $F_{p_0}(X)<\alpha$. Its coverage is at least
$1-\alpha$; discreteness can make it conservative.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: For a probability kernel K from a measurable space S to the real line, the maps (s,t) ↦ K(s,(t,∞)) and (s,t) ↦ K(s,{t}) are measurable; composing them with measurable random elements and forming the inclusive or tie-randomized tail preserves measurability.
changes.after:
Let $K$ be a probability kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$. Define
$$a(s,t):=K(s,(t,\infty)),\qquad b(s,t):=K(s,\{t\}).$$
Both maps are $\Sigma\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$-measurable. If $S_0$ and $T_0$ are measurable random elements of $S$ and $\mathbb R$ on one probability space, and $U$ is any measurable real random variable on that space, then $a(S_0,T_0)$, $a(S_0,T_0)+b(S_0,T_0)$, and $a(S_0,T_0)+U b(S_0,T_0)$ are measurable. The middle expression equals $K(S_0,[T_0,\infty))$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Let Y have any real probability law with CDF F, and let U be an independent Uniform(0,1) variable. Then F(Y−)+U(F(Y)−F(Y−)) is Uniform(0,1).
changes.after:
Let $Y$ be a real random variable with cumulative distribution function $F(y)=P(Y\le y)$, and let $U$ be independent of $Y$ with the uniform Borel probability law on $[0,1]$. Write $F(y-):=P(Y<y)$ and $\Delta F(y):=F(y)-F(y-)=P(Y=y)$. Then
$$V:=F(Y-)+U\Delta F(Y)$$
has the uniform distribution on $[0,1]$, for arbitrary continuous, discrete, mixed, or singular laws of $Y$.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: A finite-group randomization setup consists of a finite probability space, a finite group acting on its sample space, a real test statistic, and null laws invariant under every group element. The orbit of x is {g·x:g∈G}; invariance means P(g·X∈A)=P(X∈A) for every group element g, event A, and null law P.
changes.after: A **finite-group randomization setup** consists of a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ as in [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]], a finite group $G$ acting on $\Omega$ as in [[def-group-action]], a statistic $T:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and a family $\mathcal P_0$ of null probability laws on $\Omega$ that is invariant under the action. Invariance means that for every $P\in\mathcal P_0$, $g\in G$, and $A\subseteq\Omega$, $P(\{x:g\cdot x\in A\})=P(A)$. The **orbit** of $x$ is $O(x):=\{g\cdot x:g\in G\}$, a finite subset of $\Omega$. The setup itself does not assert that the action is free or that distinct group elements give distinct orbit points.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: For a nonempty finite list of real values, a uniformly selected index has a tie-randomized upper rank that is Uniform(0,1); its inclusive upper rank is superuniform.
changes.after:
Let $a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R$ with $m\ge1$. Let $J$ be uniform on $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and let $U$ be independent of $J$ and uniform on $[0,1]$. Set
$$R_0:=\frac{\#\{i:a_i\ge a_J\}}{m},\qquad R_U:=\frac{\#\{i:a_i>a_J\}+U\#\{i:a_i=a_J\}}{m}.$$
Then $R_U$ is uniform on $[0,1]$, while $R_0$ is superuniform: $P(R_0\le u)\le u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: Given a supplied conditional law K(s,·) of a real test statistic T given S under one null law, and an independent Uniform(0,1) tie breaker U, define p=K(S,(T,∞))+U K(S,{T}); the nonrandomized upper-tail value is K(S,[T,∞)).
changes.after:
Fix one null probability law $P_0$. Let $S$ be a random element of a measurable space and let $T$ be a real random variable on the same probability space. Suppose a conditional law kernel $K(s,\cdot)$ of $T$ given $S$ is supplied, in the sense of [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]. On an auxiliary extension, let $U$ be independent of $(S,T)$ and have the uniform Borel probability law on $[0,1]$, characterized by $P(U\le u)=u$ for $0\le u\le1$. The **randomized conditional upper-tail p-value** is
$$p_U:=K(S,(T,\infty))+U K(S,\{T\}),$$
and its **nonrandomized upper-tail value** is
$$p_0:=K(S,[T,\infty)).$$
The strict tail and atom terms are evaluated at the realized pair $(S,T)$; the independent $U$ randomizes only within the tie mass. Their measurability, including measurability of both displayed p-values, follows from [[lem-conditional-kernel-tail-and-atom-evaluations-are-measurable]]. The inclusive tail is the sum of the strict tail and the atom at $T$. This definition asserts no existence of the conditional kernel; it is supplied as part of the input.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: For a finite-group randomization setup and statistic T, define p0(x)=|G|^{-1}# {g:T(g·x)≥T(x)}. With an independent Uniform(0,1) variable U, define the tie-randomized value pU(x)=|G|^{-1}(# {g:T(g·x)>T(x)}+U # {g:T(g·x)=T(x)}). Group elements are counted with multiplicity, including when the action is not free.
changes.after:
For a finite-group randomization setup with statistic $T$, the **inclusive orbit upper-tail rank** at $x\in\Omega$ is
$$p_0(x):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)\ge T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
If $U$ is independent of the observed data and uniform on $[0,1]$, the **tie-randomized orbit rank** is
$$p_U(x,U):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)>T(x)\}+U\,\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)=T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
Both counts are over group elements, with multiplicity. Thus a nonfree action counts a distinct orbit point as many times as it has preimages under $g\mapsto g\cdot x$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Under a simple null and a supplied conditional law of a real statistic T given S, the randomized upper-tail p-value is Uniform(0,1) conditionally on S. The nonrandomized upper-tail p-value is conditionally superuniform.
changes.after:
Under the simple null and the supplied conditional law in [[def-randomized-conditional-p-value]], for every $u\in[0,1]$,
$$P_0(p_U\le u\mid\sigma(S))=u\quad P_0\text{-almost surely},$$
while the nonrandomized upper-tail value satisfies
$$P_0(p_0\le u\mid\sigma(S))\le u\quad P_0\text{-almost surely}.$$
Thus the randomized value is conditionally uniform and the inclusive-tail value is conditionally superuniform, including when the conditional law has atoms.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Under a finite-group randomization setup with invariant null law, conditional on each positive-probability orbit the data are uniform on its distinct points; the inclusive orbit-rank p-value is superuniform under every null law, and its independent-uniform tie-randomized version is Uniform(0,1) on every such orbit.
changes.after: In a finite-group randomization setup, fix a null law invariant under the group action. Conditional on every orbit $O$ with positive probability, the data are uniform on the distinct points of $O$. For the orbit ranks of [[def-orbit-rank-p-value]], the inclusive p-value $p_0$ is superuniform under the null, and the independent-uniform tie-randomized value $p_U$ is Uniform$(0,1)$ conditionally on each positive-probability orbit. Consequently, $p_U$ is also Uniform$(0,1)$ unconditionally.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: For a measurable statistic S with Borel target, nonempty disjoint null and alternative sets, and test function phi, define the null-wise conditional rejection probability as a supplied version of E[phi|sigma(S)]; conditional level alpha means each such version is at most alpha almost surely under its own null law.
changes.after: Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,\{P_\theta\}_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment with nonempty disjoint null and alternative parameter sets $\Theta_0,\Theta_1\subseteq\Theta$. Let $\mathcal S$ be a topological space with its Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(\mathcal S)$, and let $S:\mathcal X\to\mathcal S$ be measurable. Write $\sigma(S):=\{S^{-1}(C):C\in\mathcal B(\mathcal S)\}$, the sigma-algebra generated by $S$ as in [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]]. A possibly randomized test is a measurable function $\varphi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ as in [[def-test-size-and-power]]. For each $\theta\in\Theta_0$, a **conditional rejection probability given $S$** is a supplied version $q_\theta$ of $E_\theta[\varphi(X)\mid\sigma(S)]$, where conditional expectation is understood as in [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The test has **conditional level at most $\alpha$ given $S$ on $\Theta_0$** if such versions can be supplied with $q_\theta\le\alpha$ $P_\theta$-almost surely for every $\theta\in\Theta_0$. The almost-sure qualification is separate under each null law; no common null set or pointwise statement at conditioning values of probability zero is asserted.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: If S is sufficient for a nonempty null subfamily in the sense that one common conditional law kernel of the full data given S works under every null nuisance value, then the conditional rejection probability of any bounded measurable test is given by one nuisance-independent kernel integral, up to each null law's own conditioning-null sets.
changes.after:
Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and $(\mathcal S,\mathscr S)$ be standard Borel spaces as in [[def-standard-borel-space]]. Fix Polish topologies realizing these specified Borel sigma-algebras, as the standard-Borel definition permits. Let $\Theta_0,\Theta_1$ be nonempty disjoint parameter subsets, and write $\{P_\eta:\eta\in\Theta_0\}$ for the null subfamily. Let $S:\mathcal X\to\mathcal S$ be measurable. Suppose there is one probability kernel $K(s,\cdot)$ such that, for every $\eta\in\Theta_0$, $K(S,\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of the full data $X$ given $\sigma(S)$ under $P_\eta$. This is the common-kernel premise of sufficiency for the null subfamily in [[def-sufficient-statistic]]. For any measurable $\varphi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, define
$$q(s):=\int_{\mathcal X}\varphi(x)K(s,dx).$$
Then $q$ is measurable and $q(S)$ is a version of the conditional rejection probability of $\varphi$ given $S$ under every $P_\eta$. The same function $q$ works for every nuisance value, with conditional-expectation identities interpreted almost surely under each corresponding law.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: For a test with nonempty disjoint hypotheses, statistic S, and alpha in [0,1], conditional rejection probability at most alpha almost surely under every null law implies unconditional rejection expectation at most alpha under every null law, hence size at most alpha.
changes.after: Let $\varphi$ be a test for nonempty disjoint null and alternative parameter sets $\Theta_0,\Theta_1$ as in [[def-test-size-and-power]], let $S$ be a statistic, and let $\alpha\in[0,1]$. If for every $\theta\in\Theta_0$ there is a conditional-expectation version $q_\theta=E_\theta[\varphi(X)\mid\sigma(S)]$ with $q_\theta\le\alpha$ $P_\theta$-almost surely, then $E_\theta[\varphi(X)]\le\alpha$ for every $\theta\in\Theta_0$. Consequently, the test has size at most $\alpha$, where size is the supremum of its rejection expectation over the null family as in [[def-test-size-and-power]].

changes.heading: Statement refuted
changes.before: The claim that the group-average upper-tail p-value is superuniform for every null law, without requiring invariance, is false.
changes.after: For every finite group action and every null law, the inclusive group-average upper-tail rank is superuniform, even when the null law is not invariant under the group.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: Let S3 permute the three coordinates of Ω={e1,e2,e3}, give Ω its uniform law, and set T(x)=x1. Each point has a stabilizer of size two. The group-average p-values are p0(e1)=1/3, p0(e2)=p0(e3)=1; randomized values are U/3 on e1 and 1/3+(2/3)U on e2,e3, so the orbit-conditional randomized rank is uniform.
changes.after: Let $G=S_3$ permute the coordinates of $\Omega=\{e_1,e_2,e_3\}\subset\{0,1\}^3$, give the three points equal probability, take $T(x)=x_1$, and use an independent $U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)$. Each point has a stabilizer of size two. The group-average inclusive ranks are $p_0(e_1)=1/3$ and $p_0(e_2)=p_0(e_3)=1$. The randomized values are $p_U(e_1)=U/3$ and $p_U(e_2)=p_U(e_3)=1/3+2U/3$, illustrating how tied ranks fill adjacent intervals even when each orbit point has multiple group preimages.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: For two independent Bernoulli samples of sizes n1 and n2, the one-sided alternative that the first success probability is larger is tested under the null of a common success probability p by conditioning on the total number s of successes; the first-sample count then has a hypergeometric law. For n1=n2=2 and s=2, the conditional masses are 1/6, 4/6, 1/6, and the upper-tail p-values are 1, 5/6, 1/6.
changes.after:
Take two independent Bernoulli samples of sizes $n_1,n_2\ge1$ and test the one-sided alternative that the first success probability exceeds the second. Under the null, all $N=n_1+n_2$ trials have a common success probability $p\in[0,1]$. Let $K$ be the number of successes in the first sample and $S$ the total number in both samples. For every integer margin $s\in\{0,\ldots,N\}$, define the supplied conditional-law kernel $Q$ by
$$Q(s,\{k\})=\frac{\binom{n_1}{k}\binom{n_2}{s-k}}{\binom{N}{s}},\qquad \max(0,s-n_2)\le k\le\min(n_1,s),$$
and set $Q(s,\{k\})=0$ outside the displayed range. For each $s$, these weights sum to one because they count all $\binom Ns$ ways to choose the $s$ success positions according to how many lie in the first sample. At margins of positive probability this is the conditional law and it does not depend on $p$; at endpoint nulls $p=0,1$, the formula also supplies a version at the other, probability-zero margins. Large values of $K$ support the one-sided alternative that the first sample has a larger success probability. For $n_1=n_2=2$ and $s=2$, the conditional masses at $k=0,1,2$ are $1/6,4/6,1/6$; the inclusive upper-tail p-values are $1,5/6,1/6$.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.after:
Let $d\ge1$ be fixed, and equip $\mathbb R^d$ with the Borel sigma-algebra generated by its Euclidean open sets. Let $Z_n$ be measurable random elements of this Borel space, not necessarily defined on a common probability space, and let $
u$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d$. The sequence $(Z_n)$ has **asymptotic distribution** $
u$ if its laws converge weakly to $
u$; equivalently, $Z_n\Rightarrow Z$ for any random vector $Z$ with law $
u$ ([[def-convergence-in-distribution-of-random-elements]], [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]).

For an estimator, any centering or scaling, such as $r_n(T_n-\psi(	heta))$, is part of the sequence whose asymptotic distribution is being specified; it is not implicit in the term. Weak convergence alone does not assert convergence of moments.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.after:
For each positive integer $n$, let $(\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n,P_n)$ be a probability space and let $X_n:\Omega_n\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable into the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the Euclidean open sets, where $d\ge1$ is fixed and $\mathbb R^d$ has the Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-probability-measure]]). The spaces and measures may depend on $n$; no common probability space is required.

Write $X_n=o_P(1)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_n(\|X_n\|_2>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
Write $X_n=O_P(1)$, or say that $(X_n)$ is bounded in probability, if for every $\eta>0$ there is $M>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}P_n(\|X_n\|_2>M)\le\eta.$$
For real-valued variables on one common probability space, $o_P(1)$ is convergence in probability to zero as defined in [[def-convergence-in-probability]].

The norms and tail probabilities are part of the definition. Independence is not implicit in either notation.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let all random vectors with index $n$ be defined on a common probability space for that $n$; the spaces may vary with $n$. In any fixed finite-dimensional Euclidean space, the following rules hold:

1. If $U_n=o_P(1)$ and $V_n=o_P(1)$, then $U_n+V_n=o_P(1)$. If $U_n=O_P(1)$ and $V_n=O_P(1)$, then $U_n+V_n=O_P(1)$.
2. For positive integers $p,q,r$, let $B:\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R^r$ be a fixed map for which there is a constant $C\ge0$ with $\|B(u,v)\|_2\le C\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$ for all $u,v$. Assume in each application that $B(U_n,V_n)$ is a random vector on the same probability space as $U_n,V_n$, for every $n$. If $U_n=o_P(1)$ and $V_n=O_P(1)$, or conversely, then $B(U_n,V_n)=o_P(1)$. If both are $O_P(1)$, then $B(U_n,V_n)=O_P(1)$.
3. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ in $\mathbb R^d$, then $X_n=O_P(1)$.

The last conclusion is finite-dimensional boundedness in probability. No independence or Axiom of Choice is assumed.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $d,k,m\ge1$ be fixed. For each $n$, let $X_n\in\mathbb R^d$ and $Y_n\in\mathbb R^k$ be random vectors on one probability space; the probability space may vary with $n$. Let $X\in\mathbb R^d$ be a random vector on any probability space, and let $c\in\mathbb R^k$ be constant. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n-c=o_P(1)$, then
$$ (X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow(X,c). $$
Consequently, for every continuous $h:\mathbb R^{d+k}\to\mathbb R^m$, $h(X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow h(X,c)$. No independence between $X_n$ and $Y_n$ is required.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.after:
Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric model on a statistical experiment, and let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T$ be an estimand whose target set $\mathcal T$ is equipped with a metric $d$ ([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-parametric-statistical-model]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]], [[def-metric-space]]). For $n\ge1$, the IID sample-size-$n$ experiment has sample space $\mathcal X^n$, product sigma-algebra $\mathcal A^{\otimes n}$, and sampling law $P_\theta^{\otimes n}$ at parameter $\theta$ ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). The product law is defined recursively from $P_\theta$; each factor is a probability measure and hence sigma-finite, so the finite product theorem supplies its existence, rectangle formula, and uniqueness ([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).

A **nonrandomized estimator sequence** of $\psi$ is a sequence of measurable maps, in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]],
$$T_n:(\mathcal X^n,\mathcal A^{\otimes n})\to(\mathcal T,\mathcal B(\mathcal T)),\qquad n\ge1,$$
where $\mathcal B(\mathcal T)$ is the sigma-algebra generated by the open sets of the metric $d$, that is, the Borel sigma-algebra of its metric topology ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Its sampling distribution at $\theta$ and sample size $n$ is the pushforward of $P_\theta^{\otimes n}$ by $T_n$.

This definition fixes IID repeated sampling and data-measurable estimators. It imposes no measurability on the parameter map $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ or on $\psi$.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.after:
Let $(T_n)$ be an estimator sequence of an estimand $\psi$ with metric target $(\mathcal T,d)$, and fix $\theta\in\Theta$. The sequence is **consistent in probability at $\theta$** if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_\theta^{\otimes n}\bigl(\{x\in\mathcal X^n:d(T_n(x),\psi(\theta))>\varepsilon\}\bigr)\longrightarrow0.$$

The error event is measurable: by the triangle inequality, $t\mapsto d(t,\psi(\theta))$ is continuous, so its strict superlevel set at $\varepsilon$ is open in the target metric topology and hence Borel; its preimage under $T_n$ is measurable.

The consistency is **pointwise** because $\theta$ is fixed before the limit. It does not assert uniform convergence over $\Theta$ ([[def-estimator-sequence-in-iid-experiments]]).

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $\mathcal X=\mathbb R$ with its Borel sigma-algebra, and let $\mathsf P$ be a parametric statistical experiment on $\mathcal X$. Define the mean estimand by $\mu(\theta)=\int x\,P_\theta(dx)$ and suppose it is finite for every $\theta$. For a fixed $\theta$, suppose an IID sequence $(X_i)_{i\ge1}$ with one-observation law $P_\theta$ is given and $\mathbb E_\theta|X_1|<\infty$. The sample-mean estimator $T_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i$ is consistent in probability for $\mu$ at $\theta$ in the IID sample-size experiments.

The assertion is pointwise in $\theta$. The existence of a common probability space carrying the IID sequence is part of the hypothesis.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after: Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric statistical model, let $\psi:\Theta\to(\mathcal T,d)$ be a metric-valued estimand, and let $(T_n)$ be a nonrandomized estimator sequence for IID samples from this model. If $\psi$ is not identifiable, then there is a pair of observationally equivalent parameters with distinct target values, and no estimator sequence is consistent in probability at both parameters.

changes.heading: Example
changes.after: For each $n\ge1$, let $X_n$ be defined on a probability space $(\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n,P_n)$ with $P_n(X_n=n)=1/n$ and $P_n(X_n=0)=1-1/n$. Then $P_n(|X_n|>\varepsilon)\to0$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so $X_n=o_P(1)$ under the varying-space convention, and its asymptotic distribution is the point mass at $0$, but $\mathbb E X_n=1$ for every $n$. Although each $X_n$ is integrable, weak convergence alone does not imply convergence of expectations.

changes.heading: Example
changes.after: Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,P)$ be the two-point probability space $\Omega=\{-1,1\}$ with the power-set sigma-algebra and equal point masses, and set $Z(\omega)=\omega$. On this same space for each $n\ge1$, put $Z_n=Z$, $a_n=n^{-1/2}$, and $R_n=a_nZ_n$. Then $Z_n=O_P(1)$ and $a_n=o_P(1)$, so the finite-dimensional product rule gives $R_n=o_P(1)$. Moreover $\sqrt n R_n=Z_n=O_P(1)$, the precise root-$n$ boundedness assertion.

changes.heading: Example
changes.after:
Let $\mathcal X=\{0,1\}$ with its power-set sigma-algebra. For $p\in[0,1]$, define the Bernoulli law $P_p(\{1\})=p$ and $P_p(\{0\})=1-p$, and use the estimand $\psi(p)=p$. Suppose a common probability space carries an IID sequence with one-observation law $P_p$. Under its IID sample-size experiments, the estimator $T_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i$ is the sample proportion. It satisfies the finite-sample bound
$$P_p^{\otimes n}(|T_n-p|\ge\varepsilon)\le\frac{p(1-p)}{n\varepsilon^2}\le\frac{1}{4n\varepsilon^2},\qquad\varepsilon>0,$$
so it is consistent, including at $p=0$ and $p=1$.

changes.heading: Example
changes.after: Let $\mathcal X=\{0,1\}$ with its power-set sigma-algebra and $\Theta=[0,1]^2$. For $(u,v)\in\Theta$, let $P_{(u,v)}$ be the Bernoulli law with $P_{(u,v)}(\{1\})=u$ and $P_{(u,v)}(\{0\})=1-u$, and take the target $\psi(u,v)=v$ with its usual metric. The two parameters $\theta_0=(1/2,0)$ and $\theta_1=(1/2,1)$ have the same observation law and different target values. Thus the target is not identifiable and no estimator sequence is consistent in probability at both parameters.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.after:
Use the real random variable convention of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] and the expectation convention of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. A real random variable $X$ is **centered** when it is integrable and $\mathbb E X=0$. A vector random element $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_d)$ in $\mathbb R^d$, for an integer $d\ge1$, is centered when each coordinate is integrable and $\mathbb E Z_j=0$. For $u,z\in\mathbb R^d$, write $\langle u,z\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^d u_jz_j$ and $\|u\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d u_j^2)^{1/2}$, using the Euclidean convention in [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]].

For $\sigma^2\ge0$, a centered real random variable $X$ is **sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}\qquad\text{for every }\lambda\in\mathbb R.$$
A centered vector random element $Z\in\mathbb R^d$ is **sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda\langle u,Z\rangle}\le e^{\sigma^2\lambda^2\|u\|_2^2/2}\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathbb R^d\text{ and }\lambda\in\mathbb R.$$

For $\nu^2\ge0$ and $b>0$, a centered real random variable $X$ is **sub-exponential with parameters $(\nu^2,b)$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{\lambda^2\nu^2/2}\qquad\text{whenever }|\lambda|\le1/b.$$

The parameters $\sigma^2$ and $\nu^2$ are moment-generating-function upper-bound proxies; they are not asserted to equal the variance. The vector condition controls every one-dimensional projection and does not assert independence of coordinates.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Assume AC. Let $n\ge1$ and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent integrable real random variables on one probability space. Suppose finite real numbers $a_i\le b_i$ satisfy $a_i\le X_i\le b_i$ almost surely for every $i$. Put $V=\sum_{i=1}^n(b_i-a_i)^2$ and $S=\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mathbb E X_i)$. For every $t>0$, if $V>0$ then
$$\mathbb P(|S|\ge t)\le 2\exp\!\left(-\frac{2t^2}{V}\right),$$
and if $V=0$ then $\mathbb P(|S|\ge t)=0$. The two one-sided tails are each bounded by $\exp(-2t^2/V)$ when $V>0$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $n\ge1$ and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent centered square-integrable real random variables. Suppose $b\ge0$ is finite and $|X_i|\le b$ almost surely for each $i$. Put $v=\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(X_i)$. For $t>0$, if $v>0$ then
$$\mathbb P\left(\left|\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right|\ge t\right)\le 2\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2(v+bt/3)}\right),$$
and if $v=0$ then this probability is $0$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and $0<\epsilon<1$. There is a finite set $\mathcal N\subseteq S^{d-1}$ such that every $u\in S^{d-1}$ has some $v\in\mathcal N$ with $\|u-v\|_2\le\epsilon$, and
$$|\mathcal N|\le(1+2/\epsilon)^d.$$
Here $S^{d-1}=\{u\in\mathbb R^d:\|u\|_2=1\}$ by [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]. Such a set is called an $\epsilon$-net of the sphere.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $n\ge1$, let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be independent random elements with laws $\mu_i$ on measurable spaces $(S_i,\Sigma_i)$, and let $\mu=\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mu_i$. Let $f:\prod_{i=1}^nS_i\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$. Suppose finite deterministic $c_i\ge0$ satisfy
$$|f(x_1,\ldots,x_{i-1},x_i,x_{i+1},\ldots,x_n)-f(x_1,\ldots,x_{i-1},x_i',x_{i+1},\ldots,x_n)|\le c_i$$
for every $i$, every fixed choice of the other coordinates, and every $x_i,x_i'\in S_i$. For each $i$, define $M_i$ by integrating $f$ over the unrevealed product coordinates, using the measurable finite versions given by Fubini; set $M_0=\int f\,d\mu$ and $M_n=f(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$. Put $\mathcal F_i=\sigma(Z_1,\ldots,Z_i)$ and $D_i=M_i-M_{i-1}$. Then $M_i$ is integrable and $\mathcal F_i$-measurable, and for every $A\in\mathcal F_{i-1}$,
$$\int_A D_i\,d\mathbb P=0.$$
Moreover, there are finite $\mathcal F_{i-1}$-measurable endpoints $A_i,B_i$ such that $A_i\le0\le B_i$, $A_i\le D_i\le B_i$ almost surely, and $B_i-A_i\le c_i$ almost surely. No choice axiom is used in this product-integral construction.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent centered real random variables, with $X_i$ sub-exponential with parameters $(\nu_i^2,b_i)$ as defined in [[def-subgaussian-variable-and-vector]], where $n\ge1$ and $b_i>0$. Put $v=\sum_{i=1}^n\nu_i^2$, $b=\max_{1\le i\le n}b_i$, and $S=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$. For $t>0$, if $v>0$ then
$$\mathbb P(|S|\ge t)\le2\exp\!\left(-\frac12\min\!\left\{\frac{t^2}{v},\frac{t}{b}\right\}\right),$$
and if $v=0$ then $\mathbb P(|S|\ge t)=0$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_m$ be centered sub-Gaussian real random variables with a common proxy $\sigma^2\ge0$, where $m\ge1$. No independence is assumed. For $t>0$, if $\sigma^2>0$ then
$$\mathbb P\left(\max_{1\le j\le m}|Y_j|\ge t\right)\le2m\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),$$
and if $\sigma^2=0$ the probability is $0$.

Let $Z$ be a centered sub-Gaussian vector in $\mathbb R^d$ with proxy $\sigma^2$, where $d\ge1$. For $0<\epsilon<1$, let $\mathcal N$ be the sphere net supplied by [[lem-epsilon-net-of-unit-sphere-has-cardinality-bound]]. Then for $t>0$, if $\sigma^2>0$,
$$\mathbb P(\|Z\|_2\ge t)\le2(1+2/\epsilon)^d\exp\!\left(-\frac{(1-\epsilon)^2t^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),$$
and if $\sigma^2=0$ this probability is $0$. The deterministic reduction is $\|z\|_2\le(1-\epsilon)^{-1}\max_{u\in\mathcal N}|\langle u,z\rangle|$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^d$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Assume AC. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be independent random elements, meaning measurable maps ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]), with laws $\mu_i$ given by pushforward ([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). Put $\mu=\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mu_i$ on the finite product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). Let $f:\prod_{i=1}^nS_i\to\mathbb R$ be product-measurable with $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$. Suppose finite deterministic constants $c_i\ge0$ satisfy
$$|f(z_1,\ldots,z_i,\ldots,z_n)-f(z_1,\ldots,z_i',\ldots,z_n)|\le c_i$$
for every fixed setting of the other coordinates and every $z_i,z_i'$. The independent product-law theorem identifies the law of $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ as $\mu$. Applying change of variables for expectation first to $|f|$ and then to $f$ makes $f(Z)$ integrable and gives $\mathbb E f(Z)=\int f\,d\mu$. Put $V=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2$. For $t>0$, if $V>0$ then
$$\mathbb P\bigl(f(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)-\mathbb E f(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)\ge t\bigr)\le\exp\!\left(-\frac{2t^2}{V}\right),$$
and if $V=0$ this probability is $0$. The same bound holds for the lower tail, so the two-sided probability is at most $2e^{-2t^2/V}$ when $V>0$.

changes.heading: Example
changes.after:
Assume AC. Let $n\ge1$ and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent Rademacher variables, meaning $\mathbb P(X_i=1)=\mathbb P(X_i=-1)=1/2$, and put $S_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$. For every $t>0$,
$$\mathbb P(|S_n|\ge t)\le2e^{-t^2/(2n)}.$$

changes.heading: Example
changes.after:
Assume AC. Let $\sigma>0$, let $G\sim N(0,1)$, and set $Z_j=\sigma G$ for every $1\le j\le m$, where $m\ge1$. These variables are perfectly dependent. For every $t>0$,
$$\mathbb P\left(\max_{1\le j\le m}|Z_j|\ge t\right)\le2m\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).$$

changes.heading: Example
changes.after:
Let $d\ge1$ and let $Z\in\mathbb R^d$ be a centered sub-Gaussian vector with proxy $\sigma^2>0$. Choosing $\epsilon=1/2$ in the net reduction gives, for every $t>0$,
$$\mathbb P(\|Z\|_2\ge t)\le2\cdot5^d e^{-t^2/(8\sigma^2)}.$$
If $\sigma^2=0$, the same probability is $0$.

changes.heading: Statement refuted
changes.after: Every centered real random variable with finite variance is sub-Gaussian with some finite proxy.

$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

changes.after:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

changes.heading: Definition
changes.after:
Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space, let $n\ge1$ be an integer, and let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID random elements with law $P$. For a class $\mathcal F$ of measurable, integrable real-valued functions on $\mathcal X$, write

$$Pf:=\int f\,dP,\qquad P_nf:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f(Z_i),\qquad \mathbb G_n(f):=\sqrt n\,(P_nf-Pf).$$

The map $f\mapsto P_nf-Pf$ is the centered empirical process, and $\mathbb G_n$ is its $\sqrt n$-scaled version. More generally, for independent processes $X_1(t),\ldots,X_n(t)$ whose marginal expectations are finite for each index $t\in T$, the centered process sum is

$$S_n(t):=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(X_i(t)-\mathbb E X_i(t)\bigr),\qquad t\in T.$$

On an auxiliary probability-space extension, let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n$ be independent signs, each taking $+1$ and $-1$ with probability $1/2$, independent of the observations. The empirical Rademacher process is

$$R_n(f):=\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i f(Z_i),\qquad f\in\mathcal F.$$

The centered Rademacher process $\sum_i\sigma_i(f(Z_i)-Pf)$ is a distinct process; no equality between it and $R_n$ is part of this definition.

For a countable class of measurable functions, each displayed supremum of measurable sample paths is measurable. For an uncountable class, ordinary probability or expectation is used only when a specified countable subclass has the same supremum almost surely for the process in question; this is the separable-version convention used here. Otherwise state results using outer probability

$$P^*(A):=\inf\{P(B):A\subseteq B,\ B\in\mathcal A\}$$

and, for a nonnegative possibly nonmeasurable random quantity $Y$, outer expectation

$$\mathbb E^*Y:=\inf\{\mathbb E U: U\text{ is measurable, nonnegative, and }U\ge Y\}.$$

In particular, measurability of every $f$ separately does not by itself make an uncountable supremum measurable.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.after:
Let $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ be a family of subsets of an arbitrary set $X$. For a finite $T\subseteq X$, its trace is

$$\mathcal C|_T:=\{C\cap T:C\in\mathcal C\}.$$

The family $\mathcal C$ **shatters** $T$ when $\mathcal C|_T=\mathcal P(T)$. This extends the finite-ground-set trace convention of [[def-shattering-and-vc-dimension]]: any finite $T$ can be relabeled by $[|T|]$, and relabeling preserves all traces and their cardinalities.

For a nonempty class, its **VC dimension** $d(\mathcal C)$ is the greatest size of a finite shattered set if those sizes are bounded, is $0$ if no singleton is shattered, and is $+\infty$ if finite shattered sets have unbounded size. When the dimension is finite, its **VC index** is

$$V(\mathcal C):=d(\mathcal C)+1,$$

equivalently the least positive integer $V$ such that no $V$-point subset is shattered. The empty class is assigned $V=0$ by convention and is treated separately in the entropy theorem.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $Y$ be a measurable real random variable on a probability space with $0\le Y\le1$ almost surely. Then, for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$,

$$\mathbb E\exp\{\lambda(Y-\mathbb EY)\}\le \exp(\lambda^2/8).$$

This proof uses only finite product and scalar integral arguments; it does not assume the Axiom of Choice.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $J\ge1$ be an integer, put $u_j=-1+2j/J$ for $j=0,\ldots,J$, and give the finite set $U_J=\{u_0,\ldots,u_J\}$ the probability weights

$$\nu_J(\{u_0\})=\nu_J(\{u_J\})=\frac1{2J},\qquad \nu_J(\{u_j\})=\frac1J\quad(1\le j<J).$$

For all $-1\le a\le b\le1$,

$$\left|\nu_J([a,b)) - \frac{b-a}{2}\right|\le\frac1J.$$

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after: Let $r>0$. The map $t\mapsto t^r$ is strictly increasing on $[0,\infty)$. Consequently, if $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measurable space and $h:X\to[0,\infty)$ is measurable, then $h^r$ is measurable.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.after:
A pseudometric $d$ on a set $T$ is a nonnegative symmetric function $d:T\times T\to[0,\infty)$ with $d(t,t)=0$ and $d(s,t)\le d(s,u)+d(u,t)$; distinct points may have distance zero. For a nonempty subset $\mathcal F\subseteq T$ and $\epsilon>0$, the covering number $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the least finite $k$ for which there are centers $f_1,\ldots,f_k\in\mathcal F$ such that every $f\in\mathcal F$ satisfies $d(f,f_j)\le\epsilon$ for some $j$. It is $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists. Set $N(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=1$.

The packing number $D(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the largest size of a finite subset $\{f_1,\ldots,f_k\}\subseteq\mathcal F$ whose distinct members have pairwise distance strictly greater than $\epsilon$. If the sizes of such finite subsets are unbounded, put $D=+\infty$; put $D(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=0$. These conventions give the radius comparison proved in [[lem-packing-covering-number-comparison]]. The metric entropy is $H(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d):=\log N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ for nonempty classes, with $\log(+\infty)=+\infty$.

For a probability measure $Q$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and a measurable real function $g$, set $\|g\|_{Q,r}:=(\int |g|^r\,dQ)^{1/r}$ for $1\le r<\infty$, using the positive-base real-power convention of [[def-real-power]]. The function $|g|$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and [[lem-real-power-preserves-measurability]] makes $|g|^r$ measurable, so this integral is well-defined. On a class of functions with finite such norms, $d_{Q,r}(f,g):=\|f-g\|_{Q,r}$ is a pseudometric: nonnegativity, symmetry, and zero diagonal follow from the absolute value, and the triangle inequality is [[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]]. Functions that agree $Q$-almost everywhere have distance zero. We write $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ for this covering number.

For measurable real endpoints $\ell\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere, the bracket $[\ell,u]$ is the set of measurable functions $f$ satisfying $\ell\le f\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere. Its $L^r(Q)$ width is $\|u-\ell\|_{Q,r}$. The bracketing number $N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ is the least number of such brackets of width at most $\epsilon$ that cover $\mathcal F$, or $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists; for the empty class set it equal to $1$. Centers of metric covers are in $\mathcal F$; bracket endpoints need not be.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.after:
Let $m\ge1$, let $S=(z_1,\ldots,z_m)$ be a fixed sample in a measurable space $\mathcal X$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty finite or countable class of measurable real functions such that the displayed supremum is finite and measurable on the finite sign space. Let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m$ be independent uniform signs. The **one-sided empirical Rademacher complexity** is

$$\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal F):=\frac1m\,\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i f(z_i).$$

There is no absolute value in this definition and $0$ need not belong to $\mathcal F$. It differs from the absolute-value complexity $m^{-1}\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|\sum_i\sigma_i f(z_i)|$.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.after:
Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let $\mathcal F$ be a class of measurable real-valued functions on it. The **subgraph** of $f\in\mathcal F$ is

$$C_f:=\{(x,t)\in\mathcal X\times\mathbb R:t<f(x)\}.$$

It is measurable in $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$: the coordinate lifts are measurable by [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]], their difference is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and its strict negative set is measurable by [[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]]. The class $\mathcal F$ is a **VC-subgraph class** when the set family $\mathcal C_{\mathcal F}:=\{C_f:f\in\mathcal F\}$ has finite VC index as defined in [[def-vc-class-of-sets-and-index]]. For nonempty $\mathcal F$, write $d(\mathcal F)$ for the greatest size of a finite shattered set (zero if none is shattered) and

$$V(\mathcal F):=d(\mathcal F)+1,$$

equivalently the least positive integer $V$ for which no $V$-point set is shattered. If no finite such integer exists, set $V=+\infty$. The empty class is treated separately and assigned index $V=0$ by convention. Thus for every nonempty finite-index class, the VC dimension is exactly $V-1$.

A **measurable envelope** of $\mathcal F$ is a nonnegative measurable function $F$ on $\mathcal X$ such that $|f(x)|\le F(x)$ for every $f\in\mathcal F$ and $x\in\mathcal X$. In an $L^r(Q)$ assertion, changing $F$ on a $Q$-null set does not change its norm or the distances in that assertion.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $n\ge1$, let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID observations with law $P$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a finite nonempty class of measurable functions $f:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$. For every $\epsilon>0$,

$$P\left(\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|P_nf-Pf|\ge\epsilon\right)\le2|\mathcal F|e^{-2n\epsilon^2}.$$

Here $P_nf=n^{-1}\sum_i f(Z_i)$ and $Pf=\int f\,dP$. The proof uses only scalar exponential moments and finite independence; it does not assume the Axiom of Choice.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $n\ge1$, let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID observations with law $P$, and let $Z_1',\ldots,Z_n'$ be an independent IID copy. Let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n$ be independent uniform signs, independent of both samples. Let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty countable class of measurable $P$-integrable real functions. Assume the two suprema below are finite almost surely. If $\Phi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ is finite, convex, and nondecreasing, then

$$\mathbb E\Phi\!\left(\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\left|\sum_{i=1}^n(f(Z_i)-Pf)\right|\right)\le \mathbb E\Phi\!\left(2\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\left|\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i f(Z_i)\right|\right).$$

The same statement holds for an uncountable class when a specified countable subclass gives the same three displayed suprema almost surely for the data, copy, and signs. This is an expectation inequality only; a tail form requires separate assumptions.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty subset of a pseudometric space $(T,d)$, with covering and packing numbers as in [[def-covering-packing-bracketing-number-and-metric-entropy]]. For every $\epsilon>0$,

$$N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)\le D(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)\le N(\epsilon/2,\mathcal F,d).$$

The packing convention is strict separation $d(f,g)>\epsilon$; covers use closed balls of radius at most $\epsilon$ centered in $\mathcal F$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $m\ge1$, let $z_1,\ldots,z_m$ be fixed, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty finite class of real-valued functions on their domain. For each $i$, let $\Phi_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $|\Phi_i(x)-\Phi_i(y)|\le L|x-y|$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb R$, with a common $L\ge0$. Then

$$\frac1m\,\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i\Phi_i(f(z_i))\le L\,\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal F).$$

Equivalently, the unnormalized left expectation is at most $L$ times the unnormalized one-sided supremum on the right.

The same holds for a countable class when both suprema are finite for every sign vector. No condition $\Phi_i(0)=0$ is required; additive constants cancel because the proof compares coordinate differences.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $\mathcal C$ be a nonempty class of measurable subsets of a measurable space, with finite VC index $V$ as in [[def-vc-class-of-sets-and-index]]. Let $Q$ be a probability measure, $1\le r<\infty$, and $0<\delta<1$. Put $K:=3e^2/(e-1)$. Then

$$N(\delta,\mathcal C,L^r(Q))\le\left[K\delta^{-r}\log\left(\frac{3e}{\delta^r}\right)\right]^{V-1}.$$

For sets, $\|\mathbf1_C-\mathbf1_D\|_{Q,r}=Q(C\triangle D)^{1/r}$. In the case $V=1$, the exponent is zero and the class consists of one set modulo equality, so the bound is $N=1$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $m\ge1$, let $z_1,\ldots,z_m$ be fixed, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty finite class of real-valued functions on their domain. For each $i$, suppose $|\Phi_i(x)-\Phi_i(y)|\le L|x-y|$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb R$, with a common $L\ge0$, and $\Phi_i(0)=0$. Then

$$\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\left|\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i\Phi_i(f(z_i))\right|\le2L\,\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\left|\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i f(z_i)\right|.$$

The same holds for a countable class when the two suprema are finite for every sign vector. This is the absolute-value theorem; its factor $2$ is separate from the factor $2$ in independent-process symmetrization.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,Q)$ be a probability space, let $1\le r<\infty$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty VC-subgraph class of measurable real functions with finite VC index $V$. Suppose a measurable envelope $F$ satisfies $|f(x)|\le F(x)$ for every $f\in\mathcal F$ and $x\in\mathcal X$, and

$$0<\|F\|_{Q,r}:=\left(\int F^r\,dQ\right)^{1/r}<\infty.$$

For every $0<\epsilon<1$, put $K_0:=3e^2/(e-1)$ and $K:=4K_0$. Then

$$N\!\left(\epsilon\|F\|_{Q,r},\mathcal F,L^r(Q)\right)\le\left[K(2/\epsilon)^r\log\!\left(3e(2/\epsilon)^r\right)\right]^{V-1}\le\left(\frac{A}{\epsilon}\right)^{ArV},\qquad A:=12eK+2.$$

The exponent in the first bound is the finite-r logarithmic form. No Axiom of Choice or Countable Choice is used in this proof.

changes.heading: Example
changes.after: Let $\mathcal X=\{0,1\}$ with $P(\{0\})=P(\{1\})=1/2$. Let $Z\sim P$, and take the two-function class $\mathcal F=\{f_0,f_1\}$ with $f_0(x)=0$ and $f_1(x)=x$.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.after:
Use the empirical-measure convention of [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]]: for iid observations $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ with common law $P$, $P_nf=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i)$ and $Pf=\int f\,dP$. Let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty class of measurable real-valued functions with a nonnegative measurable integrable envelope $F$, meaning $|f|\le F$ $P$-almost surely for every $f\in\mathcal F$ and $PF<\infty$. It is **pointwise measurable** if there is a countable subclass $\mathcal F_0$ such that every $f\in\mathcal F$ is the pointwise limit of a sequence from $\mathcal F_0$. For a pointwise-measurable class, dominated convergence [[thm-dominated-convergence]] gives $Pf_k\to Pf$ along the approximating sequence, and finite empirical averages converge pointwise, so the supremum defining the uniform law is determined by $\mathcal F_0$. The class is **$P$-Glivenko–Cantelli** if

$$\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|P_nf-Pf|\longrightarrow0$$

in probability. It is **strongly $P$-Glivenko–Cantelli** if the same convergence holds almost surely. For an uncountable class with a countable pointwise-dense subclass, the supremum is interpreted using outer probability unless the chosen version makes it measurable. For a pointwise-measurable class the supremum is determined by the countable subclass and is measurable. That subclass has a common conull envelope bound, so the supremum is finite almost surely; after choosing a real-valued version, almost-sure convergence implies convergence in probability by [[thm-almost-sure-convergence-implies-convergence-in-probability]].

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid with law $P$, and let $\mathcal L$ be a nonempty class of measurable integrable loss functions $\ell$ such that $\inf_{\ell\in\mathcal L}P\ell$ is finite. Define population risk $R(\ell)=P\ell$ and empirical risk $R_n(\ell)=P_n\ell$. Suppose $\widehat\ell\in\mathcal L$ satisfies the approximate-minimization inequality

$$R_n(\widehat\ell)\le \inf_{\ell\in\mathcal L}R_n(\ell)+\eta$$

for some $\eta\ge0$. On the event

$$\sup_{\ell\in\mathcal L}|R_n(\ell)-R(\ell)|\le\epsilon,$$

one has

$$R(\widehat\ell)\le\inf_{\ell\in\mathcal L}R(\ell)+2\epsilon+\eta.$$

No existence of an exact empirical minimizer is required. The empirical averages use [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]].

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law $P$, and let $\mathcal G$ be a nonempty countable class of measurable real functions with a nonnegative measurable envelope $H$, so $|g|\le H$ $P$-almost everywhere for every $g\in\mathcal G$, and $0<\|H\|_{P,2}<\infty$. Use $\mathbb G_n(g)=\sqrt n(P_ng-Pg)$ as in [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]]. Suppose that for some integer $q_0\ge1$ there are nested finite partitions $\Pi_q$ of $\mathcal G$, for all $q\ge q_0$, with $m_q$ nonempty cells. For each cell $C\in\Pi_q$ choose a representative $\pi_q(C)\in C$ and define its pointwise oscillation

$$\Delta_{q,C}(x)=\sup_{g,h\in C}|g(x)-h(x)|.$$

Assume $\Delta_{q,C}$ is measurable, $0\le\Delta_{q,C}\le2H$ $P$-almost everywhere, and $\|\Delta_{q,C}\|_{P,2}\le2^{-q}\|H\|_{P,2}$. If $C'\in\Pi_{q+1}$ is contained in $C\in\Pi_q$, then $\Delta_{q+1,C'}\le\Delta_{q,C}$ pointwise by definition. Put

$$L_q=1+\log(2m_q),\qquad a_q=\frac{2^{-q}\|H\|_{P,2}}{\sqrt{L_{q+1}}},\qquad M_{\mathcal G}=\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}\|g\|_{P,2}.$$

The refinement property gives $m_{q+1}\ge m_q$, so $a_q$ is nonincreasing.

There is a universal constant $C<\infty$ such that

$$\mathbb E\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}|\mathbb G_n(g)|\le C\left[(M_{\mathcal G}+2^{-q_0}\|H\|_{P,2})\sqrt{L_{q_0}}+\|H\|_{P,2}\sum_{q>q_0}2^{-q}\sqrt{L_q}+\sqrt n\,P\!\left(H\mathbf1_{\{H>\sqrt n a_{q_0}/2\}}\right)\right].$$

This is a local maximal estimate: the nested partitions and their oscillation bounds are hypotheses. Empirical-process notation uses [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]].

changes.heading: Definition
changes.after:
For a class $\mathcal H$ of measurable real functions under a probability measure $Q$, an **envelope** $H$ means a nonnegative measurable function with $|h|\le H$ $Q$-almost surely for every $h\in\mathcal H$. Cauchy–Schwarz [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]] gives $QH\le\|H\|_{Q,2}<\infty$ when $H\in L^2(Q)$.

Let $(S,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space, let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law $P$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty class of measurable real-valued functions with a nonnegative measurable envelope $F$ satisfying $PF^2<\infty$. A class is **pointwise measurable** if it has a countable subclass $\mathcal F_0$ such that for each $f\in\mathcal F$ there is a sequence in $\mathcal F_0$ converging pointwise to $f$. Write $\mathbb G_n(f)=\sqrt n(P_nf-Pf)$ using [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]], and put

$$\rho_P(f,g)=\{P[(f-g)-P(f-g)]^2\}^{1/2}.$$

This is a pseudometric: distinct functions can have zero distance when their centered difference vanishes $P$-almost surely. The empirical process is **asymptotically equicontinuous in probability** with respect to $\rho_P$ if for every $\eta>0$,

$$\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\limsup_{n\to\infty}P^*\left(\sup_{f,g\in\mathcal F:\,\rho_P(f,g)<\delta}|\mathbb G_n(f)-\mathbb G_n(g)|>\eta\right)=0.$$

Here $P^*(A)=\inf\{P(B): A\subseteq B,\ B\in\mathcal A\}$ is outer probability; bounded nonmeasurable functionals are handled by the corresponding outer expectation $E^*Y=\inf\{EY':Y'\text{ measurable and }Y'\ge Y\}$. For a pointwise-measurable class these conventions agree with ordinary probability whenever the displayed supremum is measurable.

Write $\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$ for the bounded real-valued functions on the index set $\mathcal F$, with norm $\|z\|_{\mathcal F}=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|z(f)|$. The class is **$P$-Donsker** if $\mathbb G_n$, as a process in this space, converges weakly in the outer-expectation sense to a tight Borel law of a centered Gaussian process $\mathbb G_P$ with covariance

$$\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbb G_P(f),\mathbb G_P(g))=P[(f-Pf)(g-Pg)].$$

Here outer weak convergence means $E^*H(\mathbb G_n)\to EH(\mathbb G_P)$ for every bounded uniformly continuous real function $H$ on $\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$; the outer expectation is the infimum of expectations of measurable majorants. The law is tight in the sense of [[def-tight-family-of-probability-measures]]. Finite-dimensional convergence means weak convergence of the vector of process values at every finite list of indices, as in [[def-convergence-in-distribution-of-random-elements]].

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $(T,d)$ be a nonempty pseudometric space that is totally bounded in the following sense: for every $r>0$ there is a finite set $E_r\subseteq T$ such that $T\subseteq\bigcup_{e\in E_r}\{t\in T:d(t,e)\le r\}$. Its diameter is $D:=\sup_{s,t\in T}d(s,t)<\infty$. For each $t\in T$, let $X_t$ be a real random variable. Assume the process is separable: a specified countable dense subset $T_0\subseteq T$, equipped with a fixed listing, has the property that the supremum of every process increment over $T$ equals its supremum over $T_0$ almost surely. Suppose all increments are centered and sub-Gaussian with their $d$-scale, meaning that for every $s,t\in T$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R$,

$$\mathbb E\exp\{\lambda(X_s-X_t)\}\le\exp\{\lambda^2d(s,t)^2/2\}.$$

If

$$\int_0^D\sqrt{\log N(\epsilon,T,d)}\,d\epsilon<\infty,$$

where $N(\epsilon,T,d)$ is the least number of closed $d$-balls of radius $\epsilon$ covering $T$ ([[def-covering-packing-bracketing-number-and-metric-entropy]]), then for every $t_0\in T$,

$$\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}|X_t-X_{t_0}|\le C\int_0^D\sqrt{\log N(\epsilon,T,d)}\,d\epsilon$$

for a universal constant $C$. If $D=0$, the integral and the supremum are both zero.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after: Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law $P$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty pointwise-measurable class of measurable real functions with a nonnegative integrable envelope $F$. Suppose $N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^1(P))<\infty$ for every $\epsilon>0$. Then $\mathcal F$ is $P$-Glivenko–Cantelli: $\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|P_nf-Pf|\to0$ in probability. If Countable Choice is assumed, then the stronger conclusion holds that this convergence is almost sure. The terms $P_n$, $P$, and the outer-probability convention are those of [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]], and the class notion is [[def-glivenko-cantelli-class]].

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
For a class $\mathcal H$ of measurable real functions under a probability measure $Q$, an **envelope** $H$ means a nonnegative measurable function with $|h|\le H$ $Q$-almost surely for every $h\in\mathcal H$. Cauchy–Schwarz [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]] gives $QH\le\|H\|_{Q,2}<\infty$ when $H\in L^2(Q)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law $P$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty pointwise-measurable class of measurable functions with a nonnegative envelope $F$ satisfying $PF^2<\infty$. Assume $0<\|F\|_{P,2}<\infty$ and

$$\int_0^1\sqrt{\log N_{[]}\bigl(\epsilon\|F\|_{P,2},\mathcal F,L^2(P)\bigr)}\,d\epsilon<\infty.$$

Use the empirical process $\mathbb G_n$ and semimetric $\rho_P$ from [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]] and [[def-donsker-class-and-asymptotic-equicontinuity]]. Then $\mathbb G_n$ is asymptotically equicontinuous in probability with respect to $\rho_P$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
For a class $\mathcal H$ of measurable real functions under a probability measure $Q$, an **envelope** $H$ means a nonnegative measurable function with $|h|\le H$ $Q$-almost surely for every $h\in\mathcal H$. Cauchy–Schwarz [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]] gives $QH\le\|H\|_{Q,2}<\infty$ when $H\in L^2(Q)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law $P$ on a measurable space, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty pointwise-measurable class of measurable real functions with a measurable envelope $F\ge0$ satisfying $PF^2<\infty$. If $\|F\|_{P,2}=0$, the empirical process is the zero process almost surely. Otherwise assume

$$\int_0^1\sqrt{\log N_{[]}\bigl(\epsilon\|F\|_{P,2},\mathcal F,L^2(P)\bigr)}\,d\epsilon<\infty,$$

where $N_{[]}(r,\mathcal F,L^2(P))$ is the least number of measurable brackets $[l,u]$ with $l\le f\le u$ $P$-almost surely and $\|u-l\|_{P,2}\le r$ that cover $\mathcal F$. Then $\mathcal F$ is $P$-Donsker in the sense of [[def-donsker-class-and-asymptotic-equicontinuity]]: the empirical process $\mathbb G_n=\sqrt n(P_n-P)$ converges weakly in outer expectation in $\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$ to a tight centered Gaussian bridge with covariance

$$K(f,g)=P[(f-Pf)(g-Pg)].$$

The $L^2(P)$ bracketing number and width use [[def-covering-packing-bracketing-number-and-metric-entropy]].

changes.heading: Statement refuted
changes.after: The assertion that pointwise strong laws for every member of a class imply a uniform law of large numbers is false without a class-separability or entropy hypothesis.

changes.heading: Example
changes.after:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $P$ be uniform probability on $[0,1]$, let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law $P$, and let
$$\mathcal F=\{f_t:t\in[0,1]\},\qquad f_t(x)=\mathbf1_{[0,t]}(x).$$
Then $\mathcal F$ is strongly $P$-Glivenko–Cantelli:
$$\sup_{0\le t\le1}|P_nf_t-Pf_t|\longrightarrow0\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

changes.heading: Example
changes.after:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X_i$ be iid Uniform$[0,1]$, $F_n(t)=P_n([0,t])$, and $F(t)=t$. The empirical process $\mathbb G_n(t)=\sqrt n(F_n(t)-F(t))$, $0\le t\le1$, converges weakly in outer expectation in $\ell^\infty([0,1])$ to the standard Brownian bridge: the tight centered Gaussian process $B$ with covariance
$$E[B(s)B(t)]=\min(s,t)-st.$$
