Assume the uniform law $\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}|P_n\ell_\theta-M(\theta)|\to_P0$, and let $\hat\theta_n\in\Theta$ be a measurable approximate maximizer with $\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}P_n\ell_\theta-P_n\ell_{\hat\theta_n}\to_P0$.

Let $S_\theta(x)=\nabla_\theta\ell_\theta(x)$ be continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $\theta^*$. Assume $\mathbb E_PS_{\theta^*}=0$, $\mathbb E_P\|S_{\theta^*}\|_2^2<\infty$, and set $J=\mathbb E_P[S_{\theta^*}S_{\theta^*}^{T}]$. Suppose $H=\mathbb E_P[\nabla_\theta S_{\theta^*}]$ is nonsingular, $D(\theta):=\mathbb E_P[\nabla_\theta S_\theta]$ exists and is continuous at $\theta^*$, and for every sufficiently small fixed $\delta>0$,

$$\sup_{\|\theta-\theta^*\|_2\le\delta}\|P_n\nabla_\theta S_\theta-D(\theta)\|_{op}\to_P0,$$

where $\|A\|_{op}:=\sup_{\|v\|_2\le1}\|Av\|_2$. Finally assume the approximate score equation $\sqrt n\,P_nS_{\hat\theta_n}=o_P(1)$. Then

$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta^*)\Rightarrow N_d\!\left(0,H^{-1}JH^{-T}\right).$$

The covariance is the sandwich matrix formed from the Hessian $H$ under $P$ and the score second moment $J$ under $P$. The theorem does not assert that it equals the inverse Fisher information of the fitted model.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.after:
Let $d\ge1$ and let $I$ be an invertible real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. Define $\|v\|_I:=\sqrt{v^TIv}$ for $v\in\mathbb R^d$. For a nonempty set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ define

$$d_I(x,C):=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|_I.$$

This is the distance from $x$ to $C$ in the norm induced by $I$. The definition uses an infimum; attainment is proved separately when a later result requires it.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $d\ge1$, let $I$ be an invertible real symmetric matrix such that $v^TIv>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^d$, let $z\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty and closed in the Euclidean metric. Define $q_z(h):=z^Th-\tfrac12h^TIh$. Then there is a constant $\lambda>0$ such that $h^TIh\ge\lambda\|h\|_2^2$ for all $h$, $q_z$ attains its maximum on $C$, and

$$\sup_{h\in C}q_z(h)=\tfrac12z^TI^{-1}z-\tfrac12d_I^2(I^{-1}z,C).$$

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Let $d\ge1$, let $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, and let $\theta_0\in\Theta_0$. Assume the full-model parameter set $\Theta$ is open in $\mathbb R^d$, so $\theta_0$ is interior for the QMD model. Under $P_{\theta_0}$, let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID and let $\ell_n(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n\log p_\theta(X_i)$ be their sample log-likelihood. Define local parameter sets $C_n:=\sqrt n(\Theta-\theta_0)$ and $C_{0n}:=\sqrt n(\Theta_0-\theta_0)$. Assume the model is QMD at $\theta_0$ as in [[def-qmd-path]], and write $I:=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$ for its Fisher information; assume $I$ is positive definite, meaning $v^TIv>0$ for every nonzero $v$. Suppose $C_n$ and $C_{0n}$ are closed in the Euclidean metric (their complements are open), contain $0$, and converge locally to nonempty closed convex cones $C$ and $C_0$ with $C_0\subseteq C$. A cone contains $0$ and is closed under multiplication by every nonnegative scalar; convex means that the set contains the line segment between each pair of its points. Local convergence means that, for every $R>0$, there are $\delta_{n,R}\to0$ such that every point of $C_n\cap\overline B_2(0,R)$ or $C\cap\overline B_2(0,R)$ is within $\delta_{n,R}$ in Euclidean distance of the other set, and likewise for $C_{0n}$ and $C_0$. Here a point $x$ is within $\delta$ of a set $A$ when $\inf_{a\in A}\|x-a\|_2\le\delta$.

Assume a uniform local quadratic likelihood expansion: for $h\in C_n$,

$$\ell_n(\theta_0+h/\sqrt n)-\ell_n(\theta_0)=h^TZ_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+r_n(h),$$

where $Z_n\Rightarrow Z\sim N_d(0,I)$ under $P_{\theta_0}$ and, for every $R>0$, $\sup\{|r_n(h)|:h\in C_n,\ \|h\|_2\le R\}\to_P0$. Assume the full and null local log-likelihoods attain maxima at $\hat h_n\in C_n$ and $\hat h_{0n}\in C_{0n}$ and that both maximizer sequences are tight, meaning that for every $\eta>0$ some $R<\infty$ makes the limiting upper probability of either norm exceeding $R$ at most $\eta$. For

$$T_n:=2\left[\sup_{h\in C_n}\{\ell_n(\theta_0+h/\sqrt n)-\ell_n(\theta_0)\}-\sup_{h\in C_{0n}}\{\ell_n(\theta_0+h/\sqrt n)-\ell_n(\theta_0)\}\right],$$

the likelihood-ratio statistic satisfies

$$T_n\Rightarrow d_I^2(I^{-1}Z,C_0)-d_I^2(I^{-1}Z,C),$$

where $d_I$ is the Fisher-information distance of [[def-fisher-information-metric-distance]]. QMD alone is not asserted to imply the uniform expansion or tightness hypotheses.

changes.heading: Statement refuted
changes.after: For an integer $n\ge1$, iid $X_i\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,\theta]$ with fixed $\theta>0$ have an endpoint MLE with a nonzero root-$n$ fluctuation: $\sqrt n(\theta-X_{(n)})$ does not converge in probability to zero.

changes.heading: Example
changes.after: For $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ iid with density $p_\theta(x)=\theta^{-1}\mathbf1_{[0,\theta]}(x)$, $\theta>0$, the likelihood is maximized almost surely at the sample endpoint $X_{(n)}=\max_iX_i$. The error has the nonregular limit $n(\theta-X_{(n)})\Rightarrow\operatorname{Exp}(1/\theta)$, where the parameter denotes the exponential rate.

changes.heading: Example
changes.after: Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X_i$ be iid $N(\mu,1)$, let the full parameter space be $\Theta=\mathbb R$, and test $H_0:\mu\le0$ against the full model at the boundary value $\mu=0$. The likelihood-ratio statistic converges to $(G\vee0)^2$, where $G\sim N(0,1)$; by [[def-chi-square-law]] this is $\tfrac12\chi_0^2+\tfrac12\chi_1^2$, not the ordinary $\chi_1^2$ law.

changes.heading: Example
changes.after: Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix $\tau>0$ with $\tau^2\ne1$. Let the data law be $P=N(0,\tau^2)$, but fit the location model $p_\theta=N(\theta,1)$ over $\Theta=[-1,1]$. Since every fitted law has variance $1$ while $P$ has variance $\tau^2\ne1$, $P$ differs from every fitted law. The pseudo-true parameter is $0$, and the MLE is asymptotically normal with variance $\tau^2$; the fitted model's score second moment at $0$ is $1$.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: For a Borel probability density version f on R^d and iid X_1,...,X_n with law f dλ_d, define the pointwise target ψ_x(f)=f(x) and, for a Borel K∈L^1(R^d) with ∫K=1 and h>0, the indexed estimator fhat_h(x)=(nh^d)^−1 Σ_i K((x−X_i)/h). Pointwise targets depend on the selected density version; no law-identifiability is asserted without regularity.
changes.after:
Fix an integer $d\ge1$. A **density version** on $\mathbb R^d$ is a Borel
function $f:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ with
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\,d\lambda_d=1.$$
Write $P_f=f\,d\lambda_d$ for its probability law
([[def-measure-with-density]]). Let $\Theta$ be any set of such density
versions. For sample size $n\ge1$, the iid experiment has data space
$$\left((\mathbb R^d)^n,\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)\right)$$
and sampling law $P_f^{\otimes n}$ at parameter $f\in\Theta$
([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]],
[[def-independent-random-elements]],
[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).
The pointwise target at $x\in\mathbb R^d$ is the estimand
$$\psi_x(f)=f(x):\Theta\to\mathbb R$$
([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).

A **normalized kernel** is a Borel function $K:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with
$K\in L^1(\lambda_d)$ and $\int K\,d\lambda_d=1$. It may be signed. For
bandwidth $h>0$ and observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, the kernel density estimate
is the indexed family
$$\widehat f_h(x)=\frac1{nh^d}\sum_{i=1}^n K\!\left(\frac{x-X_i}{h}\right),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For each fixed $x$, this is intended as a real-valued estimator of $\psi_x$;
the next local lemma supplies its measurability
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]).

Assuming $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, if $K$ is pointwise nonnegative the estimate
is a probability density for every sample, as proved in
[[lem-nonnegative-kde-integrates-to-one]]. For a signed kernel the estimate
need not be nonnegative. Point evaluation depends on the selected density
version: this definition does not assert that $f\mapsto f(x)$ is
identifiable from the law $P_f$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: For fixed x∈R^d, a Borel kernel K, h>0 and n≥1, the map from the Borel sample space (R^d)^n to R given by (z_1,...,z_n)↦(nh^d)^−1 Σ_i K((x−z_i)/h) is Borel measurable.
changes.after:
Fix $x\in\mathbb R^d$, $h>0$, $n\ge1$, and a Borel normalized kernel $K$.
The evaluation map
$$T_x:(\mathbb R^d)^n\to\mathbb R,\qquad (z_1,\ldots,z_n)\mapsto\frac1{nh^d}\sum_{i=1}^nK\!\left(\frac{x-z_i}{h}\right)$$
is measurable for the finite product Borel sigma-algebra. Hence it is a
statistic on the iid density experiment.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: For Borel K, the map ((z_1,...,z_n),x)↦(nh^d)^−1Σ_i K((x−z_i)/h) is Borel on (R^d)^n×R^d.
changes.after:
For a Borel normalized kernel $K$, $h>0$ and $n\ge1$, the map
$$Q_h:(\mathbb R^d)^n\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R,\qquad (z_1,\ldots,z_n,x)\mapsto\frac1{nh^d}\sum_{i=1}^n K\!\left(\frac{x-z_i}{h}\right)$$
is Borel measurable for the finite product Borel sigma-algebra.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: If K is pointwise nonnegative and has Lebesgue integral one, then for every finite sample and h>0 the kernel estimate is nonnegative and its integral over R^d equals one.
changes.after:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $K\ge0$ pointwise and
$\int K\,d\lambda_d=1$, then for every sample $z_1,\ldots,z_n\in\mathbb R^d$
and bandwidth $h>0$, the function
$$x\mapsto\frac1{nh^d}\sum_{i=1}^nK\!\left(\frac{x-z_i}{h}\right)$$
is nonnegative and has Lebesgue integral one.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: If f:R^d→[0,∞) is twice continuously differentiable, ∫f dλ_d=1, and sup_x ||D²f(x)||_op<∞, then f is bounded on R^d.
changes.after:
Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ be a density version with all partial
derivatives through order two existing and continuous, so
$\int f\,d\lambda_d=1$. If its Hessian satisfies
$H:=\sup_x\|D^2f(x)\|_{op}<\infty$, then $f$ is bounded.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Assume ACω, f∈W^{2,2}(R^d), K∈L^1(R^d), ∫K=1, ∫u_jK(u)du=0 for every j, and M₂(K)=∫|K(u)| ||u||²du<∞. Define S_hf=∫K(u)f(·−hu)du as an L² class. Then ||S_hf−f||_2≤(h²/2)M₂(K)||D²f||_{2,F}, where ||D²f||_{2,F}²=Σ_{j,k}||∂_{jk}f||_2².
changes.after:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $f$ be a density version in
$W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d)$, and let $K$ be a normalized Borel kernel with
$K\in L^1$, $\int u_jK(u)\,du=0$ for every $j$, and
$$M_2(K):=\int_{\mathbb R^d}|K(u)|\,\|u\|^2du<\infty.$$
Define the convolution $S_hf=\int K(u)f(\cdot-hu)du$ as an $L^2$ equivalence
class. With
$$\|D^2f\|_{2,F}^2:=\sum_{j,k=1}^d\|\partial_{jk}f\|_{L^2}^2,$$
one has, for every $h>0$,
$$\|S_hf-f\|_{L^2}\le\frac{h^2}{2}M_2(K)\,\|D^2f\|_{2,F}.$$

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Assume ACω; X_1,...,X_n are iid with nonnegative Borel density version f on R^d; K:R^d→R is Borel, K∈L^1∩L^2, ∫K=1, ∫u_jK(u)du=0 and ∫|K(u)| ||u||²du<∞; f is C² with bounded continuous Hessian; x is fixed; and h↓0. With μ_jk=∫u_ju_kK(u)du, E[fhat_h(x)]−f(x)=(h²/2)Σ_{j,k}μ_jk ∂_{jk}f(x)+o(h²).
changes.after:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid with a Borel
probability density version $f$ on $\mathbb R^d$. Let
$K:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be Borel with $K\in L^1\cap L^2$,
$\int K(u)du=1$, $\int u_jK(u)du=0$ for each $j$, and
$\int|K(u)|\|u\|^2du<\infty$. Suppose $f$ has continuous second partial
derivatives and a globally bounded continuous Hessian. At each fixed
$x\in\mathbb R^d$, as $h\downarrow0$,
$$\mathbb E\widehat f_h(x)-f(x) =\frac{h^2}{2}\sum_{j,k=1}^d\mu_{jk}\,\partial_{jk}f(x)+o(h^2), \qquad \mu_{jk}:=\int_{\mathbb R^d}u_ju_kK(u)du.$$
Here $r(h)=o(h^2)$ means $r(h)/h^2\to0$ as $h\downarrow0$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Assume ACω; X_1,...,X_n are iid with bounded continuous density f on R^d; K:R^d→R is Borel with K∈L^1∩L^2 and ∫K=1; x is fixed; h↓0; and n h^d→∞. Then Var(fhat_h(x))=f(x)||K||_2²/(n h^d)+o((n h^d)^−1).
changes.after:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid with bounded
continuous Borel density version $f$ on $\mathbb R^d$. Let
$K:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be Borel, $K\in L^1\cap L^2$, and
$\int K(u)du=1$. For fixed $x\in\mathbb R^d$, along bandwidths $h=h_n>0$
with $h_n\to0$ and $nh_n^d\to\infty$,
$$\operatorname{Var}(\widehat f_{h_n}(x)) =\frac{f(x)\|K\|_2^2}{nh_n^d}+o((nh_n^d)^{-1}).$$

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Assume ACω; iid observations with density f∈W^{2,2}(R^d); K∈L^1∩L^2, ∫K=1, zero first moments and M₂(K)<∞. For every h>0, MISE(fhat_h)=E∫(fhat_h−f)²dλ_d≤(h⁴/4)M₂(K)²||D²f||_{2,F}²+||K||_2²/(n h^d). Hence h_n=n^−1/(d+4) gives MISE=O(n^−4/(d+4)); this is an upper rate only.
changes.after:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid with a Borel density
version $f\in W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d)$. Let $K:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be
Borel, $K\in L^1\cap L^2$, $\int K(u)du=1$,
$\int u_jK(u)du=0$ for every $j$, and
$M_2(K):=\int|K(u)|\|u\|^2du<\infty$. For every $h>0$ define
$$\operatorname{MISE}(\widehat f_h) :=\mathbb E\int_{\mathbb R^d}(\widehat f_h(x)-f(x))^2dx.$$
Then
$$\operatorname{MISE}(\widehat f_h) \le\frac{h^4}{4}M_2(K)^2\|D^2f\|_{2,F}^2+ \frac{\|K\|_2^2}{nh^d}.$$
In particular, $h_n=n^{-1/(d+4)}$ gives
$\operatorname{MISE}(\widehat f_{h_n})=O(n^{-4/(d+4)})$, where $O(n^{-4/(d+4)})$
means bounded by a finite constant times $n^{-4/(d+4)}$ for all sufficiently
large $n$. This is an upper rate under the displayed hypotheses; it is not a
minimax lower bound.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: For the d-dimensional standard Gaussian kernel, μ_jk=δ_jk and ||K||_2²=(4π)^−d/2, so the pointwise bias and variance leading constants reduce to h²Δf(x)/2 and f(x)(4π)^−d/2/(n h^d).
changes.after:
For $d\ge1$, take the standard Gaussian kernel
$$K_d(u)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}e^{-\|u\|^2/2}.$$
Its second-moment matrix is $\mu_{jk}=\delta_{jk}$ and
$\|K_d\|_2^2=(4\pi)^{-d/2}$, where $\delta_{jk}$ is $1$ for $j=k$ and $0$
otherwise. Thus, under the pointwise theorem hypotheses,
$$\mathbb E\widehat f_h(x)-f(x)=\tfrac12h^2\Delta f(x)+o(h^2),\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\widehat f_h(x)) =\frac{f(x)}{nh^d}(4\pi)^{-d/2}+o((nh^d)^{-1}).$$
Here $\Delta f=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{jj}f$.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: If f is N_d(0,τ²I_d) and K is the standard Gaussian kernel, then E[fhat_h] is N_d(0,(τ²+h²)I_d); at every fixed h>0 this differs from f.
changes.after:
Let $\tau>0$ and
$$f_\tau(x)=(2\pi\tau^2)^{-d/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{\|x\|^2}{2\tau^2}\right),\qquad K_d(u)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}e^{-\|u\|^2/2}.$$
For every fixed bandwidth $h>0$,
$$\mathbb E\widehat f_h(x) =(2\pi(\tau^2+h^2))^{-d/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{\|x\|^2}{2(\tau^2+h^2)}\right).$$
Thus the expected estimate is the centered Gaussian density with covariance
$(\tau^2+h^2)I_d$, and at $x=0$ it is strictly smaller than $f(0)$.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: For the chosen density version f=1_[0,1], a standard Gaussian kernel and x=0, E[fhat_h(0)]→1/2 while f(0)=1 as h↓0, so the uncorrected estimator has nonvanishing boundary bias.
changes.after:
In one dimension, choose the Borel density version $f=\mathbf1_{[0,1]}$ and
the standard Gaussian kernel
$K(u)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-u^2/2}$. At the support boundary $x=0$,
$$\mathbb E\widehat f_h(0)=\int_{-1/h}^{0}K(u)du\longrightarrow\frac12 \qquad(h\downarrow0),$$
while the chosen target value is $f(0)=1$. Hence the uncorrected estimator
has limiting bias $-1/2$ at the boundary. The smoothness hypotheses of the
pointwise second-order bias theorem fail at $x=0$.

changes.before:
Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$
changes.after:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

changes.before:
Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$
changes.after:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: For a finite nondecreasing clamped knot vector on a bounded interval and degree p, recursively define the B-splines, their multiplicities and the piecewise-polynomial spline space; the accompanying theorem establishes their support, continuity, partition, and basis properties.
changes.after:
Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$, $n\ge p+1$, and $a<b$. A clamped knot vector is a nondecreasing finite sequence
$$\xi_1=\cdots=\xi_{p+1}=a<\xi_{p+2}\le\cdots\le\xi_n<\xi_{n+1}=\cdots=\xi_{n+p+1}=b,$$
with $\xi_j<\xi_{j+p+1}$ for every $1\le j\le n$. Empty interior ranges are omitted. The multiplicity $\mu(\eta)$ of an interior knot $\eta$ is its number of occurrences among $\xi_{p+2},\ldots,\xi_n$.

Write $\mathcal P_p$ for the real polynomials of degree at most $p$. The degree-$p$ spline space $S_{p,\xi}$ consists of functions that restrict to a member of $\mathcal P_p$ on each nonempty knot interval and whose derivatives through order $p-\mu(\eta)$ agree across each interior knot $\eta$. The convention $C^{-1}$ means that no matching condition is imposed. For this piecewise definition, take knot cells left-closed and right-open; at a knot with no matching condition, the value is the one from the cell on its right, and at $b$ use the left limit. Thus the function value at a discontinuous knot is specified.

For each degree $d\in\{0,\ldots,p\}$, the functions $B_{j,d,\xi}$ are indexed by $1\le j\le n+p-d$. Set
$$B_{j,0,\xi}(x)=\mathbf 1_{[\xi_j,\xi_{j+1})}(x),\qquad 1\le j\le n+p.$$
For $1\le d\le p$ and $1\le j\le n+p-d$, define recursively
$$B_{j,d,\xi}(x)=\frac{x-\xi_j}{\xi_{j+d}-\xi_j}B_{j,d-1,\xi}(x)+\frac{\xi_{j+d+1}-x}{\xi_{j+d+1}-\xi_{j+1}}B_{j+1,d-1,\xi}(x),$$
where a term with zero denominator is defined to be zero. For every degree $d$ and every allowed index $j$, set $B_{j,d,\xi}(b)$ equal to its left limit. In particular, the degree-$p$ family has indices $1\le j\le n$. Its basis and regularity properties are proved in [[thm-spline-polynomial-reproduction]].

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: On a bounded interval [a,b] and at distinct ordered knots t_1<...<t_r, r>=2, a natural cubic spline is a C^2 function that is polynomial of degree at most three between successive knots, has second derivative zero at the extreme knots, and is extended linearly on data-free end intervals.
changes.after: Let $[a,b]$ be a bounded interval and let $a\le t_1<\cdots<t_r\le b$ with $r\ge2$. A natural cubic spline with knots $t_1,\ldots,t_r$ is a $C^2$ function on $[a,b]$ that is a polynomial of degree at most three on every $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$, has second derivative zero at $t_1$ and $t_r$, and is extended linearly on $[a,t_1]$ and $[t_r,b]$ when those intervals are nonempty. The knots $t_j$ are the distinct breakpoints; repeated observations at the same input do not create additional knots.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: A local quasi-interpolant is a linear map from continuous L^q functions into the spline space that depends only on bounded local neighborhoods, reproduces P_l, and satisfies a mesh-uniform cellwise L^q stability bound.
changes.after:
Fix a bounded interval $[a,b]$, a degree $p\in\mathbb N_0$, an exponent $1\le q\le\infty$, an integer $0\le l\le p$, and a nonempty family $\mathcal T$ of clamped degree-$p$ knot meshes on $[a,b]$. A **mesh-uniform bounded local quasi-interpolant** is a family of real-linear maps $Q_\xi:C([a,b];\mathbb R)\to S_{p,\xi}$, one for each $\xi\in\mathcal T$, for which there are common constants $M\in\mathbb N$ and $0\le C_Q<\infty$ such that the following hold for every $\xi\in\mathcal T$ and every nonempty cell $I_m$ of its mesh: there is a neighborhood $J_{\xi,m}\subseteq[a,b]$ containing $I_m$ and formed from at most $M$ adjacent knot cells; each point of $[a,b]$ belongs to at most $M$ of the neighborhoods $J_{\xi,m}$; (i) if $f=g$ almost everywhere on $J_{\xi,m}$, then $Q_\xi f=Q_\xi g$ almost everywhere on $I_m$; (ii) $Q_\xi v=v$ for every $v\in\mathcal P_l$; and (iii) $\|Q_\xi f\|_{L^q(I_m)}\le C_Q\|f\|_{L^q(J_{\xi,m})}$. The constants $M$ and $C_Q$ are independent of $\xi$. The derivative and continuous-representative conventions for Sobolev inputs are those of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] and [[cor-one-dimensional-w-one-p-functions-have-absolutely-continuous-representatives]].

For a fixed mesh, the coefficient-functional formulation in Lyche–Manni–Speleers is one sufficient way to obtain these local stability and reproduction properties. Uniform constants in that construction give a family as defined here; this definition records the operator hypotheses used in the approximation proof.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: For lambda>0 and data with at least two distinct inputs in [a,b], the natural cubic smoothing spline is the minimizer of the squared empirical residual plus lambda times the integrated squared second derivative over W^{2,2}(a,b), using the continuous Sobolev representative.
changes.after:
Assume AC. Let $[a,b]$ be a bounded interval, let $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n\in([a,b]\times\mathbb R)^n$, assume at least two distinct input values, and let $\lambda>0$. For $g\in W^{2,2}(a,b)$ use its unique continuous representative on $[a,b]$ supplied by the one-dimensional Sobolev representative theorem. The natural cubic smoothing spline is the unique minimizer, whose existence and uniqueness are proved in [[thm-natural-cubic-smoothing-spline-exists-uniquely]], of
$$J(g)=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-g(x_i))^2+\lambda\int_a^b|D^2g(t)|^2\,dt.$$

The requirement of two distinct inputs is essential. The penalty is the squared $L^2$ norm of the second weak derivative; the data term uses the distinct-input interpolation convention in [[def-natural-cubic-spline]].

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: At r at least 2 strictly increasing knots and arbitrary real values there is a unique natural cubic interpolant, linear outside the extreme knots; its interior nodal second derivatives solve a positive-definite tridiagonal system.
changes.after:
Let $r\ge2$, $a\le x_1<\cdots<x_r\le b$, and $y_1,\ldots,y_r\in\mathbb R$. There is exactly one natural cubic spline $s$ on $[a,b]$ with $s(x_i)=y_i$ for each $i$. On each interval $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$ it is the cubic with endpoint values $y_i,y_{i+1}$ and endpoint second derivatives $M_i,M_{i+1}$, where $M_1=M_r=0$ and the interior values solve the positive-definite tridiagonal system
$$h_{i-1}M_{i-1}+2(h_{i-1}+h_i)M_i+h_iM_{i+1}=6\left(\frac{y_{i+1}-y_i}{h_i}-\frac{y_i-y_{i-1}}{h_{i-1}}\right),\quad 2\le i\le r-1,$$
with $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i>0$. The interpolant is linear outside $[x_1,x_r]$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: For a finite clamped knot vector, the recursively defined degree-p B-splines form a basis of the piecewise-polynomial space with continuity p-m at a knot of multiplicity m, and reproduce every polynomial of degree at most p.
changes.after: Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$ and let $\xi$ be a clamped knot vector as in [[def-b-spline-space-and-basis]]. The recursively defined degree-$p$ B-splines are nonnegative, are supported on $[\xi_j,\xi_{j+p+1}]$, and are piecewise polynomials of degree at most $p$. At a knot of multiplicity $\mu\le p$, each B-spline is $C^{p-\mu}$; multiplicity $p+1$ imposes no continuity requirement. On every nonempty knot interval $[\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$, the active functions $B_{m-p,p,\xi},\ldots,B_{m,p,\xi}$ form a basis of $\mathcal P_p$ and sum to one. Globally, the $n$ B-splines form a basis of $S_{p,\xi}$. In particular, every $q\in\mathcal P_p$ has a unique expansion $q=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jB_{j,p,\xi}$ on $[a,b]$.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: Given a fixed B-spline design vector and observed data, the series least-squares fit is the projection of the response vector onto the design column space; its defined target is the fitted training vector and its loss is squared empirical prediction error.
changes.after:
Let $p_K(x)=(B_{1,p,\xi}(x),\ldots,B_{K,p,\xi}(x))^T$ be a specified degree-$p$ B-spline basis on the data domain, and let $(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n$ be observed real-valued data. Form the design matrix $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times K}$ with row $p_K(X_i)^T$. The **series least-squares fitted training vector** is
$$\widehat{\mathbf g}_K=\Pi_{\operatorname{col}(P)}\mathbf Y,$$
the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)^T$ onto the column space of $P$. Conditional on the realized design, this is the fixed-design least-squares fitted vector of [[def-fixed-design-projection-estimator]]. Equivalently, it is $P\widehat\beta$ for any minimizer $\widehat\beta$ of $\|\mathbf Y-P\beta\|_2^2$; all such minimizers have the same fitted training vector. The training prediction loss relative to a specified target vector $\mathbf g_0=(g_0(X_1),\ldots,g_0(X_n))^T$ is $n^{-1}\|\widehat{\mathbf g}_K-\mathbf g_0\|_2^2$. This definition specifies training fitted values and makes no test-risk assertion.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: With lambda>0 and at least two distinct input locations, the variational problem defining the natural cubic smoothing spline has a unique minimizer; it is a natural cubic spline with knots at the distinct inputs and linear tails.
changes.after: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $[a,b]$, $\lambda>0$, and data $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ satisfy the hypotheses of [[def-natural-cubic-smoothing-spline]], with $r\ge2$ distinct inputs $t_1<\cdots<t_r$. Then $J$ has a unique minimizer over $W^{2,2}(a,b)$. It is the natural cubic spline with knots at $t_1,\ldots,t_r$, extended linearly to $a$ and $b$ where needed.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: For 0<=l<=p, 1<=q<=infinity, f in W^{l+1,q}, and a bounded local quasi-interpolant reproducing P_l, local and global L^q errors are bounded by a constant times the (l+1)-st power of the controlled local mesh size times ||D^{l+1}f||_q; on uniform meshes the cellwise L^2 projector supplies the q=2 spline rate.
changes.after:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$, $0\le l\le p$, and $1\le q\le\infty$. Let $\mathcal T$ be a nonempty family of clamped degree-$p$ knot meshes on $[a,b]$, and let $(Q_\xi)_{\xi\in\mathcal T}$ be a mesh-uniform bounded local quasi-interpolant family as in [[def-local-spline-quasi-interpolant]], with common constants $M$ and $C_Q$. Fix $\xi\in\mathcal T$, write $Q=Q_\xi$, and let $f\in W^{l+1,q}(a,b;\mathbb R)$ with its continuous Sobolev representative. For each nonempty cell $I_m$ of $\xi$, let $J_m$ be its corresponding neighborhood and let $h_m$ be the largest cell length in $J_m$. Then
$$\|f-Qf\|_{L^q(I_m)}\le (1+C_Q)\frac{M^{l+1}}{l!}h_m^{l+1}\|D^{l+1}f\|_{L^q(J_m)}.$$
Writing $h=\max_m h_m$, the global bound is
$$\|f-Qf\|_{L^q([a,b])}\le (1+C_Q)\frac{M^{l+1+1/q}}{l!}h^{l+1}\|D^{l+1}f\|_{L^q([a,b])},$$
where $1/q=0$ for $q=\infty$. In particular, on a uniform mesh with interior knots of multiplicity $p+1$, the cellwise $L^2$ projector onto $\mathcal P_p$ is a local quasi-interpolant and gives the order-$h^s$ approximation bound for every integer $1\le s\le p+1$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: For iid real-valued pairs with a supplied Borel conditional-law kernel, a supplied Borel conditional mean with finite conditional first absolute moment, conditional variance at most Delta, and L^2(P_X) spline approximation error at most C^2K^{-2gamma}, expected empirical training-vector loss is at most Delta K/n+C^2K^{-2gamma}.
changes.after:
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $n,K\ge1$, and let $Z_i=(X_i,Y_i)$, $1\le i\le n$, be iid random elements of $([a,b]\times\mathbb R,\mathcal B([a,b])\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$. Write $P_X$ for the law of $X_1$ and suppose the one-observation law is $P_X(dx)\kappa(x,dy)$ for a supplied Borel probability kernel $\kappa$ from $([a,b],\mathcal B([a,b]))$ to $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$. Assume a Borel function $g_0:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is supplied such that, for $P_X$-almost every $x$, $\int |y|\,\kappa(x,dy)<\infty$, $g_0(x)=\int y\,\kappa(x,dy)$, and $\int (y-g_0(x))^2\,\kappa(x,dy)\le\Delta$ for a finite $\Delta\ge0$. Let $p_K:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^K$ be a fixed Borel $K$-dimensional spline basis and assume a deterministic $\bar\beta_K\in\mathbb R^K$, a constant $C\ge0$, and $\gamma>0$ satisfy
$$\int_{[a,b]}\{g_0(x)-p_K(x)^T\bar\beta_K\}^2\,P_X(dx)\le C^2K^{-2\gamma}.$$
Then, with the fitted training vector $\widehat{\mathbf g}_K$ from [[def-series-spline-least-squares]] and $\mathbf g_0=(g_0(X_1),\ldots,g_0(X_n))^T$,
$$E\left[\frac1n\|\widehat{\mathbf g}_K-\mathbf g_0\|_2^2\right]\le\frac{\Delta K}{n}+C^2K^{-2\gamma}.$$
This is expected empirical training-design loss.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: For a univariate W^{s,2} regression target on a compact interval supporting the design law with bounded density, degree p>=s-1 and a uniform full-multiplicity knot mesh of dimension K=(p+1)J, expected empirical training-vector risk is O(n^{-2s/(2s+1)}) when J is comparable to n^{1/(2s+1)}.
changes.after:
Assume AC. Let $a<b$ and let $X,Y$ be real random variables on a common probability space with $E|Y|<\infty$. Choose a regular conditional law $Q(x,dy)$ of $Y$ given $X=x$, and let $g_0$ be the selected Borel regression-function version from [[def-regression-target-version]]. Suppose $P_X$ is supported on $[a,b]$ and has a Lebesgue density bounded almost everywhere by a finite constant $M_X$, $g_0|_{(a,b)}\in W^{s,2}(a,b)$ for an integer $s\ge1$, and $\int (y-g_0(x))^2Q(x,dy)\le\Delta$ for $P_X$-almost every $x$, where $0\le\Delta<\infty$. Fix a degree $p\in\mathbb N_0$ with $p\ge s-1$. For each integer $J\ge1$, use the uniform partition into $J$ cells and the degree-$p$ B-spline space with each interior knot repeated $p+1$ times, so its dimension is $K=(p+1)J$. For $n\ge1$ iid observations from the joint law $P_X(dx)Q(x,dy)$, let $\widehat{\mathbf g}_K$ be the fitted training vector and $\mathbf g_0=(g_0(X_1),\ldots,g_0(X_n))^T$. Then
$$E\left[\frac1n\|\widehat{\mathbf g}_K-\mathbf g_0\|_2^2\right]\le\frac{\Delta K}{n}+C_{s,p,M_X,a,b}\,K^{-2s}\|D^sg_0\|_{L^2(a,b)}^2.$$
Choosing $J\asymp n^{1/(2s+1)}$ (equivalently $K\asymp n^{1/(2s+1)}$ for fixed $p$) gives expected empirical training risk $O(n^{-2s/(2s+1)})$. This is not an independent-test-risk bound.

changes.heading: Statement refuted
changes.before: If the cubic smoothing objective is extended to a single distinct input, every affine function through that input has zero residual and zero roughness, so the minimizing function is not unique.
changes.after: The formula $\sum_i(y_i-g(x_i))^2+\lambda\int_a^b|D^2g|^2$ has a unique minimizing function for every nonempty data set whenever $\lambda>0$, including data with only one distinct input.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: On [0,1], the clamped degree-two knot vector gives the Bernstein basis; the three functions are nonnegative, sum to one, and reproduce every quadratic polynomial.
changes.after: Take degree $p=2$ and clamped knot vector $(0,0,0,1,1,1)$. On $[0,1]$ its three B-splines are $(1-x)^2$, $2x(1-x)$, and $x^2$. They form a nonnegative partition of unity and hence a basis of $\mathcal P_2$.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: Two distinct knots give their unique linear interpolant; for three equally spaced knots with values 0,1,0, the middle nodal second derivative is -3 and the two cubic pieces are explicit.
changes.after:
With two knots, the natural cubic interpolant is the line joining the two values. With knots $0,1,2$ and values $0,1,0$, the middle second derivative is $-3$, and the interpolant is
$$s(x)=\begin{cases}\frac32x-\frac12x^3,&0\le x\le1,\\[2pt]\frac32(2-x)-\frac12(2-x)^3,&1\le x\le2.\end{cases}$$

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: For a W^{2,infinity} function, linear interpolation on a uniform knot mesh is a bounded local quasi-interpolant reproducing affine functions and has uniform error at most h^2 times the essential supremum of the second weak derivative divided by 8.
changes.after: For each integer $J\ge1$, let $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_J=1$ be the uniform partition with mesh $h=1/J$. For real-valued $f\in W^{2,\infty}(0,1;\mathbb R)$, its continuous representative has a piecewise-linear interpolant $I_hf$ in the degree-one spline space with simple interior knots.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: On a one-row degree-one clamped B-spline design, the fit can have zero empirical training loss while its squared error under an independent uniform test draw is 1/3.
changes.after: Use the degree-one clamped B-spline basis $p(x)=(1-x,x)$ on $[0,1]$, with a single fixed training input $x_1=1/2$ and response $y_1=1$. The coefficient vector $\widehat\beta=(0,2)^T$ is a least-squares minimizer and gives the fitted function $\widehat g(x)=2x$. Let the target be $g_0(x)=1$ and the independent test input be uniform on $[0,1]$.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: For a probability measure P, define L²₀(P) as the real L²(P) classes with P f=0, using the inherited L² norm.
changes.after:
Let $P$ be a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. Here $L^2(P)$ is the real space of square-integrable measurable functions modulo equality $P$-almost surely, with its usual quotient norm ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]). For $f\in L^2(P)$, the integral $Pf:=\int f\,dP$ is finite and independent of the representative: Cauchy–Schwarz on the probability space gives $\int|f|\,dP\le\|f\|_2$, and the expectation of integrable representatives is invariant under almost-sure equality ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]], [[lem-expectation-is-independent-of-the-ae-representative]]).

Define the **mean-zero square-integrable space** by

$$L^2_0(P):=\{f\in L^2(P):Pf=0\}.$$

It carries the norm inherited from $L^2(P)$. Countable Choice is not needed for this definition; a later local Hilbert-space argument uses it only to inherit completeness from the library's general $L^2$ Hilbert-space result.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: For a one-sided path P_t through P=P₀ dominated by a fixed sigma-finite measure μ, define DQM at zero by the L²(μ) expansion √p_t=√p+(t/2)s√p+o(t), with supplied density versions and score s∈L²(P).
changes.after:
Let $\mathcal M$ be a model of probability measures on a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let $\epsilon>0$, and let $t\mapsto P_t\in\mathcal M$ be a path for $0\le t<\epsilon$ with $P_0=P$. It is **dominated by a common measure** when one supplied sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$ satisfies $P_t\ll\mu$ for every $t$ ([[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]). Write $p_t=dP_t/d\mu$ and $p=p_0$ for simultaneously supplied nonnegative density versions; the existence and normalization of each density are the Radon–Nikodym properties in [[def-likelihood-density]] and [[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]]. The Axiom of Choice is the library convention for selecting such a family of versions along a path ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The DQM property below is unchanged by replacing any $p_t$ by another version, since each $L^2(\mu)$ norm is unchanged by a $\mu$-null modification.

The path is **differentiable in quadratic mean at $0$**, with **score** $s\in L^2(P)$, when

$$\left\|\sqrt{p_t}-\sqrt p-\frac{t}{2}s\sqrt p\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(t)\qquad(t\downarrow0).$$

Here $o(t)$ means that the displayed norm divided by $t$ tends to $0$ as $t\downarrow0$; $L^2(P)$ and $L^2(\mu)$ are quotient spaces modulo almost-everywhere equality ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). The definition is directional. A two-sided regular submodel qualifies by restricting it to $t\ge0$. No mean-zero condition is assumed in this definition.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Under Countable Choice, L²₀(P) is a closed real linear subspace of L²(P), hence a real Hilbert space.
changes.after: Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). For any probability measure $P$, the space $L^2_0(P)$ of [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]] is a closed real linear subspace of real $L^2(P)$ with pairing $\langle f,g\rangle_P:=\int fg\,dP$; consequently it is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). The only choice use is the Countable Choice assumption already required by the general $L^2(P)$ completeness supplier.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: For a DQM path with score s∈L²(P), P s=0; any two scores satisfying the expansion agree P-almost surely.
changes.after: Assume the density-version convention for the path in [[def-dqm-submodel-through-a-law]]. If $s\in L^2(P)$ is a DQM score, then $Ps=0$, so $s\in L^2_0(P)$ ([[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]). Moreover, any two scores satisfying the same DQM expansion agree $P$-almost surely. The normalization argument itself uses no choice beyond the density versions already supplied in the definition.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: For a model through P and a declared collection of allowed DQM submodels, its tangent set is the set of their unique scores in L²₀(P).
changes.after:
Fix a model $\mathcal M$ containing a law $P$ and designate a collection of allowed submodels through $P$. Each allowed submodel is a one-sided DQM path as in [[def-dqm-submodel-through-a-law]]. Its score is the $P$-almost-sure equivalence class proved unique by [[thm-dqm-score-mean-zero]], and it belongs to $L^2_0(P)$ ([[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]).

The **tangent set** $\dot{\mathcal M}(P)$ is the set of scores of the designated paths. The model specification determines which paths are allowed. In particular, the tangent set need not be a linear space: it may be a **cone**, meaning it is closed under multiplication by nonnegative real scalars, while failing closure under negative scalars. One-sided restrictions can produce this behavior. The closed linear span of the tangent set is a separate construction.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: The tangent space is the norm closure in L²₀(P) of all finite real linear combinations of scores in the tangent set; the tangent set itself need not be linear.
changes.after:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) so that $L^2_0(P)$ is the real Hilbert space established by [[thm-mean-zero-square-integrable-space-is-hilbert]]. For a tangent set $\dot{\mathcal M}(P)\subseteq L^2_0(P)$, its **linear span** is the set of all finite real linear combinations of elements of $\dot{\mathcal M}(P)$; the span of the empty set is $\{0\}$. Its **tangent space** $\mathcal T(P)$ is the closure of that span in the $L^2(P)$ norm. The closure consists of limits of sequences from the span, equivalently of points every positive-radius norm ball around which meets the span.

The tangent set itself is retained separately and may be a cone rather than a vector space.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: For every tangent set in L²₀(P), its closed linear span is a closed linear subspace of the Hilbert space L²₀(P).
changes.after: Assume Countable Choice. Let $\dot{\mathcal M}(P)$ be any tangent set in the real Hilbert space $L^2_0(P)$. Its tangent space $\mathcal T(P)$, defined as the norm closure of its finite real linear span ([[def-tangent-space]]), is a closed linear subspace of $L^2_0(P)$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]).

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: For a specified finite-dimensional target functional ψ on a model through P, the nuisance tangent space is the closed linear span of scores of designated DQM submodels with zero right derivative of ψ at P.
changes.after:
Let $\mathcal M$ be a model through $P$, let $\psi:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R^k$ be a specified finite-dimensional parameter-of-interest functional, and let the model designate its nuisance submodels. A **nuisance submodel** is a designated allowed DQM path $t\mapsto P_t$ through $P$ for which the right derivative $\lim_{t\downarrow0}(\psi(P_t)-\psi(P))/t$ exists and is the zero vector in $\mathbb R^k$. Its score belongs to the tangent set $\dot{\mathcal M}(P)$ ([[def-tangent-set]]).

The **nuisance tangent space** $\mathcal T_\eta(P)$ is the norm closure in $L^2_0(P)$ of the finite real linear span of scores of nuisance submodels. It is a closed linear subspace by [[def-tangent-space]] and [[thm-tangent-space-is-closed-linear-subspace]]. The designated nuisance submodels are part of the model specification; this definition does not assert that every path with zero first-order target derivative is nuisance unless the model designates it as such.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: Within L²₀(P), the nuisance orthogonal complement consists of all mean-zero square-integrable h with P(hg)=0 for every nuisance tangent score g; it is a closed linear subspace.
changes.after:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), so that $L^2_0(P)$ is the real Hilbert space of [[thm-mean-zero-square-integrable-space-is-hilbert]]. The **orthogonal complement of the nuisance tangent space within $L^2_0(P)$** is

$$\mathcal T_\eta(P)^\perp:=\{h\in L^2_0(P):\langle h,g\rangle_P=0\text{ for every }g\in\mathcal T_\eta(P)\},\qquad \langle h,g\rangle_P:=P(hg).$$

This is the ordinary orthogonal complement from [[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]] applied in the mean-zero Hilbert space, not in all of $L^2(P)$. It is a closed linear subspace by [[lem-orthogonal-complement-is-closed]].

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: In the model of all laws absolutely continuous with respect to P, every bounded mean-zero score is generated by an explicit DQM path, and their closure is L²₀(P).
changes.after: Assume the library's Axiom-of-Choice density convention in [[def-dqm-submodel-through-a-law]] and Countable Choice for [[thm-mean-zero-square-integrable-space-is-hilbert]]. Let $P$ be any probability law and take the unrestricted dominated model $\mathcal M=\{Q:Q\ll P\}$. Its allowed paths are all one-sided DQM paths through $P$ with common dominator $P$. Every bounded mean-zero $s\in L^2_0(P)$ is such a path score, and the tangent space is all of $L^2_0(P)$. All densities constructed below are explicit, so the example's proof makes no density-selection choice.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: For p∈(0,1), the path P_t=Bernoulli(p+t) is DQM at t=0 with score s(1)=1/p and s(0)=−1/(1−p), of variance 1/[p(1−p)].
changes.after:
Under the Axiom-of-Choice density convention of [[def-dqm-submodel-through-a-law]], let $p\in(0,1)$ and choose $0<\delta<\min(p,1-p)$. On $\{0,1\}$ with the full power-set sigma-algebra and counting measure, let $P_t\{1\}=p+t$ and $P_t\{0\}=1-p-t$ for $|t|<\delta$. This two-sided regular path, restricted to $t\ge0$, is DQM at zero with score

$$s(1)=\frac1p,\qquad s(0)=-\frac1{1-p},$$

which has $Ps=0$ and $Ps^2=1/[p(1-p)]$. The densities with respect to counting measure are displayed explicitly, so the finite-path calculation makes no choice of versions.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: For the restricted binary model Pθ{+1}=(1+θ)/2, θ∈[0,1], at θ=0 the one-sided DQM score set is {aX:a≥0}, while its closed linear span is all of L²₀(P₀)={bX:b∈ℝ}.
changes.after: Assume the general DQM density-version convention uses AC and the mean-zero Hilbert-space convention uses Countable Choice; the two-point densities below are explicit, so this proof itself makes no choice. Let $\mathcal X=\{-1,+1\}$ with all subsets measurable and let $P_\theta\{x\}=(1+\theta x)/2$ for $\theta\in[0,1]$. At the boundary law $P_0$, consider allowed one-sided paths $t\mapsto P_{\theta(t)}$ with $\theta(0)=0$, $\theta(t)\in[0,1]$, and an existing right derivative at zero. Their DQM score set is the cone $\{aX:a\ge0\}$, while its closed linear tangent space is all of $L^2_0(P_0)=\{bX:b\in\mathbb R\}$. Thus the score set and its linear tangent space are distinct.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space, let $\mathcal T\subseteq H$ be a closed linear subspace, and let $\dot\psi:\mathcal T\to\mathbb R^k$ be continuous linear with an ambient representer $\phi_0\in H^k$, meaning $\dot\psi(s)=\langle\phi_0,s\rangle_H$ coordinatewise for all $s\in\mathcal T$. Assume Countable Choice. Then all ambient representers are exactly

$$\phi_0+(\mathcal T^\perp)^k.$$

The unique representer in $\mathcal T^k$ is $\phi_{\mathrm{can}}=\Pi_{\mathcal T}\phi_0$; when $\dot\psi$ is a statistical path derivative, this is its canonical gradient. Projection is applied coordinatewise.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.after:
Fix a law $P$ and an iid sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P$. For a measurable vector function $\varphi:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^k$, write $P\varphi=E_P[\varphi(X)]$ and $P_n\varphi=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\varphi(X_i)$, where $P_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{X_i}$ is the empirical measure. For a vector remainder $R_n$, $R_n=o_P(n^{-1/2})$ means $\sqrt n R_n\to0$ in $P$-probability.

A measurable estimator sequence $\widehat\psi_n$ of $\psi(P)\in\mathbb R^k$ is **asymptotically linear at $P$** with **estimator influence function** $\varphi$ if

$$\widehat\psi_n-\psi(P)=(P_n-P)\varphi+o_P(n^{-1/2}),$$

where $\varphi\in L^2_0(P)^k$: $E_P\varphi=0$ and $E_P\|\varphi\|^2<\infty$. The space $L^2_0(P)$ and its almost-sure equivalence convention are as in [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]. This definition alone does not assert regularity under local alternatives, pathwise differentiability of $\psi$, or asymptotic normality.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.after:
Let $P$ be a probability law for one observation, let $\mathcal P$ be a model of laws containing $P$, and let $\psi:\mathcal P\to\mathbb R^k$ be a target functional, where $k\ge1$ is finite. A one-sided path $t\mapsto P_t$, $0\le t<\epsilon$, through $P=P_0$ is **differentiable in quadratic mean (DQM)** with score $s\in L^2(P)$ when its densities $p_t,p$ relative to one common sigma-finite measure $\mu$ satisfy

$$\left\|\sqrt{p_t}-\sqrt p-\frac{t}{2}s\sqrt p\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(t)\qquad(t\downarrow0).$$

The score initially belongs to $L^2(P)$; [[thm-dqm-score-mean-zero]] proves it is unique modulo $P$-almost-sure equality and has mean zero, so it lies in $L^2_0(P)$ as defined by [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]. The allowed scores form the **tangent set** of the designated paths ([[def-tangent-set]]); their **tangent space** $\mathcal T$ is the closure of their real linear span in $L^2_0(P)$ ([[def-tangent-space]]). It is a closed linear subspace by [[thm-tangent-space-is-closed-linear-subspace]], and hence a Hilbert space under Countable Choice ([[thm-mean-zero-square-integrable-space-is-hilbert]]).

The functional $\psi$ is **pathwise differentiable at $P$ relative to $\mathcal T$** if the right derivative $\dot\psi_P(s):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}(\psi(P_t)-\psi(P))/t$ exists for every allowed path, depends only on its score, and extends to a continuous linear map $\dot\psi_P:\mathcal T\to\mathbb R^k$. A vector $\phi\in L^2_0(P)^k$ is a **parameter influence curve** (or representer) when

$$\dot\psi_P(s)=E_P[\phi s]\qquad(s\in\mathcal T),$$

with the expectation interpreted coordinatewise. The Hilbert-space Riesz theorem gives a unique representer in $\mathcal T^k$; it is the **canonical gradient**. This representation requires Countable Choice, as in [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]] and [[def-countable-choice]]. The supplied density versions along a path use the separate Axiom of Choice in [[def-dqm-submodel-through-a-law]] and [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. The full set of ambient representers and its projection characterization are proved in [[thm-influence-curve-representers]].

changes.heading: Definition
changes.after:
Let $\theta\in\mathbb R^p$, $p\ge1$ finite, be a parameter of interest at a law $P$. Assume its score vector $S_\theta=(S_{\theta,1},\ldots,S_{\theta,p})^T$ has components in $L^2_0(P)$; under a dominated differentiable parametric submodel these are the coordinate log-density scores of [[def-score-and-fisher-information]]. Let $\mathcal T_\eta\subseteq L^2_0(P)$ be the closed nuisance tangent space of [[def-nuisance-tangent-space]]. The ambient $L^2_0(P)$ is as in [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]. The score-density convention uses the Axiom of Choice, while Hilbert projection uses Countable Choice; both dependencies are retained separately.

The Hilbert decomposition [[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]] defines $\Pi_{\mathcal T_\eta}f$ as the unique $g\in\mathcal T_\eta$ with $f-g\in\mathcal T_\eta^\perp$, where orthogonality and $\mathcal T_\eta^\perp$ have the meanings in [[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. The **efficient score vector** and **efficient information matrix** are

$$S_{\mathrm{eff}}=S_\theta-\Pi_{\mathcal T_\eta}S_\theta,\qquad I_{\mathrm{eff}}=E_P[S_{\mathrm{eff}}S_{\mathrm{eff}}^T],$$

where $\Pi_{\mathcal T_\eta}$ is the Hilbert-space orthogonal projection applied coordinatewise. This projection exists and is unique because $\mathcal T_\eta$ is a closed linear subspace; the projection theorem used by [[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]] assumes Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $H=L^2_0(P)$, let $S_\theta\in H^p$ be a finite-dimensional interest-score vector, and let $\mathcal T_\eta\subseteq\mathcal T\subseteq H$ be closed linear nuisance and full tangent spaces, with $\mathcal T_\eta$ a subspace of $\mathcal T$. Assume the designated allowed score set is exactly

$$\mathcal S=\{a^TS_\theta+t:a\in\mathbb R^p,\ t\in\mathcal T_\eta\},\qquad \mathcal T=\overline{\mathcal S}^{\,L^2(P)},$$

and every allowed one-sided path with score $a^TS_\theta+t\in\mathcal S$ has right target derivative $a$ for the parameter $\theta$. If $I_{\mathrm{eff}}=E_P[S_{\mathrm{eff}}S_{\mathrm{eff}}^T]$ is nonsingular, then $\theta$ is pathwise differentiable and its canonical gradient is

$$\phi_{\mathrm{can}}=I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}S_{\mathrm{eff}}.$$

Its covariance matrix is $E_P[\phi_{\mathrm{can}}\phi_{\mathrm{can}}^T]=I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}$. This theorem does not assert that an estimator attaining the covariance bound exists.

changes.heading: Example
changes.after: Let $\Omega=\mathbb N$ with $\mathcal F=2^{\mathbb N}$, and define $X:\Omega\to[0,\infty)$ by $X(k)=k$. Let $\mathcal M_X$ be the model of probability laws $Q$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ satisfying $E_QX<\infty$, and define $\psi:\mathcal M_X\to\mathbb R$ by $\psi(Q)=E_QX$. Take $P\{X=k\}=c k^{-3}$, where $c=(\sum_{k\ge1}k^{-3})^{-1}$. Then $E_PX<\infty$ but $E_PX^2=\infty$. At $P$, designate the bounded-score one-sided paths $dP_{t,s}=(1+ts)dP$ with $E_Ps=0$ and sufficiently small $t\ge0$ as the allowed paths. Their tangent space is $L^2_0(P)$. The right derivative on bounded scores is $s\mapsto E_P[Xs]$, but this map is not continuous in the $L^2(P)$ norm. Thus $\psi$ is not pathwise differentiable relative to this tangent space and has no finite-variance influence curve there.

changes.heading: Example
changes.after:
Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable observation space and let $X:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable. Let $\mathcal M_X$ be the model of probability laws $Q$ on this space satisfying $E_QX<\infty$, and define $\psi:\mathcal M_X\to\mathbb R$ by $\psi(Q)=E_QX$. Take $P\in\mathcal M_X$ with $X\in L^2(P)$, and write $\mu=E_PX$. Specify the allowed one-sided paths through $P$ to be $dP_{t,s}=(1+ts)dP$ for bounded real $s$ with $E_Ps=0$ and sufficiently small $t\ge0$. Their scores are the bounded mean-zero functions, whose closure is $\mathcal T=L^2_0(P)$. The right path derivative is represented by $X-\mu$. It is the unique representer in $\mathcal T$, hence the canonical gradient in this example. For iid observations from $P$, the sample mean has the exact expansion

$$\overline X_n-\mu=(P_n-P)(X-\mu),$$

so $X-\mu$ is also its estimator influence function. Only the specified bounded-score path class is asserted here.

changes.heading: Example
changes.after:
Let $U,V$ be the coordinate functions on $\Omega=\{-1,1\}^2$, with $P$ uniform and counting measure as a common dominator. For $2|\theta|+|\eta|<1$, define
$$P_{\theta,\eta}\{(u,v)\}=\frac14\bigl(1+\theta(u+v)+\eta u\bigr).$$
Take $\theta$ as the scalar parameter of interest and $\eta$ as nuisance. At $(0,0)$ designate the straight one-sided paths $(\theta_t,\eta_t)=(at,bt)$ as allowed paths, with those having $a=0$ designated as nuisance paths. Then the interest score is $S_\theta=U+V$, the nuisance tangent space is $\mathcal T_\eta=\operatorname{span}\{U\}$, and the full tangent space is $\mathcal T=\operatorname{span}\{U,V\}$. The efficient score is $V$, the efficient information is $1$, and the canonical gradient for $\theta$ is $V$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law $P$, let $k<\infty$, and let $\widehat\psi_n$ estimate $\psi(P)\in\mathbb R^k$. If it is asymptotically linear at $P$ with influence function $\varphi\in L^2_0(P)^k$, then

$$\sqrt n\{\widehat\psi_n-\psi(P)\}\Rightarrow N_k(0,\Sigma_\varphi),\qquad \Sigma_\varphi=P[\varphi\varphi^T].$$

The covariance may be singular. This is a distributional limit only; the theorem asserts neither local regularity nor estimator attainment of an efficiency bound.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Assume AC and let $d,k\ge1$ be finite. Let $\{P_{n,h}:h\in\mathbb R^d\}$ be LAN at $h=0$ with positive-definite information matrix $K$ and central sequence $\Delta_n$. Let $\psi_{n,h}\in\mathbb R^k$ be a local target such that for every fixed $h$,

$$\delta_n(h):=\sqrt n(\psi_{n,h}-\psi_{n,0})\longrightarrow Dh$$

for a fixed matrix $D\in\mathbb R^{k\times d}$. Suppose $T_n=\sqrt n(\widehat\psi_n-\psi_{n,0})$ is regular for this target: under each fixed $P_{n,h}$, $T_n-\delta_n(h)\Rightarrow W$ for the same Borel law $W$. Then there is a probability law $\nu$ on $\mathbb R^k$ such that

$$\mathcal L(W)=N_k(0,DK^{-1}D^T)*\nu.$$

The Gaussian covariance may be singular. No finite-moment hypothesis on $W$ or $\nu$ is needed.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Assume AC. Let $t\mapsto P_t$ be a one-sided path ($0\le t<\epsilon$) of probability laws on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ dominated by one supplied sigma-finite measure $\mu$, with supplied densities $p_t$ and $P_0=P$. Suppose the path is differentiable in quadratic mean at $0$ with score $s\in L^2(P)$, in the sense of [[def-dqm-submodel-through-a-law]]. Put $I=P[s^2]$. For a fixed $h\ge0$, let $t_n=h/\sqrt n$ and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid $P$. On $S=\{p_0>0\}$ set $\alpha_t=P_t(S^c)$ and, for sufficiently small $t$, define

$$q_t(x)=\frac{\mathbf1_S(x)p_t(x)}{(1-\alpha_t)p_0(x)}\quad\text{on }S,\qquad q_t(x)=0\quad\text{on }S^c.$$

Then $q_t$ is a probability density relative to $P$. With $L_n=\prod_{i=1}^nq_{t_n}(X_i)$ and $\Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^ns(X_i)$,

$$\left\|P_{t_n}^{\otimes n}-L_nP^{\otimes n}\right\|_{\rm TV}\longrightarrow0,\qquad \log L_n=h\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^2I+o_P(1),\qquad \Delta_n\Rightarrow N(0,I).$$

For $h=0$ take $L_n=1$ and use the convention $\log0=-\infty$. The proxy $L_nP^{\otimes n}$ is the normalized absolutely continuous component; the conclusion does not assert a full likelihood ratio for $P_{t_n}^{\otimes n}$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Assume AC and Countable Choice. Let $P$ be a law in a statistical model, let $\mathcal T\subseteq L^2_0(P)$ be its closed score tangent space, and let $\psi$ be a pathwise differentiable $\mathbb R^k$-valued functional with canonical gradient $\phi_{\rm can}\in\mathcal T^k$. Write $V_{\rm can}=P[\phi_{\rm can}\phi_{\rm can}^T]$. Let $\widehat\psi_n$ be asymptotically linear at $P$ with influence function $\varphi\in L^2_0(P)^k$. Assume that for every allowed one-sided DQM path $P_t$ with score $s$ and every fixed $h\ge0$, under $P_{h/\sqrt n}^{\otimes n}$ the centered estimator $\sqrt n\{\widehat\psi_n-\psi(P_{h/\sqrt n})\}$ converges to one law independent of $h$, equal to its limit at $h=0$. Then $\varphi$ represents the pathwise derivative on $\mathcal T$, so

$$\varphi\in\phi_{\rm can}+(\mathcal T^\perp)^k,\qquad P[\varphi\varphi^T]-V_{\rm can}=P[(\varphi-\phi_{\rm can})(\varphi-\phi_{\rm can})^T]\succeq0.$$

By [[thm-asymptotic-linearity-implies-normality]], this is the covariance lower bound for the estimator's asymptotic normal limit. The theorem does not assert that an estimator attaining the bound exists.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Assume AC and Countable Choice. Let $\psi$ be pathwise differentiable at $P$ with tangent space $\mathcal T$ and canonical gradient $\phi_{\rm can}\in\mathcal T^k$, and write $V_{\rm can}=P[\phi_{\rm can}\phi_{\rm can}^T]$. If $\mathcal T\ne\{0\}$, suppose a directed family of finite-dimensional, dominated QMD models $\{P_{\gamma,\theta}:\theta\in\Theta_\gamma\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_\gamma}\}$, with each $\Theta_\gamma$ open and $P_{\gamma,\theta_{\gamma,0}}=P$, has score spans $\mathcal S_\gamma\subseteq\mathcal T$ whose union is dense in $\mathcal T$. In each model let $S_\gamma\in L^2_0(P)^{d_\gamma}$ be a score basis, let $I_\gamma=P[S_\gamma S_\gamma^T]$ be nonsingular, and let $D_\gamma=P[\phi_{\rm can}S_\gamma^T]$. Assume for each fixed $h\in\mathbb R^{d_\gamma}$ that $\sqrt n\{\psi(P_{\gamma,\theta_{\gamma,0}+h/\sqrt n})-\psi(P)\}\to D_\gamma h$, and that under each local law the centered estimator $\sqrt n\{\widehat\psi_n-\psi(P_{\gamma,\theta_{\gamma,0}+h/\sqrt n})\}$ converges to one common law $L$, independent of $\gamma$ and $h$. Suppose $L$ has finite covariance. By [[thm-qmd-implies-lan-for-iid]], each model has the required LAN proxy; [[lem-finite-dimensional-functional-convolution-bound]] then applies with derivative matrix $D_\gamma$. If $\mathcal T=\{0\}$, no submodel family is needed. Then

$$\operatorname{Cov}(L)\succeq V_{\rm can}.$$

This is a lower bound for general regular estimators; asymptotic linearity is not assumed.

changes.heading: Statement refuted
changes.after: Every finite-mean law has a finite-variance influence curve for its mean functional in the dominated local model generated by bounded mean-zero score tilts.

changes.heading: Example
changes.after: Let $P$ be any law on $\mathbb R$ with $P[X^2]<\infty$, let $\mu=PX$, and consider the local model whose allowed paths are all bounded mean-zero tilts $dP_{t,s}=(1+ts)dP$ for sufficiently small $t\ge0$. For $\psi(Q)=QX$, the sample mean $\bar X_n$ is regular along each allowed one-sided path (the centered root-$n$ error has one common limit law for every fixed $h\ge0$), and is asymptotically linear with influence function $X-\mu$. Its asymptotic variance equals the unrestricted mean bound.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: Given a statistical experiment $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and any probability measure $Q$ on that space ([[def-probability-measure]]), Huber's one-observation contamination law is
changes.after:
Given a statistical experiment $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and any probability measure $Q$ on that space ([[def-probability-measure]]), Huber's one-observation contamination law is
$$
P_{\epsilon,\theta,Q}=(1-\epsilon)P_\theta+\epsilon Q,\qquad 0\le\epsilon\le1.
$$
The mixture is a probability measure by [[lem-convex-mixture-of-probability-laws]]. In the sample-size-$n$ model, observations are iid from this law ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]). A worst-case $Q$ may be chosen separately for each $\theta$. This is an iid sampling model, distinct from a fixed gross-error direction and from sample replacement.

changes.before: For a statistical experiment $\{P_\theta\}$ from [[def-statistical-experiment]], sample size $N\ge1$, and replacement fraction $0\le\eta\le1$, equip $\mathcal X^N$ with its finite product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). A sample-replacement coupling is a pair of $\mathcal X^N$-valued random elements on a common probability space ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]) $(X,Y)$ such that $X_1,\ldots,X_N$ are iid with law $P_\theta$ under [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]] and
changes.after:
For a statistical experiment $\{P_\theta\}$ from [[def-statistical-experiment]], sample size $N\ge1$, and replacement fraction $0\le\eta\le1$, equip $\mathcal X^N$ with its finite product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). A sample-replacement coupling is a pair of $\mathcal X^N$-valued random elements on a common probability space ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]) $(X,Y)$ such that $X_1,\ldots,X_N$ are iid with law $P_\theta$ under [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]] and
$$
\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf1\{X_i\ne Y_i\}\le\lfloor\eta N\rfloor
$$
almost surely. Assume the diagonal $\Delta_{\mathcal X}=\{(x,x):x\in\mathcal X\}$ belongs to the product sigma-algebra $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A$ ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]), so each mismatch indicator is measurable. The joint law may depend on the entire clean sample; the observed vector $Y$ need not be iid.

changes.before: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $P_0,P_1$ be probability measures on one measurable space. If $0\le\epsilon<1$ and $\|P_0-P_1\|_{TV}\le\epsilon/(1-\epsilon)$, there are probability measures $Q_0,Q_1$ for which
changes.after:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $P_0,P_1$ be probability measures on one measurable space. If $0\le\epsilon<1$ and $\|P_0-P_1\|_{TV}\le\epsilon/(1-\epsilon)$, there are probability measures $Q_0,Q_1$ for which
$$
(1-\epsilon)P_0+\epsilon Q_0=(1-\epsilon)P_1+\epsilon Q_1.
$$
At $\epsilon=1$, the same equality is possible without a TV condition.

changes.before: Let the experiment in [[def-statistical-experiment]] have nonempty parameter set $\Theta$. Choose a sigma-algebra $\mathcal T$ on $\Theta$ and take $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ as its measurable action space ([[def-measurable-space]]). Write $X(x)=x$ for the canonical sample vector on this product space.
