changes.after:
Let the experiment in [[def-statistical-experiment]] have nonempty parameter set $\Theta$. Choose a sigma-algebra $\mathcal T$ on $\Theta$ and take $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ as its measurable action space ([[def-measurable-space]]). Specialize the target-first loss of [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] to $L:\Theta\times\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$ by taking its action space to be $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$. Fix an integer sample size $N\ge1$ and a measurable rule $\hat\theta:\mathcal X^N\to\Theta$. Equip $\mathcal X^N$ with the finite product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]); the iid sample law is the finite product measure supplied by [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] and [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]. Write $X(x)=x$ for the canonical sample vector on this product space. The Huber sampling law is from [[def-huber-contamination-model]], and nonnegative expectations use [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. For $0\le\epsilon\le1$ and $0\le\eta\le1$, its **Huber robust expected risk** at fraction $\epsilon$ is
$$
\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\sup_Q\mathbb E_{P_{\epsilon,\theta,Q}^{\otimes N}}L(\theta,\hat\theta(X)).
$$
Its **replacement robust expected risk** at fraction $\eta$ is the supremum of $\mathbb E L(\theta,\hat\theta(Y))$ over $\theta$ and all couplings in [[def-adversarial-sample-replacement]]. For $t\in[0,+\infty]$, the Huber tail risk at threshold $t$ is $\sup_{\theta,Q}P_{\epsilon,\theta,Q}^{\otimes N}\{x:L(\theta,\hat\theta(x))\ge t\}$; the replacement tail risk is the supremum of $\Pr\{L(\theta,\hat\theta(Y))\ge t\}$ over $\theta$ and the same replacement couplings. Expected risk and tail risk are different criteria. The gross-error path in [[def-gross-error-path]] is a path of laws; it is not a sample-replacement mechanism.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: For an experiment $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$ with nonempty $\Theta$ ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), choose a sigma-algebra $\mathcal T$ on $\Theta$ and take $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ as the measurable action space ([[def-measurable-space]]). Take the target-first loss $L:\Theta\times\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$ from [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] with that action space. For $0\le\epsilon<1$, define
changes.after:
For an experiment $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$ with nonempty $\Theta$ ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), choose a sigma-algebra $\mathcal T$ on $\Theta$ and take $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ as the measurable action space ([[def-measurable-space]]). Take the target-first loss $L:\Theta\times\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$ from [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] with that action space. For $0\le\epsilon<1$, define
$$
\omega(\epsilon,\Theta)=\sup\{L(\theta_1,\theta_2):\theta_1,\theta_2\in\Theta,\ \|P_{\theta_1}-P_{\theta_2}\|_{TV}\le\epsilon/(1-\epsilon)\}.
$$
Set $\omega(1,\Theta)=\sup_{\theta_1,\theta_2\in\Theta}L(\theta_1,\theta_2)$, allowing $+\infty$. Total variation is the event-supremum convention $\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|$ from [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]], with no factor $1/2$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a contamination level $0\le\epsilon\le1$, an integer sample size $N\ge1$, and a nonempty statistical model $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$ on a common measurable sample space, and give $\Theta$ a measurable structure as the parameter action space ([[def-measurable-space]]). Let the target-first loss $L:\Theta\times\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$ of [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] have measurable sections $a\mapsto L(\theta,a)$. Suppose a fixed $0<\kappa\le1$ satisfies
changes.after:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a contamination level $0\le\epsilon\le1$, an integer sample size $N\ge1$, and a nonempty statistical model $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$ on a common measurable sample space, and give $\Theta$ a measurable structure as the parameter action space ([[def-measurable-space]]). Let the target-first loss $L:\Theta\times\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$ of [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] have measurable sections $a\mapsto L(\theta,a)$. Suppose a fixed $0<\kappa\le1$ satisfies
$$
\max\{L(\theta_0,a),L(\theta_1,a)\}\ge\kappa L(\theta_0,\theta_1)
$$
for all $a,\theta_0,\theta_1\in\Theta$. Suppose also that $0\le M_0<\infty$, $0<c_0\le1$, and
$$
\inf_{\hat\theta:\mathcal X^N\to\Theta\ {\rm measurable}}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}P_{\theta}^{\otimes N}\{L(\theta,\hat\theta)\ge M_0\}\ge c_0.
$$
If $\omega(\epsilon,\Theta)<\infty$, then with
$$
M_\epsilon=\frac{\kappa}{4}\bigl(M_0\vee\omega(\epsilon,\Theta)\bigr)
$$
one has
$$
\inf_{\hat\theta:\mathcal X^N\to\Theta\ {\rm measurable}}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\sup_QP_{\epsilon,\theta,Q}^{\otimes N}\{L(\theta,\hat\theta)\ge M_\epsilon\}\ge\min(c_0,1/2).
$$
Thus the lower-bound threshold is comparable to $M_0\vee\omega(\epsilon,\Theta)$. If $\omega(\epsilon,\Theta)=+\infty$, the same supremum is at least $1/2$ at every finite threshold. In particular, if $c_0\ge c_*>0$ for a fixed constant $c_*\le1/2$ independent of the model, the finite-modulus conclusion has the universal probability constant $c_*$. A metric loss has the separation property with $\kappa=1/2$; its square has it with $\kappa=1/4$.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: For integers $N\ge1$ and $0\le k\le N$, if $x_i,y_i\in[0,1]$ and at most $k$ coordinates differ, then
changes.after:
For integers $N\ge1$ and $0\le k\le N$, if $x_i,y_i\in[0,1]$ and at most $k$ coordinates differ, then
$$
\left|N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N y_i-N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N x_i\right|\le k/N.
$$
For the coupling example, take $\mathcal X=\Theta=\{0,1\}$ with their full power-set sigma-algebras ([[def-measurable-space]]) and the experiment $P_\theta=\delta_\theta$ ([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-dirac-measure]], [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]). For $N=2$ and replacement fraction $\eta=1/2$, the clean samples $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ can both be changed to $(0,1)$ with one replacement, so the two parameter values induce the same observed law.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: Take $\Theta=[0,1]$ with its Borel sigma-algebra and sample space $\{0,1\}$ with full power set. Let $\delta_0,\delta_1$ be the point masses, set $P_\theta=(1-\theta)\delta_0+\theta\delta_1$, and use absolute parameter loss $L(\theta,a)=|\theta-a|$. Then
changes.after:
Take $\Theta=[0,1]$ with its Borel sigma-algebra and sample space $\{0,1\}$ with full power set. Let $\delta_0,\delta_1$ be the point masses, set $P_\theta=(1-\theta)\delta_0+\theta\delta_1$, and use absolute parameter loss $L(\theta,a)=|\theta-a|$. Then
$$
\omega(\epsilon,\Theta)=\min\{\epsilon/(1-\epsilon),1\}\quad(0\le\epsilon<1),\qquad \omega(1,\Theta)=1.
$$
For $0<\epsilon\le1/2$, set $\theta_0=0$, $\theta_1=\epsilon/(1-\epsilon)$, $Q_0=\delta_1$, and $Q_1=\delta_0$; both Huber mixtures are Bernoulli$(\epsilon)$. For $1/2\le\epsilon\le1$, endpoint laws can also be made identical.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: For a total scalar statistic T_n on R^n and a fixed sample x, the replacement breakdown fraction is the minimum m/n for which the supremum displacement over samples changing at most m coordinates is infinite, when such an m exists.
changes.after:
Let $n\ge1$, let $T_n:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be a total statistic, and fix a sample $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$. For $0\le m\le n$, define its maximum replacement displacement by

$$B_m(T_n,x):=\sup\bigl\{|T_n(y)-T_n(x)|:y\in\mathbb R^n,\ \#\{i:y_i\ne x_i\}\le m\bigr\}\in[0,+\infty].$$

When the set is nonempty, the finite-sample replacement breakdown fraction is

$$\epsilon_n^*(T_n,x):=\frac1n\min\{m\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:B_m(T_n,x)=+\infty\}.$$

Only coordinate replacements are counted, and the replacement values range over all of $\mathbb R$. This is a property of the statistic at the fixed sample; it is not a probability or contamination-neighborhood statement.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: For a Borel probability law G on R whose set {t: G((-infinity,t]) >= 1/2} is nonempty and bounded below, its lower median is m(G)=inf{t: G((-infinity,t]) >= 1/2}.
changes.after:
Let $G$ be a probability measure on the Borel subsets of $\mathbb R$, and put $F_G(t):=G(( -\infty,t])$. For any $G$ such that $S_G:=\{t\in\mathbb R:F_G(t)\ge1/2\}$ is nonempty and bounded below, define its **lower median** by

$$m(G):=\inf S_G.$$

The stated condition makes $m(G)$ a finite real number. This convention chooses the left endpoint when the set of medians is an interval; it assumes neither a density nor uniqueness.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: For n>=1 and points x_1,...,x_n in a measurable space, P_n(A)=n^{-1} sum_i delta_{x_i}(A) is a probability measure.
changes.after:
Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space, let $n\ge1$, and let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X$. Define

$$P_n(A):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}(A),\qquad A\in\mathcal A.$$

Then $P_n$ is a probability measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: For n=2r+1 and empirical law P_n, the lower median m(P_n)=inf{t:P_n((-infinity,t])>=1/2} equals the (r+1)-st order statistic.
changes.after: Let $n=2r+1\ge1$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R$. Let $P_n=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{x_i}$ be their empirical probability law and write $x_{(1)}\le\cdots\le x_{(n)}$ for the sorted sample. Then the lower median $m(P_n)$ is $x_{(r+1)}$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: For every fixed real sample of size n, the sample mean has replacement breakdown 1/n. If n=2r+1 and the sample median is the (r+1)-st order statistic, its replacement breakdown is (r+1)/n=floor((n+1)/2)/n.
changes.after: For any fixed sample $x\in\mathbb R^n$, the sample mean $\bar x=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i$ has finite-sample replacement breakdown fraction $1/n$. If $n=2r+1$ is odd and the conventional sample median is the $(r+1)$-st order statistic, its finite-sample replacement breakdown fraction is $(r+1)/n=\lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor/n$.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: For a single-valued functional T on a model of probability laws, the point-contamination influence function at F is the right derivative lim_{epsilon downarrow 0}[T((1-epsilon)F+epsilon delta_x)-T(F)]/epsilon wherever that derivative exists.
changes.after:
Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space, let $\mathcal P$ be a collection of probability measures on it, and let $T:\mathcal P\to\mathbb R^k$ be a single-valued map with finite $k\ge1$. Such a map is a **statistical functional**. For $F\in\mathcal P$ and $x\in\mathcal X$, suppose the point-contamination path $F_{\epsilon,x}=(1-\epsilon)F+\epsilon\delta_x$ belongs to $\mathcal P$ for all sufficiently small $\epsilon\ge0$ ([[def-gross-error-path]]). The **gross-error influence function** at $(x;T,F)$ is

$$\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F):=\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\frac{T(F_{\epsilon,x})-T(F)}{\epsilon}\in\mathbb R^k,$$

when this finite right limit exists. Its domain may be a proper subset of $\mathcal X$.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: The gross-error sensitivity of T at F is the extended supremum of |IF(x;T,F)| over point-contamination directions where the influence function exists.
changes.after:
For a statistical functional $T$ at a law $F$, let $D_{T,F}:=\{x\in\mathcal X:\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F)\text{ exists as a finite vector}\}$. When $D_{T,F}\ne\varnothing$, its **gross-error sensitivity** is the extended nonnegative number

$$\gamma^*(T,F):=\sup_{x\in D_{T,F}}\|\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F)\|_2.$$

For a real-valued functional the norm is absolute value. This supremum only ranges over directions where the influence function exists; it makes no claim that the derivative exists in every direction.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Under an M-location root equation, local domination that justifies differentiation under the integral, and a nonzero expected derivative, the point-contamination influence function is psi(x-theta)/E_F[psi'(X-theta)]; for psi(u)=u this is x-mu.
changes.after:
Let $F$ be a Borel probability law on $\mathbb R$, let $\psi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$, and let $\theta\in\mathbb R$ satisfy

$$J(\theta):=\int\psi(y-\theta)\,dF(y)=0.$$

Assume $\int|\psi(y-\theta)|\,dF(y)<\infty$ and that there is an open interval $I$ containing $\theta$ and a nonnegative $g\in L^1(F)$ such that $|\psi'(y-t)|\le g(y)$ for $F$-almost every $y$ and every $t\in I$. Put $A:=\int\psi'(y-\theta)\,dF(y)$ and assume $A\ne0$. For each fixed $x\in\mathbb R$, let $\theta_x(\epsilon)$ be the locally unique root near $\theta$ of

$$\int\psi(y-t)\,dF_{\epsilon,x}(y)=0,\qquad F_{\epsilon,x}=(1-\epsilon)F+\epsilon\delta_x.$$

Then, for all sufficiently small $\epsilon\ge0$, this local root exists and

$$\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F)=\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\frac{\theta_x(\epsilon)-\theta}{\epsilon}=\frac{\psi(x-\theta)}{A}.$$

Here $T(F_{\epsilon,x})$ denotes this local root. In the special case $\psi(u)=u$ and $F$ has a finite first absolute moment, $\theta=\mu:=\int y\,dF(y)$ and $\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F)=x-\mu$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: If F has a unique median m, F(m)=1/2, and a continuous local density f with f(m)>0, then the right point-contamination derivative is -1/(2f(m)) below m, +1/(2f(m)) above m, and 0 at x=m; hence its gross-error sensitivity is 1/(2f(m)).
changes.after:
Let $F$ be a Borel probability law on $\mathbb R$, let $m=m(F)$ be its lower median, and assume $F(m)=1/2$. Suppose that on an open interval $I$ containing $m$ there is a continuous density version $f$ satisfying

$$F((s,t])=\int_s^t f(u)\,du\quad(s<t,\ s,t\in I),\qquad f(m)>0.$$

For each fixed $x\in\mathbb R$, the right point-contamination influence function of the lower-median functional is

$$\operatorname{IF}(x;m,F)=\begin{cases}-\dfrac1{2f(m)},&x<m,\\[4pt]0,&x=m,\\[4pt]+\dfrac1{2f(m)},&x>m.\end{cases}$$

Consequently, its gross-error sensitivity is $\gamma^*(m,F)=1/(2f(m))$.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: For a finite-mean law on R, the mean has influence function x-mu and infinite gross-error sensitivity, while its sample mean has replacement breakdown 1/n.
changes.after: Let $F$ be any probability law on $\mathbb R$ with finite first absolute moment $\mu=\int y\,dF(y)$. Its mean functional has $\operatorname{IF}(x)=x-\mu$, so its gross-error sensitivity is infinite. At every fixed sample, its sample mean has replacement breakdown fraction $1/n$.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: At a median with positive continuous density, the pointwise influence function is bounded by 1/(2f(m)); for odd n the sample median breakdown is floor((n+1)/2)/n.
changes.after: Suppose $F$ has a unique median $m$, satisfies $F(m)=1/2$, and has a continuous density with $f(m)>0$. The median's gross-error sensitivity is $1/(2f(m))<\infty$. For odd sample sizes $n=2r+1$, the sample median's replacement breakdown fraction is $(r+1)/(2r+1)$, which tends to $1/2$ as $n$ increases through odd integers.

changes.heading: Statement refuted
changes.before: Bounded gross-error sensitivity of a population functional does not force its empirical plug-in statistic to have replacement breakdown bounded away from zero.
changes.after: At a probability law $F$, finite gross-error sensitivity forces the empirical plug-in statistic $T(P_n)$ to have replacement breakdown bounded below by a positive constant as $n\to\infty$.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.after:
Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, let $n\ge1$, and let $1\le k\le n$ be an integer. Given $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in H^n$, put $q=\lfloor n/k\rfloor$ and $r=n-kq$. Form consecutive blocks $B_1,\ldots,B_k$ in index order, with $|B_j|=q+1$ for $j\le r$ and $|B_j|=q$ for $j>r$. Compute the block means $m_j=|B_j|^{-1}\sum_{i\in B_j}x_i$. Return the unique minimum-norm point of
$$
\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in H}\sum_{j=1}^k\|z-m_j\|.
$$

The objective minimizers are called geometric medians of the block means. The minimum-norm rule makes the output single-valued. Existence, uniqueness of that selected point, and Borel measurability as a function of the input tuple are proved in [[lem-measurable-minimum-norm-geometric-median-selection]].

changes.heading: Definition
changes.after:
Let $d,N\ge1$ be integers, let $0\le\eta\le1/10$, and let $0<\delta<1$ satisfy $N\ge2560\log(2/\delta)$. Given two observed halves $\widetilde X_1,\ldots,\widetilde X_N$ and $\widetilde Y_1,\ldots,\widetilde Y_N$ in $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$
\varepsilon=\max\left\{10\eta,\frac{2560\log(2/\delta)}{N}\right\}\in(0,1].
$$
For $v\in S^{d-1}$, sort $\langle\widetilde Y_i,v\rangle$ nondecreasingly and let $\alpha_v$ and $\beta_v$ be its order statistics of ranks $\lceil\varepsilon N/2\rceil$ and $\lceil(1-\varepsilon/2)N\rceil$. Write $\phi_{a,b}(t)=\min\{b,\max\{a,t\}\}$. For $Q>0$ define
$$U_Q(v)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\phi_{\alpha_v-Q,\,\beta_v+Q}(\langle\widetilde X_i,v\rangle),\qquad \Gamma(v,Q)=\{z\in\mathbb R^d:|\langle z,v\rangle-U_Q(v)|\le2\varepsilon Q\}.$$
and $\Gamma(Q)=\bigcap_{v\in S^{d-1}}\Gamma(v,Q)$. For each $j\in\mathbb Z$, put
$$
K_j=\bigcap_{i\ge j}\Gamma(2^i),\qquad S=\{j\in\mathbb Z:K_j\ne\varnothing\}.
$$
Return the unique minimum-norm point of $K_j$ if $S$ has least element $j$; if $S=\mathbb Z$, return the unique minimum-norm point of $\bigcap_{i\in\mathbb Z}\Gamma(2^i)$; if $S=\varnothing$, return the first-half sample mean $N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\widetilde X_i$. This three-branch selector is total on the displayed input domain; its existence and Borel measurability are proved in [[lem-multivariate-trimmed-mean-selector-total-and-measurable]].

changes.heading: Definition
changes.after:
Let $N\ge1$ be an integer, let $\eta\ge0$, $0<\delta<1$, and set
$$
\varepsilon=8\eta+\frac{12\log(4/\delta)}{N}.
$$
The procedure is admissible when $0<\varepsilon\le1/4$. Its input is two observed real samples $\widetilde X_1,\ldots,\widetilde X_N$ and $\widetilde Y_1,\ldots,\widetilde Y_N$. Sort the second sample nondecreasingly as $\widetilde Y^*_{(1)}\le\cdots\le\widetilde Y^*_{(N)}$ and define $r(u)=\lceil uN\rceil$ for $0<u\le1$. Set
$$
\alpha=\widetilde Y^*_{(r(\varepsilon))},\qquad \beta=\widetilde Y^*_{(r(1-\varepsilon))},
$$
and, for $\alpha\le\beta$, let $\phi_{\alpha,\beta}(x)=\min\{\beta,\max\{\alpha,x\}\}$. Return
$$
\widehat\mu=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\phi_{\alpha,\beta}(\widetilde X_i).
$$
The operation is defined for every admissible input, including tied observations.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $Z$ be a real random variable whose law is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$. For $0<u<1$, define
$$
Q_u(Z)=\sup\{t\in\mathbb R:P(Z\ge t)\ge1-u\}.
$$
Then $Q_u(Z)$ is finite and
$$
P(Z\ge Q_u(Z))=P(Z>Q_u(Z))=1-u.
$$

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $d\ge1$ and let $X$ be a Borel random vector in $\mathbb R^d$ with $E\|X\|_2^2<\infty$. Define $\mu=EX$ coordinatewise, $Y=X-\mu$, and the finite matrix $\Sigma$ by $\Sigma_{rs}=E[Y_rY_s]$ for $1\le r,s\le d$. Then $\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite,
$$
\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=E\|X-\mu\|_2^2,
$$
and $0\le\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\le\operatorname{tr}\Sigma$. If $\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=0$, then $X=\mu$ almost surely.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after: For every real $a>0$, there is an integer $i$ such that $a\le2^i<2a$.

changes.heading: Statement refuted
changes.after:
The auxiliary bound used in the source proof,
$$
\mathbb P\!\left(B_N>\frac34\varepsilon N\right)\le e^{-\varepsilon N/12},\qquad B_N\sim\operatorname{Bin}(N,\varepsilon/2),
$$
is false for admissible theorem parameters: with $\eta=0$, $\varepsilon=1/10$, $N$ sufficiently large and divisible by $40$, and $\delta=4e^{-N/120}$, one has
$$
\mathbb P\!\left(B_N>\frac{3N}{40}\right)>e^{-N/120}=e^{-\varepsilon N/12}.
$$
For absolutely continuous clean data, [[lem-absolutely-continuous-upper-quantile-exact-tail-mass]] makes this binomial variable exactly the source's upper-quantile count. This refutes that proof step, not the univariate estimator theorem.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after:
Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space, let $k\ge1$ be an integer, let $m_1,\ldots,m_k\in H$, and let $m$ minimize $F(z)=\sum_{j=1}^k\|z-m_j\|$. For $0<a<1/2$ and $r>0$, put
$$
C_a=\frac{1-a}{\sqrt{1-2a}}.
$$
If $z\in H$ satisfies $\|m-z\|>C_a r$, then more than $ak$ of the points $m_j$ satisfy $\|m_j-z\|>r$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after: Fix a separable real Hilbert space $H$ and an integer $k\ge1$. The rule in [[alg-geometric-median-of-block-means]] defines a single-valued Borel map $H^k\to H$: for every tuple $(m_1,\ldots,m_k)$ the function $F_m(z)=\sum_{j=1}^k\|z-m_j\|$ has a nonempty closed convex minimizer set, and that set has a unique point of minimum norm. The choice-free Borel construction below does not use weak compactness or reflexivity. Countable Choice is used only for the published Hilbert projection supplier that identifies the minimum-norm point.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after: For each fixed admissible $d,N,\varepsilon$ and each observed data tuple in $(\mathbb R^d)^{2N}$, the procedure [[alg-multivariate-trimmed-mean]] returns a unique vector in $\mathbb R^d$. As a function of the observed data tuple it is Borel measurable. The fallback branch covers the case where no dyadic tail intersection is nonempty; the all-scale branch covers the case where every tail intersection is nonempty.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after: Fix an integer $N\ge1$, $0<\varepsilon\le1/4$, and the split-sample rule in [[alg-univariate-trimmed-mean]]. It defines a total continuous, hence Borel measurable, map $\mathbb R^{2N}\to\mathbb R$ for every admissible pair of observed samples, including tied values.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.after: Let $X$ be a Borel random vector in $\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, with finite second moment, mean $\mu$, and covariance matrix $\Sigma$ as defined in [[lem-finite-covariance-matrix-basic-properties]]. Let two halves of size $N$ be iid clean copies, and let the observed vector be a sample-replacement version with at most $\lfloor2\eta N\rfloor$ changed coordinates in total. Assume $0\le\eta\le1/10$, $0<\delta<1$, and $N\ge2560\log(2/\delta)$. With $\varepsilon=\max\{10\eta,2560\log(2/\delta)/N\}$, if $\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=0$, then [[alg-multivariate-trimmed-mean]] returns $\mu$ almost surely.

changes.heading: Example
changes.after: Take five real block means $0,0,0,0,M$ with $M>0$. Their geometric median is exactly $0$, regardless of how large $M$ is.

changes.heading: Statement refuted
changes.after: For sample-replacement fractions $1/2\le\eta\le1$, no deterministic Borel estimator $T:\mathbb R^{2N}\to\mathbb R$ can satisfy $T=\mu$ almost surely for every clean law and every admissible replacement coupling: two different zero-covariance means can generate the same observed sample within the replacement budget. In particular, no covariance-only error bound that forces zero error whenever the clean covariance is zero can hold uniformly.

changes.heading: Example
changes.after: Let $X$ have density $f(x)=\frac{3}{2(1+|x|)^4}$ on $\mathbb R$. This law has mean $0$ and variance $1$, but it is not sub-Gaussian in the moment-generating-function sense. The geometric-median-of-means theorem therefore applies even though no finite sub-Gaussian proxy exists.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_m\in\mathbb R^p$ be iid with
mean $\mu$, finite covariance $\Sigma$, and $T=\operatorname{tr}\Sigma$.
For $\beta>1$, put $k=\lfloor3.5\beta\rfloor+1\le m/2$. Partition the
sample deterministically into $k$ blocks whose sizes differ by at most one,
and let $\widehat\mu$ be the minimum-norm geometric median of the block
means as in [[alg-geometric-median-of-block-means]]. Then
$$P\!\left(\|\widehat\mu-\mu\|_2>11\sqrt{\frac{T(\beta+1)}m}\right)\le e^{-\beta}.$$
In particular the larger radius $B=11\sqrt{2T\beta/m}$ has the same
failure bound. This uses the prescribed covariance-pilot block count,
without changing the robust-mean theorem's separate confidence convention.
changes.after: Assume Countable Choice. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_m\in\mathbb R^p$ be iid with mean $\mu$, finite covariance $\Sigma$, and $T=\operatorname{tr}\Sigma$. For $\beta>1$, put $k=\lfloor3.5\beta\rfloor+1\le m/2$. Partition the sample into $k$ consecutive blocks by the deterministic balanced rule of [[alg-geometric-median-of-block-means]], and let $\widehat\mu$ be the selected minimum-norm geometric median of their block means. Then $$P\!\left(\|\widehat\mu-\mu\|_2>11\sqrt{\frac{T(\beta+1)}m}\right)\le e^{-\beta}.$$ In particular the larger radius $B=11\sqrt{2T\beta/m}$ has the same failure bound. This proves the prescribed covariance-pilot block count without relying on the robust-mean theorem's different confidence convention.

changes.before:
Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$
changes.after:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: Assuming AC, on a common discrete filtered probability space and for a null family of laws P0, an adapted, integrable process E_t that is nonnegative P-almost surely at every time, is a supermartingale under every P in P0, and satisfies E_P E_0 <= 1 for every P in P0 is a nonnegative test supermartingale for P0. Time starts at zero.
changes.after:
Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC) [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0})$ be a discrete filtration
on a measurable space, and let $\mathcal P_0$ be a family of probability laws
on $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$. A real-valued process $E=(E_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0}$ is
a **nonnegative test supermartingale for $\mathcal P_0$** if, for every
$P\in\mathcal P_0$, it is adapted and integrable under $P$
[[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]
[[def-martingale-submartingale-and-supermartingale]], satisfies
$P(E_t\ge0)=1$ for every $t$, and has $\mathbb E_P E_0\le1$.

The same process must satisfy the supermartingale condition under every law
in the null family; that is what makes the definition uniform over a composite
null. The initial value may be random and need not be bounded by one
pointwise. Time starts at zero.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Assume AC. For every P in P0, every nonnegative test supermartingale E under P, and every alpha in (0,1), P(sup_{t>=0} E_t >= 1/alpha) <= alpha.
changes.after:
Assume AC. Let $\mathcal P_0$ be a family of probability laws on a common
discrete filtered measurable space and let $E=(E_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a nonnegative
test supermartingale for $\mathcal P_0$
[[def-nonnegative-test-supermartingale]]. For every $P\in\mathcal P_0$ and
every $\alpha\in(0,1)$,
$$P\!\left(\sup_{t\ge0}E_t\ge\frac1\alpha\right)\le\alpha.$$

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Assume AC. Let pi be a probability measure on a measurable space Lambda. If (lambda,omega) maps to E_t^lambda(omega) is measurable with respect to A tensor F_t for every t and each E^lambda is a nonnegative test supermartingale for the same null family P0, then its pi-mixture, with an everywhere-finite version chosen by setting the mixture to zero where its integral is infinite, is a nonnegative test supermartingale for P0.
changes.after:
Assume AC. Let $(\Lambda,\mathcal A,\pi)$ be a probability space and let
$\mathcal P_0$ be a family of laws on a common discrete filtered measurable
space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0})$. For each
$\lambda\in\Lambda$, let $E^\lambda=(E_t^\lambda)_{t\ge0}$ be a nonnegative
test supermartingale for $\mathcal P_0$. Suppose that, for every $t$, the map
$(\lambda,\omega)\mapsto E_t^\lambda(\omega)$ is measurable with respect to
$\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal F_t$. Before mixing, take its pointwise
nonnegative version $E_t^{\lambda,+}(\omega)=\max\{E_t^\lambda(\omega),0\}$,
and define
$$\overline E_t(\omega)=\int_\Lambda E_t^{\lambda,+}(\omega)\,\pi(d\lambda),\qquad \widetilde E_t(\omega)=\begin{cases}\overline E_t(\omega),&\overline E_t(\omega)<\infty,\\0,&\overline E_t(\omega)=\infty.\end{cases}$$
Then $\widetilde E=(\widetilde E_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a nonnegative test
supermartingale for $\mathcal P_0$. The modification on the infinite-integral
set makes a real-valued version common to all null laws.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: On a common discrete filtered probability space and for a null family P0, an adapted process p_t with values in [0,1] is an anytime-valid p-value process if for every P in P0 and alpha in (0,1), P(exists t>=0: p_t <= alpha) <= alpha. For each threshold alpha, the rejection rule 1{p_t <= alpha} is an F_t-measurable deterministic test via its binary probability kernel; every finite stopping-time rejection event is contained in the all-times crossing event.
changes.after:
Let $\mathcal P_0$ be a family of probability laws on a common discrete filtered
probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0})$. A process
$p=(p_t)_{t\ge0}$ is an **anytime-valid p-value process** for $\mathcal P_0$ if
each $p_t$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable with values in $[0,1]$ and, for every
$P\in\mathcal P_0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$,
$$P(\exists t\ge0:p_t\le\alpha)\le\alpha.$$

At time $t$, the rejection rule at threshold $\alpha$ is the
$\mathcal F_t$-measurable test function $\varphi_{t,\alpha}
=\mathbf 1_{\{p_t\le\alpha\}}$ in the sense of
[[def-randomized-test]]: the indicator supplies a binary probability kernel by
[[lem-measurable-rejection-function-defines-randomized-test]]. For any stopping time $\tau:\Omega\to\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$
[[def-discrete-stopping-time]], the rejection event is
$$\{\tau<\infty,\ p_\tau\le\alpha\}=\bigcup_{t\ge0}\bigl(\{\tau=t\}\cap\{p_t\le\alpha\}\bigr).$$
For $t=0$, $\{\tau=t\}=\{\tau\le0\}\in\mathcal F_0$; for $t\ge1$,
$\{\tau=t\}=\{\tau\le t\}\setminus\{\tau\le t-1\}\in\mathcal F_t$ by the
stopping-time condition and filtration property. Thus each term is in
$\mathcal F_t$, so this event is measurable and is contained
in the all-times crossing event; the definition therefore controls rejection
after data-dependent stopping.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Assume AC. If E is a nonnegative test supermartingale for P0, define p_t=1 when E_t<=0 and p_t=min(1,1/E_t) otherwise. Then p is an anytime-valid p-value process for P0; for every P in P0, fixed t>=0 and u in [0,1], P(p_t<=u)<=u. For every possibly unbounded stopping time tau and u in [0,1], P(tau<infinity, p_tau<=u)<=u under every P in P0.
changes.after:
Assume AC. Let $E=(E_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a nonnegative test supermartingale
[[def-nonnegative-test-supermartingale]] for a null family $\mathcal P_0$.
Define
$$p_t=\begin{cases}1,&E_t\le0,\\\min(1,1/E_t),&E_t>0.\end{cases}$$
Then $p=(p_t)_{t\ge0}$ is an anytime-valid p-value process for $\mathcal P_0$
[[def-anytime-valid-p-value-process]]. For every $P\in\mathcal P_0$, fixed
$t\ge0$, and $u\in[0,1]$, $P(p_t\le u)\le u$. For every possibly unbounded
stopping time $\tau$ and $u\in[0,1]$,
$$P(\tau<\infty,\ p_\tau\le u)\le u\qquad(P\in\mathcal P_0).$$

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: For a parameter family (P_theta) on a common discrete filtered probability space, a (1-alpha) confidence sequence is a sequence of set-valued rules C_t such that each fixed-parameter membership event {theta in C_t} is F_t-measurable and P_theta(theta in C_t for every t>=0) >= 1-alpha.
changes.after:
Let $\Theta$ be a parameter set and $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ a family of
probability laws on a common discrete filtered measurable space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0})$
[[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]. For
$\alpha\in(0,1)$, a **$(1-\alpha)$ confidence sequence** is a sequence of
set-valued rules $C_t(\omega)\subseteq\Theta$ such that, for each fixed
$\theta\in\Theta$, the membership event $\{\theta\in C_t\}$ belongs to
$\mathcal F_t$ for every $t$ and
$$P_\theta(\theta\in C_t\text{ for every }t\ge0)\ge1-\alpha.$$

The coverage is simultaneous over all discrete times. The definition makes no
claim of conditional-on-covariates coverage or validity under a changed
sampling law.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Assume AC and alpha in (0,1). Let (P_theta) be a parameter-indexed family on a common discrete filtered space. If for each theta, E_t^theta is a nonnegative test supermartingale for the singleton null {P_theta}, then C_t={theta:E_t^theta<1/alpha} is a (1-alpha) confidence sequence.
changes.after:
Assume AC and fix $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Let $\Theta$ be a parameter set,
$(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ a family of laws on a common discrete filtered
measurable space, and, for each $\theta\in\Theta$, let
$E^\theta=(E_t^\theta)_{t\ge0}$ be a nonnegative test supermartingale for the
singleton null family $\{P_\theta\}$. Define
$$C_t(\omega)=\{\theta\in\Theta:E_t^\theta(\omega)<1/\alpha\}.$$
Then $(C_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a $(1-\alpha)$ confidence sequence
[[def-confidence-sequence]].

No measurable structure on $\Theta$ or joint measurability across $\theta$ is
needed for this pointwise membership and coverage statement.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: On Omega={0,1}^K with the uniform law P0 and its prefix filtration, let Q be the product Bernoulli(3/4) law and P0 the product Bernoulli(1/2) law. The likelihood ratio E_t=dQ|F_t/dP0|F_t, held constant after K, is a nonnegative test martingale under P0 and hence a test supermartingale.
changes.after:
Fix an integer $K\ge1$. Let $\Omega=\{0,1\}^K$ and let $P_0$ be uniform on
$\Omega$, so the coordinate variables $X_1,\ldots,X_K$ are independent
Bernoulli$(1/2)$. Let $Q$ be the product Bernoulli$(3/4)$ law and let
$\mathcal F_t=\sigma(X_1,\ldots,X_{\min(t,K)})$. The likelihood ratio of $Q$
to $P_0$ on $\mathcal F_t$ is
$$E_t=\prod_{i=1}^{\min(t,K)}\ell(X_i),\qquad \ell(1)=\frac32,\quad \ell(0)=\frac12,$$
with the empty product $E_0=1$. It is a nonnegative test martingale, hence a
nonnegative test supermartingale, for the simple null $\{P_0\}$.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: For two fair coin observations and the likelihood-ratio process from Bernoulli(3/4) against Bernoulli(1/2), the stopping rule tau=inf{t>=0:E_t>=2} rejects only on two heads, an event of probability 1/4 under the null. The level-1/2 threshold is selected from the data through the first-crossing rule, and the finite-horizon crossing probability is at most 1/2.
changes.after:
Take two fair coin observations under the null $P_0$, with the likelihood-ratio
process $E_0=1$, $E_1=\ell(X_1)$, $E_2=\ell(X_1)\ell(X_2)$ and $E_t=E_2$
for $t\ge2$, where $\ell(1)=3/2$ and $\ell(0)=1/2$. Set
$\tau=\inf\{t\ge0:E_t\ge2\}$. This is a data-dependent stopping rule. It
crosses only on two heads, so $P_0(\tau<\infty)=1/4$. Since $2=1/\alpha$ for
$\alpha=1/2$, the crossing probability is below Ville's bound $1/2$.

changes.heading: Statement refuted
changes.before: Let X be Bernoulli(1/4) or Bernoulli(3/4) under two null laws, take F_0 trivial, F_t=sigma(X) for t>=1, M_0=1, and M_t=2X for t>=1. M is a nonnegative supermartingale under Bernoulli(1/4), but not under Bernoulli(3/4), so it is not a test supermartingale for the composite null family.
changes.after: The claim “a nonnegative process that is a supermartingale under one member of a composite null family is a test supermartingale for the whole family” is false.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: Define H=L2([0,1], B, dt; R), iid innovations on a measurable space S, a product-measurable causal map f:S^N0→H, its independent replacement copies X_t,m (including X_t,0), the physical-dependence errors δ_m, and L2-m-approximability by E||X_0||^2<∞ and Σ_{m≥1}δ_m<∞.
changes.after:
Let $\mathcal B$ be the Borel sigma-algebra of $[0,1]$, generated by intervals with rational endpoints; let $dt$ be Lebesgue measure restricted to $\mathcal B$, and set $H=L^2([0,1],\mathcal B,dt;\mathbb R)$, with inner product $\langle x,y\rangle_H=\int_0^1x(u)y(u)\,du$. We use the quotient-by-null-functions convention for $L^2$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). The measure space is finite and countably generated, so under Countable Choice $H$ is separable ([[thm-l-p-of-a-sigma-finite-countably-generated-measure-space-is-separable]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-separable-space]]); [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]] verifies that this real pairing makes the quotient a Hilbert space.

Let $(S,\mathcal S,\nu)$ be a probability space and $(\delta_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ an independent identically distributed family of $S$-valued random elements with law $\nu$ ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]], [[def-independent-random-elements]]). A **causal Bernoulli shift** with innovation law $\nu$ is a process
$$X_t=f(\delta_t,\delta_{t-1},\delta_{t-2},\ldots),\qquad t\in\mathbb Z,$$
where $f:S^{\mathbb N_0}\to H$ is measurable from the product sigma-algebra $\mathcal S^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}$ to the Borel sigma-algebra of $H$. This product-measurability formulation is meaningful for a merely measurable innovation space $S$.

On an independent product extension, take replacement innovations $\delta'_{t,m,k}$, indexed by $t\in\mathbb Z$, $m\in\mathbb N_0$, and integers $k\le t-m$, all with law $\nu$, mutually independent, and independent of the original innovations. Such a countable family and its product with the original probability space exist under Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]], [[cor-countable-independent-copies-exist]], [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]). For $m\ge1$ define
$$X_{t,m}=f(\delta_t,\ldots,\delta_{t-m+1},\delta'_{t,m,t-m},\delta'_{t,m,t-m-1},\ldots),$$
and define the full replacement $X_{t,0}=f(\delta'_{t,0,t},\delta'_{t,0,t-1},\ldots)$. Each $X_{t,m}$ has the same marginal law as $X_t$; for fixed $m\ge1$ the sequence $(X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary and $m$-dependent because its original-innovation windows have length $m$ and its replacement arrays are independent across $t$.

For every fixed $m\ge0$, the joint process $(X_t,X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary: shifting all indices relabels a family of mutually independent innovations with the same law and commutes with the defining measurable maps. Consequently $D_{t,m}:=X_t-X_{t,m}$ is stationary and $\|D_{t,m}\|_{L^2(H)}=\delta_m$ for every $t$.

Write $\|X\|_{L^2(H)}=(\mathbb E\|X\|_H^2)^{1/2}$ and
$$\delta_m=\|X_0-X_{0,m}\|_{L^2(H)},\qquad m\ge0.$$
The process is **$L^2$-$m$-approximable** when
$$\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2<\infty\qquad\hbox{and}\qquad\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m<\infty.$$
The same marginal law gives $\delta_0\le2\|X_0\|_{L^2(H)}<\infty$. For a Bochner-integrable $H$-valued random element $Y$, write $\mathbb E_B Y=\int Y\,d\mathbb P$; the moment condition makes $X_t$ and every $X_{t,m}$ Bochner integrable ([[def-bochner-integrable-function]], [[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]).

Here **strict stationarity** means invariance of every finite-dimensional law under integer shifts. A process is **$m$-dependent** if, for every $a\in\mathbb Z$, the sigma-algebras generated by $(X_s)_{s\le a}$ and $(X_s)_{s\ge a+m+1}$ are independent ([[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]]). The stated input windows for $X_{t,m}$ are disjoint across these two index ranges, so they satisfy this definition.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$ and $m\ge0$ be finite integers, and let $(Y_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered strictly stationary sequence of $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|Y_0\|^2<\infty$. Strict stationarity means that every finite-dimensional law is invariant under integer shifts. Assume $m$-dependence: for each $a\in\mathbb Z$, the sigma-algebras generated by $(Y_t)_{t\le a}$ and $(Y_t)_{t\ge a+m+1}$ are independent, in the sense of [[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]]. Set
changes.after:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$ and $m\ge0$ be finite integers, and let $(Y_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered strictly stationary sequence of $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|Y_0\|^2<\infty$. Strict stationarity means that every finite-dimensional law is invariant under integer shifts. Assume $m$-dependence: for each $a\in\mathbb Z$, the sigma-algebras generated by $(Y_t)_{t\le a}$ and $(Y_t)_{t\ge a+m+1}$ are independent, in the sense of [[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]]. Set
$$\Sigma_m=\sum_{|j|\le m}\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_j),$$
where $\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)=\mathbb E[(U-\mathbb EU)(V-\mathbb EV)^T]$ ([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]). Then $\Sigma_m$ is symmetric positive semidefinite and
$$\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{t=1}^nY_t\ \Rightarrow\ N_d(0,\Sigma_m).$$
The conclusion allows singular $\Sigma_m$, including $\Sigma_m=0$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Assume AC. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space and let $\Gamma:H\to H$ be positive, self-adjoint and trace class. Then there is a Borel $H$-valued random element $G$ such that every $\langle G,h\rangle_H$ is a centered real normal random variable and
changes.after:
Assume AC. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space and let $\Gamma:H\to H$ be positive, self-adjoint and trace class. Then there is a Borel $H$-valued random element $G$ such that every $\langle G,h\rangle_H$ is a centered real normal random variable and
$$\mathbb E[\langle G,h\rangle_H\langle G,k\rangle_H]=\langle\Gamma h,k\rangle_H\qquad(h,k\in H).$$
This is the centered Gaussian law with covariance operator $\Gamma$; it includes finite-rank and zero covariance.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Let $I=[0,1]$ with its Borel sigma-algebra and Lebesgue measure $dt$, and let
changes.after:
Let $I=[0,1]$ with its Borel sigma-algebra and Lebesgue measure $dt$, and let
$H=L^2(I,dt;\mathbb R)$ and $K=L^2(I^2,dt\times dt;\mathbb R)$ be the
quotient spaces by null functions. Assume Countable Choice, so these $L^2$
spaces have their usual real Hilbert-space structures. For $k\in K$ and
$f\in H$, define, for almost every $u$,
$$ (T_k f)(u)=\int_0^1 k(u,v)f(v)\,dv. $$
This defines a bounded linear operator $T_k:H\to H$ and
$\|T_k\|\le\|k\|_K$. For $x,y\in H$, the class $x\boxtimes y$ represented by
$x(u)y(v)$ is well-defined in $K$, satisfies
$$ \|x\boxtimes y\|_K=\|x\|_H\|y\|_H, $$
and $T_{x\boxtimes y}=x\otimes y$, where
$(x\otimes y)h=\langle h,y\rangle_H x$.
For $x,y,g,h\in H$ the product-kernel inner product also satisfies
$$ \langle x\boxtimes y,g\boxtimes h\rangle_K =\langle x,g\rangle_H\langle y,h\rangle_H. $$

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space and let $(e_k)$ be a finite or countable
changes.after:
Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space and let $(e_k)$ be a finite or countable
orthonormal family whose finite linear span is dense in $H$. Here
orthonormal means $\langle e_j,e_k\rangle_H=1$ when $j=k$ and $0$ otherwise;
density means every $x\in H$ is arbitrarily close in norm to a finite linear
combination of the $e_k$. For $x\in H$, define
$$P_Nx=\sum_{k\le N}\langle x,e_k\rangle_H e_k,$$
using all basis vectors once $N$ reaches the size of a finite family. Then
$P_Nx\to x$ in norm and
$$\|x\|_H^2=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{k\le N}|\langle x,e_k\rangle_H|^2.$$

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space with a fixed complete finite or countable
changes.after:
Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space with a fixed complete finite or countable
orthonormal basis $(e_k)$. On a probability
space let $U,V$ be independent, strongly measurable and Bochner-integrable
$H$-valued random elements with
$\mathbb E_B U=\mathbb E_B V=0$ and
$\mathbb E\|U\|_H^2,\mathbb E\|V\|_H^2<\infty$. Then
$$\mathbb E\langle U,V\rangle_H=0.$$

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $H=L^2([0,1],dt;\mathbb R)$,
changes.after:
Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $H=L^2([0,1],dt;\mathbb R)$,
let $(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered causal Bernoulli shift as in
[[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]], and suppose it is
$L^2$-$m$-approximable. Write $\sigma=(\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2)^{1/2}$,
let $S_1(H)$ be the trace-class Banach space with trace norm $\|\cdot\|_1$
([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]),
write $\mathbb E_B$ for a Bochner integral, and define $x\otimes y:H\to H$ by
$(x\otimes y)h=\langle h,y\rangle_Hx$. The Bochner series
$$ \Gamma=\mathbb E_B[X_0\otimes X_0]+ \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\bigl(\mathbb E_B[X_0\otimes X_j] +\mathbb E_B[X_j\otimes X_0]\bigr) $$
converges absolutely in trace norm to a positive self-adjoint trace-class
operator. For $S_n=\sum_{t=1}^nX_t$, the Bochner covariance operators
$\Gamma_n=n^{-1}\mathbb E_B[S_n\otimes S_n]$ satisfy
$\|\Gamma_n-\Gamma\|_1\to0$. If $\boxtimes$ is the product-kernel class from
[[lem-real-l-two-kernel-operator-is-bounded-and-rank-one-compatible]], then
$$ \kappa_j=\mathbb E_B[X_0\boxtimes X_j],\qquad \widetilde\kappa_j=\mathbb E_B[X_j\boxtimes X_0] $$
are well-defined elements of $K=L^2([0,1]^2,dt\times dt;\mathbb R)$, and
$$ c=\kappa_0+\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}(\kappa_j+\widetilde\kappa_j) $$
converges absolutely in $K$ and satisfies $T_c=\Gamma$. Equivalently, $c$ is
the design's long-run covariance-kernel series interpreted as an
$L^2([0,1]^2)$ equivalence class; no pointwise representatives are fixed.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H=L^2([0,1],dt;\mathbb R)$ and let
changes.after:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H=L^2([0,1],dt;\mathbb R)$ and let
$(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered, $L^2$-$m$-approximable causal
Bernoulli shift as defined in
[[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]], with Bochner mean
$\mathbb E_BX_0=0$. Let $\Gamma$ be its long-run covariance operator from
[[lem-long-run-covariance-is-trace-class]], and let $G$ be a centered
$H$-valued Gaussian random element with covariance $\Gamma$, whose existence
is given by [[lem-positive-trace-class-covariance-defines-hilbert-gaussian]].
Then, for $S_n=\sum_{t=1}^nX_t$,
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\ \Rightarrow\ G$$
in the weak topology of Borel probability measures on $H$. The covariance
kernel is the $L^2([0,1]^2)$ equivalence class $c$ in the long-run covariance
lemma, and its integral operator is $T_c=\Gamma$. This is a CLT for the
$H$-valued sample sums; it is not a functional CLT for the time-indexed
partial-sum process.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: For measurable coordinate maps into a finite product, the tuple map is measurable; every coordinate permutation of a finite product of one measurable space is measurable.
changes.after:
Let $(S_i,\Sigma_i)$, $1\le i\le n$, be finitely many measurable spaces, with
$n\ge1$, and equip $\prod_{i=1}^nS_i$ with its finite product sigma-algebra.
If $f_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ are measurable, then the tuple
$f=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$ is measurable. If all factors equal one measurable space
$(S,\Sigma)$, every coordinate permutation $\tau_\pi:S^n\to S^n$ is
measurable, where $(\tau_\pi z)_i=z_{\pi(i)}$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: A regular conditional distribution remains a regular conditional distribution after a jointly measurable map that may depend on the conditioning point; adjoining an independent random element appends its law by product measure.
changes.after:
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, let $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$, let $X$ be a random element of $(S,\Sigma)$, and let $K$ be a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\mathcal G$. If $T$ is a measurable space and $g:(\Omega,\mathcal G)\times(S,\Sigma)\to(T,\Tau)$ is measurable, then
$$K_g(\omega,B):=K\bigl(\omega,\{x:g(\omega,x)\in B\}\bigr),\qquad B\in\Tau,$$
is a regular conditional distribution of $g(\omega,X(\omega))$ given $\mathcal G$.

If, in addition, $U$ is a random element of a measurable space $(V,\mathcal V)$, is independent of $\mathcal G\vee\sigma(X)$, and has law $\lambda$, then $K(\omega,\cdot)\otimes\lambda$ is a regular conditional distribution of $(X,U)$ given $\mathcal G$.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: A finite tuple of random elements in one measurable space is exchangeable when its joint law is invariant under every coordinate permutation.
changes.after:
Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be random elements, $n\ge1$, of one measurable space
$(\mathcal Z,\mathscr Z)$. Their tuple $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ is a random element
of $(\mathcal Z^n,\mathscr Z^{\otimes n})$ by
[[lem-coordinate-maps-and-permutations-are-measurable-on-finite-products]],
and its law is the pushforward probability measure from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. For a permutation $\pi$ of
$\{1,\ldots,n\}$, let $\tau_\pi(z)_i=z_{\pi(i)}$. The tuple is
**exchangeable** if
$$\mathbb P_Z\circ\tau_\pi^{-1}=\mathbb P_Z\qquad\text{for every permutation }\pi.$$

This is invariance of the joint law, not an assertion of independence or identical marginal construction by independent sampling. The coordinate maps $\tau_\pi$ are measurable by the cited finite-product lemma.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: Defines measurable split score rules, permutation-equivariant full score assignments, the nonrandomized upper-rank p-value, and the optional tie-randomized p-value using an independent shared uniform variable.
changes.after:
Let $\mathcal Z=\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$ be a feature-response measurable
space, let $m\ge0$, and put $n=m+1$. A **split score rule** is a jointly
measurable map $s:\mathcal H\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R$, where $H$ is a
training statistic with values in the specified measurable rule space
$(\mathcal H,\mathscr H)$. The measurable-statistic convention is that of
[[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. Once $H=h$ is fixed, calibration and test
scores are $R_i=s(h,Z_i)$; the rule does not change when it scores the
calibration or test example.

A **full score assignment** of length $n$ is a measurable map
$A=(A_1,\ldots,A_n):\mathcal Z^n\to\mathbb R^n$ that is
permutation-equivariant:
$$A(\tau_\pi z)=\tau_\pi A(z)\qquad\text{for every }z\in\mathcal Z^n\text{ and permutation }\pi.$$
For a candidate response $y$, append $(x,y)$ as the $n$th example and write
$R_i(y)=A_i(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m,(x,y))$ and $r=R_n(y)$.

For either a split score vector or a full augmented score vector, the
**nonrandomized upper-rank p-value** of the candidate is
$$p(y)=\frac1{m+1}\sum_{i=1}^{m+1}\mathbf1\{R_i(y)\ge R_{m+1}(y)\}.$$
An optional **tie-randomized rank p-value** is defined when a supplied random
variable $U$ has Lebesgue probability law on $[0,1]$ and is independent of the
data and training information:
$$p_U(y)=\frac{\#\{i\le m:R_i(y)>r\}+U\bigl(1+\#\{i\le m:R_i(y)=r\}\bigr)}{m+1}.$$
The added $1$ counts the candidate itself in its tie group. A single such $U$
is shared across a candidate scan. This is an explicit randomization; the
general Markov-kernel definition of a randomized procedure
[[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]] does not assert that arbitrary
kernels have a random-seed representation.

Here “uniform on $[0,1]$” means $\mathbb P(U\le u)=u$ for $0\le u\le1$.

Smaller scores are treated as more conforming. The rank formula counts all
ties conservatively in the nonrandomized version; the randomized formula
spreads the candidate uniformly over its entire tie block.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: For a finite real score vector, each order statistic, upper-rank p-value, and independent-uniform randomized rank is a Borel-measurable function of its inputs.
changes.after:
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ be a measurable space, let $R_1,\ldots,R_m$ be
measurable real-valued functions with $m\ge1$, and let $1\le k\le m$. The
$k$th order statistic $R_{(k)}$ is measurable. For a finite real score vector
$R_1,\ldots,R_n$ and another measurable real-valued function $U$ on the same
space, its upper-rank p-value and tie-randomized rank are measurable.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: A measurable permutation-equivariant score assignment sends an exchangeable data vector to an exchangeable score vector.
changes.after:
Let $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ be an exchangeable random element of $\mathcal Z^n$,
and let $A:\mathcal Z^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be measurable and
permutation-equivariant in the sense of
[[def-conformal-nonconformity-score-and-rank-pvalue]]. Then $A(Z)$ is an
exchangeable real random vector.

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: For m calibration examples and 0<alpha<1, use k=ceil((m+1)(1-alpha)), the kth calibration score when k<=m and +infinity otherwise, then return candidates with score at most that threshold; an optional exact randomized version uses the shared-U rank p-value.
changes.after:
Let $m\ge0$ calibration examples $Z_i=(X_i,Y_i)$ be scored by one fixed,
measurable score rule $s_H$ obtained from the training statistic $H$, and let
$0<\alpha<1$. Set
$$n=m+1,\qquad k=\lceil(m+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil.$$
Compute $R_i=s_H(Z_i)$ for $1\le i\le m$. Sort calibration observations by
the ordered keys $(R_i,i)$, so ties are broken by the fixed index order. If
$k\le m$, let $q$ be the score component of the $k$th ordered pair; if
$k=m+1$, set $q=+\infty$. For a feature value $x$, return
$$C(x)=\{y\in\mathcal Y:s_H(x,y)\le q\}.$$

The optional tie-randomized version uses one independent $U$ with Lebesgue
probability law on $[0,1]$, shared across the candidate scan, and returns
$$C_U(x)=\{y\in\mathcal Y:p_U(y)>\alpha\},$$
where $p_U$ is the score-rank formula in
[[def-conformal-nonconformity-score-and-rank-pvalue]]. The candidate score is
included in its tie group. The score maps must be jointly measurable in the
training, calibration, feature, and response variables; then membership in
each returned set is a measurable event by
[[lem-finite-order-statistic-and-rank-maps-are-measurable]].

changes.heading: Definition
changes.before: For each candidate, compute the permutation-equivariant augmented score vector and include the candidate when its nonrandomized upper-rank p-value exceeds alpha, or use the shared-U randomized rank version.
changes.after:
Let $m\ge0$ observed examples $Z_1,\ldots,Z_m$ and $0<\alpha<1$ be given.
For each candidate $(x,y)$, append it to the examples and apply a measurable,
permutation-equivariant full score assignment of length $m+1$ from
[[def-conformal-nonconformity-score-and-rank-pvalue]], obtaining
$R_1(y),\ldots,R_{m+1}(y)$. Compute
$$p(y)=\frac1{m+1}\sum_{i=1}^{m+1}\mathbf1\{R_i(y)\ge R_{m+1}(y)\}$$
and return
$$C(x)=\{y\in\mathcal Y:p(y)>\alpha\}.$$

An optional exact-randomized version uses one independent $U$ with Lebesgue
probability law on $[0,1]$, shared across the candidate scan, and returns
$C_U(x)=\{y:p_U(y)>\alpha\}$. The full score map must be jointly measurable
in the observed examples, $x$, and $y$; the membership event is measurable by
[[lem-finite-order-statistic-and-rank-maps-are-measurable]].

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: For an exchangeable real score vector of length n, the nonrandomized upper-rank p-value is superuniform; the specified tie-randomized rank is Uniform(0,1) when its uniform variable is independent.
changes.after:
Let $R_1,\ldots,R_n$ be an exchangeable real random vector with $n\ge1$.
Define its last-coordinate upper-rank p-value by
$$p_n=\frac1n\#\{i\le n:R_i\ge R_n\}.$$
Then $\mathbb P(p_n\le u)\le u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$. If $U$ has Lebesgue
probability law on $[0,1]$ and is independent of $R$, define
$$p_{U,n}=\frac{\#\{i\le n:R_i>R_n\}+U\,\#\{i\le n:R_i=R_n\}}n.$$
Then $p_{U,n}$ has the uniform law on $[0,1]$.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: If the training-fitted score rule is measurable and the calibration and test examples are conditionally exchangeable given the training sigma-field, the split quantile set has conditional and hence marginal coverage at least 1-alpha; the shared-U rank version has conditional and marginal coverage exactly 1-alpha.
changes.after:
Let $Z_i=(X_i,Y_i)$, $1\le i\le m+1$, be random elements of one measurable
example space $(\mathcal Z,\mathscr Z)$, and let $\mathcal T$ be the training
sigma-field. Suppose the tuple $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_{m+1})$ has a regular
conditional distribution $Q_\omega$ given $\mathcal T$ in the sense of
[[def-regular-conditional-distribution]], whose sections have joint laws
invariant under every coordinate permutation, as in
[[def-exchangeable-random-elements]], for almost every $\omega$. Let $H$ be a $\mathcal T$-measurable
training statistic, and let $s:\mathcal H\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R$ be a
jointly measurable split score rule. Use the split set in
[[alg-split-conformal-prediction-set]] at $0<\alpha<1$. Then
$$\mathbb P\{Y_{m+1}\in C(X_{m+1})\mid\mathcal T\}\ge1-\alpha\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
If the tie-randomized set $C_U$ is used with one $U$ of Lebesgue probability
law on $[0,1]$ independent of $\mathcal T\vee\sigma(Z)$, then
$$\mathbb P\{Y_{m+1}\in C_U(X_{m+1})\mid\mathcal T\}=1-\alpha\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
In either case, integration over the training sigma-field gives the same
marginal lower bound or exact marginal coverage.

changes.heading: Statement
changes.before: For exchangeable examples and a measurable permutation-equivariant score assignment, full conformal has marginal coverage at least 1-alpha; independent shared-U randomized ties give exact marginal coverage 1-alpha.
changes.after:
Let $(\mathcal X,\mathscr X)$ and $(\mathcal Y,\mathscr Y)$ be measurable
feature and response spaces, let $m\ge0$, and let
$Z_i=(X_i,Y_i)$, $1\le i\le m+1$, be random elements of the product measurable
space $\mathcal Z=(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y,\mathscr X\otimes\mathscr Y)$.
Suppose their joint law is invariant under every coordinate permutation, as in
[[def-exchangeable-random-elements]]. Suppose a measurable, permutation-equivariant
full score assignment $A:\mathcal Z^{m+1}\to\mathbb R^{m+1}$ is used for every
augmented candidate sample, as in [[alg-full-conformal-prediction-set]]. Then,
for $0<\alpha<1$, its nonrandomized full conformal set satisfies
$$\mathbb P\{Y_{m+1}\in C(X_{m+1})\}\ge1-\alpha.$$
If the tie-randomized set uses one $U$ with Lebesgue probability law on
$[0,1]$, independent of $\sigma(Z_1,\ldots,Z_{m+1})$ and shared across the
candidate scan, then
$$\mathbb P\{Y_{m+1}\in C_U(X_{m+1})\}=1-\alpha.$$
These are marginal guarantees over the exchangeable examples and any stated
tie randomization.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: With three identical exchangeable scores, m=2 and alpha=1/2, the nonrandomized split quantile set covers with probability 1, while the specified independent-uniform rank randomization covers with probability 1/2.
changes.after:
Take a constant score rule $s(z)=0$, two calibration examples, one exchangeable
test example, and $\alpha=1/2$. All three scores are tied. The ordinary split
quantile set covers with probability $1$, while the specified independent
uniform tie-randomized rank set covers with probability exactly $1/2$.

changes.heading: Example
changes.before: For a uniformly random ordering of the fixed distinct score multiset {1,2,3}, an equivariant identity-score assignment gives the true candidate upper p-value 1, 2/3, or 1/3, each with probability 1/3; at alpha=0.4 the coverage is 2/3.
changes.after:
Take feature space $\mathcal X=\{x_0\}$ and response space
$\mathcal Y=\{1,2,3\}$, each with its power-set sigma-algebra, so the product
example space is identified with $\mathcal Y$ by $(x_0,y)\mapsto y$. Let
$Z_1,Z_2,Z_3$ be a uniformly random ordering of the pairs
$(x_0,1),(x_0,2),(x_0,3)$, and use the response-coordinate score assignment
$A_i(z_1,z_2,z_3)=y_i$ when $z_i=(x_0,y_i)$. The true
candidate's nonrandomized upper-rank p-value is $1$, $2/3$, or $1/3$, each with
probability $1/3$. At $\alpha=0.4$, the full conformal set covers with
probability $2/3$.

changes.heading: Statement refuted
changes.before: A split conformal rule can satisfy its marginal lower bound under exchangeability while its conditional coverage on a rare group is below the nominal level.
changes.after:
Marginal split-conformal coverage at level $1-\alpha$ forces coverage at least
$1-\alpha$ conditional on every feature subgroup.

changes.heading: Statement refuted
changes.before: A calibration sample drawn entirely at label 0 and a test label fixed at 1 yield zero coverage for a simple split score set, so the exchangeability hypothesis cannot be dropped.
changes.after:
The split-conformal lower coverage bound holds for arbitrary calibration and
test distributions, even when their joint law is not exchangeable.
